Opioid example: enkephalin most potent + full efficacy, morphine less potent, buprenorphine partial agonist (~55% Emax). Constitutive activity = receptor active without ligand (Ri inactive <-> Ra active); inverse agonist has negative efficacy, stabilises Ri, lowers response below baseline. Competitive antagonist binds the same (orthosteric) site reversibly, zero efficacy, shifts the agonist CRC right WITHOUT changing slope or Emax = surmountable (more agonist overcomes). Irreversible antagonist forms covalent bonds, dissociates very slowly/never (e.g. aspirin acetylating COX), shifts right AND lowers slope/Emax = insurmountable. Receptor reserve (spare receptors): full response without full occupancy, so a CRC cannot be used to calculate affinity when spare receptors exist. Allosteric modulator binds a site distinct from the agonist's orthosteric site and increases (positive) or decreases (negative) the agonist's effect; benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the GABA-A receptor (enhance GABA-gated Cl- influx). Naloxone = competitive antagonist reversing opioids.

questions.question: Pharmacodynamics is the study of:
options: A. How the body absorbs, distributes and eliminates a drug
B. What the drug does to the body and how it does it
C. How a drug is metabolised by the liver
D. How a drug is excreted by the kidney
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (mechanism of action). Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug.

questions.question: Most drug targets are:
questions.explanation: Most drug targets are proteins — a number likely to grow with gene therapy.

questions.question: The four main protein drug targets are:
options: A. Receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters
B. Receptors, lipids, DNA and enzymes
C. Agonists, antagonists, modulators and inhibitors
D. Carriers, cofactors, ligands and channels
questions.explanation: The four main protein targets are receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers) — remember 'RITE'.

questions.question: A drug acting as a 'false substrate' for an enzyme:
options: B. Is processed into an abnormal metabolite
questions.explanation: A false substrate is handled by the enzyme but yields an abnormal metabolite (as opposed to an inhibitor, which blocks the normal reaction).

questions.question: An ion-channel MODULATOR (as opposed to a blocker):
options: A. Physically plugs the pore to stop permeation
B. Increases or decreases the channel's opening probability
C. Forms a covalent bond with the channel
D. Is metabolised into an abnormal product
questions.explanation: Modulators change the opening probability of the channel; blockers stop permeation through the pore.

questions.question: An 'acceptor' differs from a receptor in that it:
options: A. Binds the drug but produces no direct functional response (e.g. plasma protein)
B. Always produces a stronger response
C. Is a type of enzyme
questions.explanation: Acceptors (e.g. plasma proteins) bind drug without generating a direct response, affecting distribution rather than action.

questions.question: Affinity is best defined as:
options: A. The tendency (strength) of a drug to bind its receptor
B. The capacity of a drug to activate a receptor
C. The maximal response a drug can produce
D. The dose needed for an effect
questions.explanation: Affinity is the tendency of a drug to bind its receptor — the strength of the reversible interaction, set by chemical structure.

questions.question: The dissociation constant KD is the concentration of drug that:
options: D. Produces 50% of the maximal response
questions.explanation: KD is the concentration occupying half the receptors — a binding (occupancy) measure, distinct from EC50 (a response measure).

questions.question: A drug with a LOWER KD has:
questions.explanation: A lower KD means less drug is needed to occupy half the receptors — i.e. higher affinity.

questions.question: The 'ideal' specific drug would:
options: A. Interact with one target at one site with one effect
B. Bind every receptor in the body
C. Have the highest possible potency
questions.explanation: Specificity is the ideal of one target, one site, one effect — it is reciprocal and never fully achieved in practice.

questions.question: Propranolol is described as:
questions.explanation: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker — it acts on more than one beta receptor at therapeutic concentration.

questions.question: Selectivity refers to a drug's:
options: A. Ability to bind only one target for its entire lifetime
B. Preference for a molecular target in particular cells or tissues
questions.explanation: Selectivity is a preference for a target in particular cells/tissues; a non-selective drug hits more than one target at therapeutic doses.

questions.question: A drug with high affinity but ZERO efficacy is:
questions.explanation: An antagonist binds well (affinity) but cannot activate the receptor (zero efficacy), so it produces no response of its own.

questions.question: Efficacy is:
options: A. The capacity of a drug to activate a receptor and generate a response
B. The tendency of a drug to bind a receptor
C. The dose needed to produce an effect
questions.explanation: Efficacy is the capacity to activate a receptor and produce a response — measured by Emax.

questions.question: On a concentration-response curve, Emax measures:
questions.explanation: Emax is the maximal response a drug can produce — the curve's height — a measure of efficacy.

questions.question: EC50 is:
options: A. The concentration producing 50% of the maximal response (a measure of potency)
C. The concentration occupying 50% of receptors
D. A measure of efficacy only
questions.explanation: EC50 is the concentration giving 50% of maximal response — the curve's horizontal position, a measure of potency.

questions.question: Receptor occupation is governed by affinity; activation (AR → AR*) is governed by:
questions.explanation: Occupation depends on affinity; whether the occupied receptor becomes active (AR*) depends on efficacy.

questions.question: Compared with a full agonist, a partial agonist:
options: A. Reaches a lower Emax even at full receptor occupancy
C. Produces no response at all
questions.explanation: A partial agonist has lower efficacy, so it plateaus below the full Emax even when all receptors are occupied.

questions.question: Saying drug X is 'more potent' than drug Y means:
options: A. X's curve sits further left (lower EC50) — it says nothing about Emax
B. X has a higher maximal effect
D. X is necessarily a full agonist
questions.explanation: Potency is horizontal position (EC50). More potent just means less drug is needed; the maximal effect (efficacy/Emax) is a separate axis.

questions.question: An inverse agonist:
options: A. Has zero efficacy like a competitive antagonist
B. Has negative efficacy, reducing constitutive activity below baseline
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists have negative efficacy — they stabilise the inactive receptor and lower the constitutive (baseline) response.

questions.question: Constitutive activity means a receptor:
options: A. Is active only when an agonist is bound
B. Is active even without a ligand (Ri ⇌ Ra equilibrium)
questions.explanation: Some receptors idle in an active state without ligand — an equilibrium between inactive (Ri) and active (Ra) — which inverse agonists can turn down.

questions.question: On the opioid concentration-response curves, buprenorphine behaves as:
options: C. A partial agonist (plateaus well below maximum)
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine plateaus around ~55% of maximum — a partial agonist, giving it a useful ceiling effect.

questions.question: An antagonist is characterised by:
options: C. Both high affinity and high efficacy
questions.explanation: Antagonists bind (affinity) but do not activate (zero efficacy), blocking the receptor.

questions.question: A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist concentration-response curve:
options: A. To the right, with Emax unchanged
B. To the right, with a reduced Emax
questions.explanation: Competitive antagonism produces a parallel right-shift without changing the slope or Emax — it is surmountable.

questions.question: Competitive antagonism is 'surmountable' because:
options: A. Adding more agonist can overcome it (same site, reversible)
questions.explanation: Because the block is reversible and at the same site, enough extra agonist out-competes it, restoring the full response.

questions.question: An irreversible antagonist affects the curve by:
options: A. Shifting it right AND reducing the slope/Emax
B. Shifting it right with no change in Emax
questions.explanation: Irreversible (covalent) block removes receptors permanently, shifting the curve right and lowering Emax — insurmountable.

questions.question: A clinical example of an irreversible antagonist is:
questions.explanation: Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly — a rare clinically used irreversible antagonist; its effect lasts the platelet's lifetime.

questions.question: Receptor reserve ('spare receptors') means that:
options: A. A full response can occur without full occupancy, so a CRC can't give affinity
B. There are no receptors present
C. More drug is always required
questions.explanation: With spare receptors a maximal response is reached before all receptors are occupied, so the CRC cannot be used to calculate affinity.

questions.question: An allosteric modulator binds:
options: A. A site distinct from the agonist's (orthosteric) site
B. The same site as the agonist
C. Only the enzyme active site
questions.explanation: Allosteric modulators bind a separate site and increase (positive) or decrease (negative) the agonist's effect — unlike competitive drugs at the orthosteric site.

questions.question: Benzodiazepines act on the GABA_A receptor as:
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators — they don't open the channel themselves but enhance GABA's effect.

questions.question: Naloxone reverses an opioid overdose by acting as a:
options: A. Competitive antagonist at the opioid receptor
questions.explanation: Naloxone competitively (reversibly) out-competes the opioid at the receptor — a surmountable, competitive antagonist.

hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.title: MHHS2401 W4 · Anatomy of the Hand
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.content: Anatomy of the hand (Dr Strkalj). Skeleton: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals (I-V from thumb), 14 phalanges (thumb has proximal + distal only, no middle). Carpals proximal row radial->ulnar: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ('Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle'). Carpals not visible at birth; capitate ossifies first (1-3 months) then anticlockwise. Carpal bones form a bony arch closed by the flexor retinaculum = carpal tunnel; contents = 9 tendons + median nerve (4 flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 flexor digitorum profundus, 1 flexor pollicis longus tendon + median nerve). Ulnar nerve and extensor tendons lie OUTSIDE the tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome = median nerve compression. Scaphoid is the most fractured carpal (risk of avascular necrosis). Joints: wrist (radiocarpal) = condyloid synovial (distal radius + articular disc / proximal carpal row EXCEPT pisiform); movements flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction. Intercarpal = plane (gliding); midcarpal (between rows) aids extension/abduction. Carpometacarpal (CMC) joints of medial 4 = plane; thumb CMC = SADDLE synovial joint (trapezium + base of 1st metacarpal) giving opposition. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) of medial 4 = condyloid (flex/ext/abd/add) with collateral ligaments, palmar ligament, deep transverse metacarpal ligaments (tie metacarpal heads 2-5). Interphalangeal (IP) = hinge (flexion/extension). Rheumatoid arthritis = chronic autoimmune disease of synovial joints (~1 in 50 Australians, women>men), small joints of hand/feet, MCP ulnar deviation + erosion. Muscles: extrinsic (forearm bellies, long tendons) - anterior superficial (pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU), intermediate (FDS), deep (FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus); posterior superficial (ECRL, ECRB, ED, EDM, ECU), deep (supinator, APL, EPB, EPL, EI). Intrinsic: thenar (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), hypothenar (abductor/flexor/opponens digiti minimi), adductor pollicis, 4 lumbricals, 4 dorsal + 3 palmar interossei, palmaris brevis. Innervation: ULNAR nerve supplies all intrinsics EXCEPT thenar muscles and lateral 2 lumbricals (median). Median = 'MEat LOAF' (Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis). Dorsal interossei ABduct = DAB (from adjacent metacarpal shafts, insert extensor hood + base proximal phalanx of index/middle/ring); palmar interossei ADduct = PAD. First dorsal interosseous is pierced by the radial artery. Lumbricals arise from FDP tendons, insert extensor hoods, flex MCP + extend IP. Ulnar nerve lesion = claw hand (worst ring/little fingers); median lesion = thenar wasting/ape hand. Fascia (5): palmar aponeurosis (deep fascia continuous with palmaris longus tendon, 4 bands -> fibrous digital sheaths, aids grip + protects neurovascular), flexor retinaculum (roof of carpal tunnel, limits flexor tendon bowstringing), fibrous digital sheaths (enclose flexor tendons + synovial sheaths, limit movement/friction), extensor retinaculum (holds extensor tendons, 6 osteofibrous tunnels, synovial sheaths), extensor hoods (expansions of extensor digitorum + extensor pollicis longus; lumbricals/interossei insert). Tenosynovitis = inflammation of tendon + synovial sheath. Mallet/baseball finger = avulsion of terminal extensor slip.

questions.question: How many carpal bones are there?
questions.explanation: There are 8 carpals (in two rows of four); the hand has 27 bones in total (8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges).

questions.question: The proximal carpal row, from radial to ulnar, is:
questions.explanation: Proximal row (radial→ulnar): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

questions.question: Which carpal bone begins to ossify first?
questions.explanation: The capitate ossifies first (1–3 months), with the others following in an anticlockwise order; carpals are not visible at birth.

questions.question: The contents of the carpal tunnel are:
options: A. 9 tendons and the median nerve
B. 9 tendons and the ulnar nerve
C. 8 tendons and the median nerve
D. The flexor tendons and the radial artery
questions.explanation: Nine tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) plus the median nerve pass through the tunnel; the ulnar nerve lies outside it.

questions.question: Which tendons pass through the carpal tunnel?
options: A. 4 FDS, 4 FDP and 1 flexor pollicis longus
B. 4 FDS, 4 FDP and flexor carpi radialis
D. Palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.explanation: The 4 flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 flexor digitorum profundus and 1 flexor pollicis longus tendons (FCR and palmaris longus do NOT pass through it).

questions.question: How many phalanges does the thumb have?
questions.explanation: The thumb has only a proximal and distal phalanx — no middle phalanx; the other digits have three each.

questions.question: Which carpal is most commonly fractured and prone to avascular necrosis?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal (fall on outstretched hand); its distal blood supply means a fracture can cause avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment.

questions.question: The flexor retinaculum forms the:
options: A. Floor of the carpal tunnel
B. Roof of the carpal tunnel
C. The carpal tunnel walls only
D. A tendon of the hand
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum bridges the carpal arch, forming the roof of the carpal tunnel and limiting anterior bowstringing of the flexor tendons.

questions.question: The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is classified as a:
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint is condyloid (ellipsoid), allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction — but not true rotation.

questions.question: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a:
questions.explanation: The thumb CMC is a saddle joint, giving the wide mobility (including opposition) not shared by the other digits.

questions.question: The thumb saddle joint's articular surfaces are on the:
options: A. Trapezium and base of the 1st metacarpal
questions.explanation: The saddle surfaces are on the trapezium and the base of the 1st metacarpal.

questions.question: The interphalangeal joints are which type, and what do they allow?
options: A. Hinge joints — flexion and extension
B. Condyloid joints — flexion, extension, abduction, adduction
questions.explanation: IP joints are hinge synovial joints allowing only flexion and extension.

questions.question: Which carpal is NOT part of the proximal row articulating at the wrist joint?
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint involves the proximal row EXCEPT the pisiform (a sesamoid that sits on the triquetrum).

questions.question: The deep transverse metacarpal ligaments:
options: A. Tie together the heads of the medial four metacarpals
C. Stabilise the thumb saddle joint
D. Join the phalanges of one finger
questions.explanation: They unite the heads of metacarpals 2–5, so the fingers move as a unit and cannot splay apart.

questions.question: A characteristic hand deformity in rheumatoid arthritis is:
options: A. Ulnar deviation at the MCP joints
B. Radial deviation at the MCP joints
questions.explanation: RA erodes the MCP joints and their ligaments, causing the fingers to drift into ulnar deviation (and dislocation).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a movement of the wrist joint?
questions.explanation: The wrist allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction. Pronation/supination occur at the radioulnar joints, not the wrist.

questions.question: Extrinsic muscles of the hand have their muscle bellies in the:
questions.explanation: Extrinsic muscles arise in the forearm and act on the hand through long tendons; intrinsic muscles lie wholly within the hand.

questions.question: Most intrinsic muscles of the hand are supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all intrinsics EXCEPT the thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals (median).

questions.question: The median-innervated intrinsic hand muscles ('MEat LOAF') are:
options: A. Lumbricals 1&2, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis
D. Adductor pollicis and palmaris brevis
questions.explanation: 'MEat LOAF' = lumbricals 1 & 2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis — the median exceptions to ulnar supply.

questions.question: The dorsal interossei act to:
questions.explanation: Dorsal interossei ABduct the fingers — 'DAB' (Dorsal ABduct).

questions.question: The palmar interossei act to:
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei ADduct the fingers — 'PAD' (Palmar ADduct).

questions.question: The lumbricals arise from and insert into:
options: A. The FDP tendons → the extensor hoods
B. The metacarpals → the proximal phalanges
D. The flexor retinaculum → the skin
questions.explanation: The lumbricals are unique — arising from the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and inserting into the extensor hoods.

questions.question: The action of the lumbricals is to:
options: A. Flex the MCP joint while extending the interphalangeal joints
B. Extend the MCP joint while flexing the IP joints
questions.explanation: Because they link a flexor tendon to the extensor hood, the lumbricals flex the MCP joint and extend the IP joints ('intrinsic-plus').

questions.question: An ulnar nerve lesion classically produces:
options: A. A claw hand, worst in the ring and little fingers
B. An ape hand with thenar wasting
questions.explanation: Losing most intrinsics (interossei + medial lumbricals) causes clawing — MCP hyperextension with IP flexion — worst in the ulnar (ring/little) fingers.

questions.question: The first dorsal interosseous muscle is pierced by which vessel entering the palm?
questions.explanation: The radial artery passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous to reach the deep palm.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the fascial components of the hand?
questions.explanation: The five components are the palmar aponeurosis, flexor retinaculum, fibrous digital sheaths, extensor retinaculum and extensor hoods. The plantar aponeurosis is in the FOOT.

questions.question: The palmar aponeurosis blends proximally with the tendon of:
questions.explanation: The apex of the palmar aponeurosis is continuous with the palmaris longus tendon; distally its four bands become the fibrous digital sheaths.

questions.question: The extensor retinaculum forms how many tunnels for the extensor tendons?
questions.explanation: It sends septa to bone forming 6 osteofibrous tunnels, each transmitting synovial-sheathed extensor tendons.

questions.question: The extensor hoods are expansions of the tendons of:
options: A. Extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus
B. Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus
questions.explanation: The extensor hoods are aponeurotic expansions of extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus, receiving the lumbricals and interossei.

questions.question: Mallet (baseball) finger results from:
options: A. Avulsion of the terminal (distal) extensor tendon slip
B. Rupture of a flexor tendon
C. Dislocation of the MCP joint
questions.explanation: Forced flexion of an extended fingertip avulses the terminal extensor slip, leaving a dropped DIP joint that cannot straighten.

questions.question: Tenosynovitis is inflammation of:
options: A. A tendon and its synovial sheath
questions.explanation: Tenosynovitis inflames a tendon and its synovial sheath, swelling the digit and making movement painful; infection can track along the sheaths into the palm.

cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.title: MEDI2200 W3 · Cell Division — DNA Organisation & Mitosis
cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.content: Cell division (Week 3). Eukaryotes hold DNA in a nucleus; prokaryotes have a free nucleoid. ~2 m of DNA is packed: DNA -> wound on histones as nucleosomes -> chromatin fibre -> further looping/supercoiling -> condensed chromosome. Packing also controls gene expression (accessibility). Euchromatin = loose, light, gene-rich, active; heterochromatin = tight, dark, silent (constitutive at centromeres/telomeres; facultative e.g. X-inactivation). Epigenetic control without changing sequence: HATs (acetylation) open chromatin -> active transcription; HDACs, KMTs, DNMTs (deacetylation/methylation) close it -> repressed. Chromosome: replication makes 2 identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere (spindle-attachment point) until anaphase; short arm p ('petit'), long arm q ('queue'); telomere caps each end. Centromere-position classes: metacentric (central), submetacentric (off-centre), acrocentric (near end), telocentric (at end; not in humans). Telomeres are repetitive caps that prevent end fusion, nuclease digestion and false double-strand-break signalling; end-replication problem shortens them each division -> replicative senescence (Hayflick limit); telomerase re-adds repeats (stem/germ cells, and reactivated in most cancers -> unlimited division). Human genome = 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs; homologous pairs (one per parent); 22 autosome pairs + 1 sex pair (XX/XY). Karyotype/karyogram arranges chromosomes by size to check number/structure. Locus = chromosome + arm(p/q) + region + band + sub-band, e.g. 3p22.1; bands numbered outward from the centromere. Somatic cells divide by mitosis (growth/maintenance/repair; identical diploid daughters = genomic stability); germ cells by meiosis (haploid gametes; genetic variation); prokaryotes by binary fission (replicate, segregate, split). Cell cycle = interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication making sister chromatids, G2 prep) + M phase (mitosis + cytokinesis); G0 = resting. Mitosis PMAT: prophase (condense, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks) -> metaphase (align on metaphase plate) -> anaphase (sister chromatids to opposite poles) -> telophase (nuclei re-form, decondense) -> cytokinesis (2 identical diploid daughters). Progression driven by cyclins + CDKs; checkpoints: G1/S restriction (size/nutrients/DNA damage), G2/M (DNA fully/correctly replicated), spindle/M (all chromosomes attached). Checkpoint failure (e.g. p53 loss) -> division with damaged DNA -> cancer.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes a eukaryotic cell from a prokaryotic one?
options: A. It lacks any membrane-bound organelles
B. Its DNA is enclosed within a nucleus
C. Its DNA sits free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid
D. Its DNA is a single circular chromosome
questions.explanation: Eukaryotes keep their DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus; the other options describe prokaryotes, whose DNA is a free nucleoid.

questions.question: Which sequence orders DNA packing from least to most condensed?
options: A. DNA → nucleosomes → chromatin fibre → chromosome
B. Chromosome → chromatin fibre → nucleosomes → DNA
C. Nucleosomes → DNA → chromosome → chromatin fibre
D. DNA → chromatin fibre → nucleosomes → chromosome
questions.explanation: DNA winds on histones to make nucleosomes, which coil into the chromatin fibre, which condenses further into the chromosome.

questions.question: A nucleosome is:
options: A. Two sister chromatids joined at the centromere
B. A chromosome fully condensed for division
C. The protein scaffold of a chromatin loop
D. DNA wound around a core of histone proteins
questions.explanation: The nucleosome — DNA wrapped on histones — is the basic repeating unit of chromatin.

questions.question: Besides fitting ~2 m of DNA into the nucleus, condensation also:
options: A. Increases the total amount of DNA present
B. Removes the need for DNA replication
C. Controls which genes can be transcribed
D. Directly converts the DNA into RNA
questions.explanation: How tightly a region is packed sets its accessibility, so condensation is also a gene switch (the basis of §1). It doesn't change DNA amount or replace replication.

questions.question: Euchromatin is:
options: A. The protein core at the centre of a nucleosome
B. Loosely packed and transcriptionally active
C. The form chromatin takes only during mitosis
D. Tightly packed and transcriptionally silent
questions.explanation: Euchromatin is open, gene-rich and active; the tightly packed, silent form is heterochromatin.

questions.question: Which enzyme OPENS chromatin to favour transcription?
questions.explanation: HATs acetylate histones, loosening their grip and opening chromatin for transcription; HDACs, DNMTs and KMTs all tighten/close it.

questions.question: A gene can be silenced WITHOUT any change to its DNA sequence when:
options: A. Its chromatin is tightened by histone/DNA methylation
B. The gene is physically deleted from the chromosome
C. A whole chromosome is lost from the cell
D. A point mutation introduces a premature stop codon
questions.explanation: Epigenetic tightening (methylation/deacetylation) locks the gene in heterochromatin without altering the sequence. B, C and D all change the DNA content.

questions.question: An inactivated X chromosome is an example of:
questions.explanation: X-inactivation is facultative heterochromatin — condensed only in some cells/contexts. Constitutive heterochromatin (centromeres, telomeres) is always condensed.

questions.question: Sister chromatids are:
options: A. The two identical DNA copies joined at the centromere
B. The short and long arms of one chromosome
C. The two homologous chromosomes of a pair
D. Two separate chromosomes that have fused
questions.explanation: Replication makes two identical copies (sister chromatids) held at the centromere until anaphase. Homologous chromosomes (B) are the maternal/paternal pair — a common confusion.

questions.question: The centromere is essential for division because it:
options: A. Is where the spindle attaches to pull the chromatids apart
B. Carries most of the chromosome's genes
C. Protects the chromosome ends from fusing together
D. Is the site where DNA replication begins
questions.explanation: The centromere is the spindle-attachment (kinetochore) point for accurate segregation. Protecting the ends (B) is the telomere's job.

questions.question: The p arm of a chromosome is the:
questions.explanation: p ('petit') is the short arm; q ('queue') is the long arm.

questions.question: A chromosome whose centromere is slightly off-centre, giving unequal arms, is:
questions.explanation: Off-centre = submetacentric. Metacentric is central, acrocentric is near one end, telocentric is at the very end.

questions.question: Which centromere type is NOT found in human chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Humans have no telocentric chromosomes (centromere right at the end); they are common in mice.

questions.question: Which is a protective role of telomeres?
options: A. Attaching the chromosome to the mitotic spindle
B. Condensing the chromosome for mitosis
C. Preventing chromosome ends from fusing together
D. Starting DNA replication at the chromosome centre
questions.explanation: Telomeres cap the ends — preventing fusion, nuclease digestion and false double-strand-break signalling. Spindle attachment (B) is the centromere's role.

questions.question: Telomeres shorten with each division because:
options: A. Nucleases digest the coding DNA every cycle
B. Telomerase actively trims them after each replication
C. The centromere loses repeats at each division
D. DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the end of a linear chromosome
questions.explanation: The end-replication problem — polymerase can't finish the very end — costs a little telomere each division. Telomerase does the opposite of B (it re-adds repeats).

questions.question: When a normal cell's telomeres become critically short, the cell:
options: B. Re-lengthens them using DNA polymerase
C. Enters replicative senescence and stops dividing
questions.explanation: Critically short telomeres trigger replicative senescence (the Hayflick limit). Re-lengthening needs telomerase, not DNA polymerase (D).

questions.question: Most cancers can divide indefinitely partly because they:
options: B. Switch from mitosis to meiosis
C. Reactivate telomerase to rebuild their telomeres
questions.explanation: Reactivating telomerase resets the shortening clock, giving cancer cells unlimited divisions.

questions.question: The human genome consists of:
options: A. 44 chromosomes plus 2 unpaired sex chromosomes
questions.explanation: 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs.

questions.question: Of the 23 human chromosome pairs:
options: A. 11 are autosomes and 12 are sex-chromosome pairs
C. 22 are autosomes and 1 is the sex-chromosome pair
D. 21 are autosomes and 2 are sex-chromosome pairs
questions.explanation: 22 autosome pairs plus 1 sex pair (XX or XY).

questions.question: Homologous chromosomes are:
options: A. Two chromosomes that have swapped segments
B. The short and long arms of a single chromosome
C. The two identical sister chromatids of one chromosome
D. A matched pair carrying the same genes, one from each parent
questions.explanation: Homologues are the maternal/paternal pair carrying the same genes. Sister chromatids (B) are the two identical copies of one chromosome.

questions.question: The locus 3p22.1 means chromosome 3,:
options: A. Short arm, region 2, band 2, sub-band 1
B. Short arm, region 1, band 2, sub-band 2
C. Long arm, region 2, band 2, sub-band 1
D. Long arm, region 1, band 2, sub-band 2
questions.explanation: p = short arm; the digits read region 2, band 2, sub-band 1.

questions.question: Chromosome bands are numbered:
options: A. By staining intensity, darkest first
B. Inward from the telomere toward the centromere
C. Outward from the centromere toward the telomere
D. From the p-arm tip straight through to the q-arm tip
questions.explanation: Bands are counted outward from the centromere on each arm.

questions.question: Somatic cells divide by mitosis to:
options: A. Produce genetically identical diploid daughter cells
B. Halve the chromosome number each division
C. Produce haploid gametes carrying genetic variation
D. Generate genetic diversity for reproduction
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives identical diploid daughters for growth, maintenance and repair. B, C and D describe meiosis.

questions.question: Meiosis differs from mitosis in that it:
options: A. Produces two identical diploid daughter cells
B. Produces haploid, genetically varied gametes
C. Occurs in all somatic tissues of the body
questions.explanation: Meiosis makes haploid, varied gametes; the other options are features of mitosis.

questions.question: Prokaryotic binary fission involves:
options: A. Producing four haploid daughter cells
B. Replicating the single chromosome, segregating the copies, then splitting
C. Aligning chromosomes on a spindle before separating them
D. Condensing 46 chromosomes into a karyotype
questions.explanation: Binary fission = replicate, segregate, split into two identical cells — no spindle. B describes mitosis, C meiosis.

questions.question: During which phase of interphase is the DNA replicated?
questions.explanation: DNA is synthesised (replicated) in S phase; G1 and G2 are growth/preparation, and M is division.

questions.question: The event that defines anaphase is:
options: A. The cytoplasm splitting into two cells
B. Sister chromatids being pulled to opposite poles
C. Chromosomes lining up on the metaphase plate
D. The nuclear envelope breaking down
questions.explanation: Anaphase = chromatids separate to opposite poles. Alignment is metaphase, envelope breakdown is prophase, cytoplasmic splitting is cytokinesis.

questions.question: The correct order of the mitotic phases is:
questions.explanation: PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase.

questions.question: The spindle-assembly (M) checkpoint holds the cell until:
options: A. The cell has grown large enough to divide
B. Every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle
C. The telomeres have been re-lengthened
D. All the DNA has finished replicating
questions.explanation: The M/spindle checkpoint verifies correct spindle attachment before anaphase. B is the G2/M check, C is the G1/S check.

questions.question: Cancer arises from cell-cycle dysregulation when:
options: A. Checkpoint controls fail, letting cells divide with damaged DNA
B. Telomeres lengthen at their normal rate
C. Mitosis starts producing haploid daughter cells
D. Cells permanently arrest in the resting G0 state
questions.explanation: Losing checkpoint control (e.g. p53 mutation) lets cells divide with damaged genomes and proliferate unchecked.

meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.title: MEDI2200 W4 · Meiosis — Cell Division & Genetic Variation
meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.content: Meiosis (Week 4). Meiosis makes haploid (n) gametes from diploid (2n) germ cells (ovaries/testes) so fertilisation (n + n -> 2n zygote) keeps the chromosome number constant; it also mixes the genome for variation. Gametogenesis: spermatogenesis (sperm), oogenesis (ova). Meiosis vs mitosis: both have one DNA replication (S phase); mitosis = 1 division -> 2 identical diploid somatic cells; meiosis = 2 divisions (no replication between) -> up to 4 varied haploid cells; homologues pair only in meiosis. Stages: interphase replicates DNA (each chromosome = 2 sister chromatids). Meiosis I (PMAT I) is reductional: homologous chromosomes pair then SEPARATE (sister chromatids stay together) -> 2 haploid cells whose chromosomes still have 2 chromatids. Meiosis II (PMAT II) is like mitosis: sister chromatids separate -> 4 haploid cells with single/unreplicated chromosomes. Anaphase I = homologues apart; anaphase II = sister chromatids apart. Three sources of genetic variation: (1) crossing over in prophase I - homologues pair (synapsis, bivalent/tetrad, synaptonemal complex) and non-sister chromatids exchange DNA at chiasmata; prophase I substages leptotene (condense) -> zygotene (synapsis) -> pachytene (crossing over) -> diplotene (chiasmata visible) -> diakinesis; without chiasmata segregation can be erroneous. (2) Independent assortment at metaphase I - homologue pairs orient randomly (2^23 combinations). (3) Random assortment at metaphase II of the now non-identical sister chromatids. Non-disjunction = failure of chromosomes to separate: homologues fail in meiosis I, sister chromatids fail in meiosis II -> gametes with an extra/missing chromosome -> aneuploidy. Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome (47,+21); monosomy X = Turner syndrome (45,X); 47,XXY = Klinefelter. Trisomy-21 risk rises with maternal age (long-arrested oocyte meiosis I). Chiasmata tether homologues for correct segregation, so failed crossover is one cause of non-disjunction.

questions.question: Gametes must be haploid so that:
options: A. The daughter cells are genetically identical
B. Each generation has twice the chromosomes of the last
C. Cell division can happen more quickly
D. Fertilisation restores the normal diploid number
questions.explanation: Two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation to give a diploid zygote; if gametes were diploid, chromosome number would double each generation.

questions.question: In terms of ploidy, fertilisation is:
questions.explanation: Two haploid (n) gametes fuse to form one diploid (2n) zygote.

questions.question: Meiosis takes place in:
options: B. Germ cells of the ovaries and testes
C. Only the skin and gut lining
D. All somatic tissues of the body
questions.explanation: Meiosis is confined to germ cells (gametogenesis); somatic cells divide by mitosis.

questions.question: Compared with mitosis, meiosis produces:
options: A. Two diploid cells from two divisions
B. Two haploid cells from one division
C. Four haploid cells from two divisions
D. Four diploid cells from one division
questions.explanation: Meiosis has two divisions yielding up to four haploid cells; mitosis has one division yielding two diploid cells.

questions.question: Across the whole of meiosis, the DNA is replicated:
options: D. Twice, once before each division
questions.explanation: There is a single S-phase replication before meiosis I and none between meiosis I and II — two divisions on one replication gives haploid cells.

questions.question: Which event occurs in meiosis but NOT in mitosis?
options: A. A spindle forms to move chromosomes
C. Sister chromatids are formed by replication
D. The nuclear envelope breaks down
questions.explanation: Homologue pairing (synapsis) in prophase I is unique to meiosis; the other events happen in both.

questions.question: Meiosis I separates:
questions.explanation: Meiosis I (reductional) pulls homologous chromosomes apart; sister chromatids stay together until meiosis II.

questions.question: Meiosis II separates:
questions.explanation: Meiosis II resembles mitosis — the sister chromatids separate, giving four haploid cells with single chromosomes.

questions.question: Which statement about anaphase is correct?
options: A. In anaphase I homologues separate; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate
B. Homologues separate in both anaphase I and II
C. Sister chromatids separate in both anaphase I and II
D. In anaphase I sister chromatids separate; in anaphase II homologues separate
questions.explanation: Anaphase I pulls homologues apart (sisters stay joined); anaphase II pulls the sister chromatids apart.

questions.question: The cells produced at the end of meiosis I are:
options: A. Tetraploid, with four chromatids each
C. Haploid, with chromosomes still made of two sister chromatids
questions.explanation: Meiosis I halves the chromosome number (haploid) but each chromosome still has two sister chromatids until meiosis II.

questions.question: Meiosis II is often said to resemble mitosis because:
options: A. It is preceded by a round of DNA replication
B. It separates sister chromatids of each chromosome
C. It produces diploid daughter cells
D. It separates homologous chromosome pairs
questions.explanation: Like mitosis, meiosis II separates sister chromatids — but starting from a haploid cell with no preceding replication.

questions.question: Crossing over takes place during:
questions.explanation: Homologues pair and exchange segments during prophase I.

questions.question: Crossing over exchanges DNA between:
options: A. The two sister chromatids of one chromosome
B. Non-sister chromatids of paired homologous chromosomes
D. The two strands of a single DNA molecule
questions.explanation: Recombination swaps segments between non-sister chromatids of the paired homologues, mixing maternal and paternal alleles.

questions.question: During which substage of prophase I does crossing over actually occur?
questions.explanation: Homologues condense (leptotene), pair (zygotene), cross over (pachytene), show chiasmata (diplotene), then fully condense (diakinesis).

questions.question: Chiasmata are:
options: A. The centromeres joining sister chromatids
B. The protective caps on the chromosome ends
C. The visible crossover points that hold paired homologues together
D. The spindle-attachment sites on the chromosome
questions.explanation: Chiasmata are the crossover points seen once the synaptonemal complex dissolves; they tether the homologues and produce recombination.

questions.question: Independent assortment of homologous pairs occurs at:
questions.explanation: At metaphase I the homologue pairs orient randomly on the plate, so each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal homologues.

questions.question: Random assortment in meiosis II adds genetic variation because by then the sister chromatids:
options: B. Have been replicated a second time
C. Are no longer identical, owing to crossing over
questions.explanation: Crossing over in prophase I made the sister chromatids non-identical, so their random orientation in meiosis II reshuffles them further.

questions.question: Synapsis refers to:
options: A. The pairing of homologous chromosomes
B. The assembly of the mitotic spindle
C. The replication of DNA in S phase
D. The joining of two sister chromatids
questions.explanation: Synapsis is the close pairing of homologues (forming a bivalent/tetrad) in prophase I, enabling crossing over.

questions.question: For 23 chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone gives how many possible gamete combinations?
questions.explanation: Each of the 23 pairs orients two ways independently, so 2^23 (≈ 8 million) combinations — before crossing over adds more.

questions.question: Non-disjunction is:
options: A. The failure of chromosomes to condense
B. An error confined to crossing over
C. The failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis
D. The failure of DNA to replicate before meiosis
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction is failed separation — of homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II).

questions.question: Non-disjunction in meiosis I specifically means that:
options: A. Sister chromatids fail to separate
B. The DNA fails to replicate
C. Homologous chromosomes fail to separate
D. Two spindles form instead of one
questions.explanation: In meiosis I the failure is of homologues to separate; if it happens in meiosis II it is the sister chromatids that fail.

questions.question: Non-disjunction produces:
options: A. Gametes that are all genetically identical
B. Gametes with an extra or missing chromosome
C. Extra copies of the whole genome
D. Diploid zygotes with the normal chromosome count
questions.explanation: A gamete gains or loses a chromosome, so the fertilised individual is aneuploid (a wrong chromosome number).

questions.question: Three copies of chromosome 21 cause:
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 (47,+21) is Down syndrome — the commonest autosomal aneuploidy.

questions.question: The karyotype of Turner syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is a single X chromosome — 45,X, i.e. 45 chromosomes instead of 46.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome has the karyotype:
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is an extra X in a male — 47,XXY.

questions.question: Failure to form chiasmata can cause non-disjunction because chiasmata normally:
options: A. Tether homologues so they orient and segregate correctly
B. Prevent crossing over from happening
C. Attach the spindle directly to the telomeres
D. Replicate the DNA before the first division
questions.explanation: Chiasmata physically hold paired homologues together and correctly oriented until anaphase I; without them a pair can mis-segregate.

questions.question: The risk of trisomy 21 rises with maternal age mainly because of:
options: A. Faster mitosis in the ageing embryo
B. Increased crossing over in older sperm
C. Shorter telomeres in the father's gametes
D. Errors in the long-arrested oocyte's meiosis I
questions.explanation: Oocytes are arrested in meiosis I for years; the longer arrest raises the chance of meiosis-I non-disjunction with age.

questions.question: A gamete is:
options: A. A germline stem cell before meiosis
questions.explanation: Gametes are the haploid products of meiosis — sperm or ova — that fuse at fertilisation.

soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.title: SOCI1010 W1 · What is Everyday Life? — Intro to Sociology
soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.content: SOCI1010 Introduction to Sociology: Understanding Everyday Life — Week 1 'Making something out of nothing?' (A/Prof Selvaraj Velayutham). SOURCE 1 LECTURE: Sociology = the study of society and how society shapes our lives, and a tool for understanding the world. C. Wright Mills (1959) — the SOCIOLOGICAL IMAGINATION: a quality of mind, the vivid awareness of the relationship between personal experience and the wider society; neither an individual's life nor a society's history can be understood without understanding both; 'thinking yourself away from the familiar routines of everyday life'. The MONOBLOC chair (ubiquitous cheap stackable plastic chair, petroleum-derived, ignored, despised by designers, yet world's most popular furniture) = making something out of nothing: the mundane object is significant. Ben Highmore (2011): in ordinary life there is never 'nothing' going on, just nothing 'much'. Everyday life = taken-for-granted, mundane, routine daily life; the sociology of everyday life interrogates daily practices, activities and interactions. TOOTHBRUSHING unpacked: routine (mundane/taken-for-granted); RITUALISTIC (repetition & habituation, personal techniques — brush, bristle, paste, floss); EMBODIED PRACTICE (socialisation/training in the correct way, internalised); SOCIAL NORM (can't imagine anyone not doing it; tied to age, class, gender, race); personal hygiene & idealised beauty (the 'perfect smile' originates in Hollywood); PUBLIC HEALTH (WHO 2022: oral disease affects ~3.5 billion; cavities prevented by constant low fluoride; periodontal disease in 15-20% of 35-44s; ~30% of 65-74s have no natural teeth; worse among the poor; risk factors diet/tobacco/alcohol/poor hygiene/social determinants); STRUCTURAL INEQUALITY ('the unseen dentist' — dentists cluster in middle-class areas, haves vs have-nots); GLOBAL CAPITALISM (toothpaste brands owned by a few multinationals — Colgate-Palmolive, P&G [Crest, Oral B], GlaxoSmithKline [Macleans, Aquafresh, Sensodyne], Unilever, Johnson & Johnson [Listerine]; 'unlimited choice' is an illusion). SOCIOLOGY & COMEDY: Peter Berger (1970) — the social scientist who misses the comic dimension misses essential features of social reality; Zijderveld (1997) — the sociologist is like the fool holding up a mirror. Sociology is LIKE comedy (puts everyday manners/customs under the microscope, questions authority) but DIFFERS (more systematic/objective methods, specialised concepts). Seinfeld = 'the show about nothing'; characters constantly monitor the rules of interaction = REFLEXIVITY (what are the rules? how to interpret them? do they make sense/why exist? consequences of breaking them?). SOURCE 2 READING — Susie Scott, Making Sense of Everyday Life (2009), Ch.1 'What is Everyday Life?': everyday life IS the wider picture — micro-level small-scale practices relate to and are shaped by macro-level patterns; social order/disorder/change reflect individual-society, agency-structure. Moran (2005) four 'quotidian spaces': workspaces, urban/mobile spaces, living spaces, non-places (transit spaces between contexts — buses, service stations). Silva & Bennett (2004): home/family/community, sexuality/'race'/age, technology. Three defining FEATURES: (1) mundane/familiar/unremarkable ('daily lives of ordinary people', Bennett & Watson 2002); (2) routine/repetitive/rhythmic — habitual (Felski 1999), reproduces social life; (3) private/personal — Mills: relate 'private troubles' to 'public issues'. Everyday phenomena 'obvious to the point of elusiveness' (Martin 2003), the 'connective tissue' (Bennett 2004), yet infused with power/politics/history (Martin). DEVELOPMENT: an 'absent presence' — implicit in studies of poverty (Rowntree 1901), kinship (Willmott & Young 1960), deviance (Becker 1963); now studied in its own right like the sociology of the body (Turner 1996). Bennett & Watson's three reasons: (1) ordinary lives become worthy of public representation (photojournalism, diaries, reality TV); (2) Foucauldian 'disciplinary society' of control/surveillance; (3) social movements (feminism, black civil rights, Gay Pride). Prominent theorists: Lukács (pre-reflective acceptance stops authentic living), Lefebvre (capitalist workplace alienation, false consciousness, la vie quotidienne), de Certeau (people 'do'/practise everyday life; resistance via minor rule-breaking = 'making do'). Douglas (1981): study common-sense meanings. Berger & Luckmann (1967): we construct our own social reality through everyday encounters; no single objective reality — central to interpretivist sociology (Symbolic Interactionism, phenomenology, ethnomethodology). Cultural Studies: places/images/artefacts read as 'texts' transmitting ideologies. HOW TO STUDY: (1) make the familiar strange — view objectively, bracket assumptions/value judgements, morally neutral; 'anthropologist on Mars' (Sacks 1996), detective story (Highmore 2002); (2) search for underlying rules/routines/regularities, link micro to macro; (3) challenge taken-for-granted assumptions (Garfinkel 1967) by studying norm-breaking; Durkheim (1893): deviance is FUNCTIONAL — unites 'us' vs 'them', reinforces shared values, makes the group cohesive; some rules only visible when broken (faux pas). Three THEMES per topic: rituals & routines; social order; challenges (norm-breaking, 'exceptions that prove the rule'). SOURCE 3 — Jorge Gracia, 'The Secret of Seinfeld's Humor: The Significance of the Insignificant' (Seinfeld and Philosophy, 2000): THESIS — we laugh at something because in it we see the SIGNIFICANCE OF THE INSIGNIFICANT, and we cry at something because through it we grasp the INSIGNIFICANCE OF THE SIGNIFICANT. Not a universal/scientific law — a matter of emotion/feeling, not intellect. Comedy is about the ordinary/everyday: it makes our unnoticed idiosyncrasies, manners, customs come alive, revealing the follies, absurdities and idiosyncrasies of cultures. Seinfeld's success = capturing the significance of the insignificant ('a show about nothing'); characters never think their doings significant. Tragedy is the opposite: momentous subject matter (love, death, betrayal, vice, virtue, pain, injustice, cruelty, revenge), characters 'larger than life' (heroes, villains, victims, ogres); no tragedy is written about the sale of a van, mail delivery or non-fat yogurt. Tragedy underscores significance then reveals the insignificance of what we hold dear (a shattering realisation); comedy teaches without pain. Comedy dates more easily than tragedy because it turns on culture-specific everyday customs, whereas tragedy taps the more universal core of human nature.

questions.question: In the lecture, sociology is defined as:
options: A. The study of past civilisations and their remains
B. The study of the individual mind and personality
C. The study of formal political institutions alone
D. The study of society and how society shapes our lives
questions.explanation: Sociology is the study of society and how society shapes our lives — and also a tool or way of understanding the world.

questions.question: C. Wright Mills (1959) gave the name 'sociological imagination' to:
options: A. The tendency to accept daily routines without reflection
B. A quality of mind that links personal experience to the wider society
C. Characters' habit of reflecting on the rules of interaction
D. The way media place everyone under constant surveillance
questions.explanation: Mills called the sociological imagination a quality of mind: the vivid awareness of the relationship between personal experience and the wider society. The distractors are other real ideas from the material (pre-reflective acceptance, the disciplinary society, reflexivity).

questions.question: Which statement best captures Mills's sociological imagination?
options: A. Individual behaviour is ultimately explained by underlying biology and genetics
B. Society is really just the sum of many individuals' private choices
C. Personal troubles are best kept quite separate from wider public issues
D. Neither an individual's life nor a society's history makes sense without the other
questions.explanation: The sociological imagination insists the individual and society are mutually intelligible — you cannot grasp one without the other.

questions.question: For Mills, to 'relate private troubles to public issues' means to:
options: A. Treat personal problems as purely individual failings
B. Judge which personal choices are morally best
C. Keep sociology focused only on large historical events
D. Look for the social patterns reflected in the lives of individuals
questions.explanation: Thinking sociologically links 'private troubles' to 'public issues' — seeing the social structure behind individual experience.

questions.question: Why does the lecture open with the mass-produced monobloc plastic chair?
options: A. To claim that recycling would solve overconsumption
B. To argue that good design must always be expensive
C. To show that even a mundane, ignored object is sociologically significant
D. To prove that plastics are environmentally harmless
questions.explanation: The monobloc — cheap, mass-produced, despised by designers, ignored by everyone — is 'making something out of nothing': the ordinary object turns out to be socially significant.

questions.question: Ben Highmore's point about answering 'nothing much' to 'what have you been up to?' is that:
options: A. Only dramatic events deserve our attention
B. In ordinary life there is never 'nothing' going on, only nothing 'much'
C. Most people genuinely do nothing worth studying
D. Everyday life is too trivial for serious sociology
questions.explanation: Highmore (2011) insists the 'nothing much' of ordinary life is full of social activity worth examining.

questions.question: 'Everyday life' is best defined as:
options: B. The taken-for-granted, mundane, routine aspects of daily life
C. The formal institutions of the state and economy
D. Rare, dramatic and life-changing events
questions.explanation: Everyday life refers to the common-sensical, mundane, routine activities we all take for granted.

questions.question: The lecture calls tooth-brushing 'ritualistic' because it is:
options: A. A driver of structural inequality in health
B. Something we cannot imagine anyone skipping
C. Learned as the single correct bodily technique
D. Based on repetition and habituation, with personal techniques and methods
questions.explanation: As a ritual, brushing rests on repetition and habituation; each person develops their own methods (brush, bristle, paste, floss). The distractors name the OTHER framings used in the same slide (embodied practice, social norm, inequality).

questions.question: Learning the 'proper way' to brush until it feels natural and internalised is described as:
options: A. An embodied practice acquired through socialisation
C. A social norm we assume everyone shares
D. A ritual based on repetition
questions.explanation: Embodied practice = socialisation and training in the correct technique, which becomes familiar and internalised in the body.

questions.question: That we 'can't imagine anyone NOT brushing their teeth' expresses:
options: B. A social norm, i.e. a shared social expectation
D. A form of false consciousness
questions.explanation: The sense that everyone does it (barring specific circumstances) marks brushing as a social norm — an expectation tied to age, class, gender and race.

questions.question: Saying norms around brushing are 'tied to age, class, gender and race' makes the sociological point that:
options: A. Personal habits have no link to social position
B. Hygiene is determined entirely by biology
C. Everyone practises hygiene in exactly the same way
D. Seemingly personal habits are socially structured, not purely individual
questions.explanation: A private-seeming act is patterned by social position — the recurring lecture theme that the personal is social.

questions.question: The lecture traces the modern demand for a 'perfect smile' of pearly whites to:
options: A. Hollywood and idealised standards of beauty
B. The rise of reality television
questions.explanation: The 'perfect smile' has its origin in Hollywood; perfect white teeth became an idealised beauty requirement.

questions.question: The 'unseen dentist' — dentists clustering in middle-class areas rather than disadvantaged rural and remote ones — illustrates:
options: A. Structural inequality between the 'haves' and 'have-nots'
B. The influence of social movements
C. Consumer choice in a free market
questions.explanation: Unequal access to dental care exposes structural inequalities and power differences between rich and poor.

questions.question: The lecture shows most toothpaste brands are owned by a few multinationals (Colgate-Palmolive, P&G, GlaxoSmithKline, Unilever, Johnson & Johnson) to make the point that:
options: A. Toothpaste brands are mostly locally owned and independently produced
B. Everyday consumption sits inside global capitalism, so choice is an illusion
C. Market competition guarantees consumers a genuinely unlimited range of choice
D. Who owns a brand makes no difference to everyday life
questions.explanation: A handful of corporations control production, supply and consumption chains — the apparent variety of choice sits inside global capitalism.

questions.question: According to the WHO figures cited, oral diseases affect roughly how many people worldwide?
questions.explanation: The WHO (2022) estimate cited is that oral diseases affect nearly 3.5 billion people.

questions.question: The slide states dental cavities can be prevented by:
options: A. Visiting a dentist once a year
B. Brushing exactly twice every day
C. Removing all sugar from the diet
D. Maintaining a constant low level of fluoride in the oral cavity
questions.explanation: Cavities are prevented by a constant low level of fluoride in the mouth — the specific mechanism given.

questions.question: Peter Berger argued that a social scientist who fails to perceive the comic dimension of social reality will:
options: A. Avoid bias in their findings
C. Miss essential features of that reality
D. Better capture large-scale historical change
questions.explanation: Berger (1970) held that the comic dimension reveals essential features of social reality, and that laughter yields genuine insight.

questions.question: Zijderveld compared the scrutinising sociologist to which figure?
options: A. The judge carefully weighing up competing moral values
B. The anthropologist on Mars observing a wholly alien world
C. The fool who holds up a mirror to show people themselves
D. The detective quietly investigating an unexplained mystery
questions.explanation: Zijderveld (1997) likened the sociologist to the traditional fool holding up a mirror. The distractors are other real analogies for the sociologist — but from Scott's reading (Sacks's 'anthropologist on Mars', Highmore's detective).

questions.question: In what way is sociology LIKE comedy, according to the lecture?
options: A. Both hold everyday manners and customs up to scrutiny, questioning authority
B. Both employ systematic and rigorously objective research methods
C. Both depend on a specialised, technical professional vocabulary
D. Both carefully avoid ever making their audience laugh
questions.explanation: Like comedy, sociology holds everyday arrangements up to scrutiny and asks whether they make sense, often questioning power.

questions.question: How does the lecture say sociology DIFFERS from comedy?
options: A. Its methods are more systematic and objective, using specialised concepts
B. It concerns itself only with large-scale historical events
C. It never examines the everyday manners of ordinary people
D. It refuses, as a matter of principle, to question authority
questions.explanation: Unlike comedy, sociology employs more systematic, objective methods and a specialised set of concepts and language.

questions.question: When Seinfeld's characters constantly reflect on how to act and what follows, they are engaged in what sociologists call:
questions.explanation: Reflexivity is the ongoing monitoring of the rules of interaction — asking what the rules are, how to read them, and what breaking them entails. The distractors are other real concepts from the same material.

questions.question: Which question is one of the 'types of reflexivity' the lecture lists?
options: A. Which culture has the best rules?
B. Who first wrote the rules into law?
C. What are the consequences of breaking the rules?
D. How can the rules be legally enforced?
questions.explanation: The listed reflexive questions are: What are the rules? How does one interpret them? Do they make sense and why do they exist? What are the consequences of breaking them?

questions.question: Scott answers the charge that everyday life is 'trivial' by arguing that:
options: A. Everyday life IS the wider picture: big events rest on small local acts
B. Macro-level patterns bear no genuine connection to micro practices
C. Only large-scale historical events truly shape a society
D. Everyday life really is less important than wars and inequality
questions.explanation: Scott's core claim: micro-level, small-scale practices relate to and are shaped by macro-level patterns — the everyday is the wider picture, not a distraction from it.

questions.question: Social order, disorder and change, Scott says, reflect the relationship between:
options: D. Individual and society, agency and structure
questions.explanation: Everyday life expresses the relationship between individual and society, agency and structure, process and regularity.

questions.question: In Moran's four types of 'quotidian space', a 'non-place' is:
options: A. A transit space between two contexts, such as a bus or station
B. The private domestic living space of the family home
C. An online or digital environment such as social media
D. A sacred space deliberately set apart for ritual and worship
questions.explanation: Moran (2005) lists workspaces, urban/mobile spaces, living spaces and non-places — the last being transit spaces like buses or service stations, between two contexts.

questions.question: Scott says everyday life is mundane/familiar, private/personal, and also:
options: C. Formally regulated by written law
questions.explanation: The three defining features are: mundane and unremarkable; routine, repetitive and rhythmic (which reproduces social life); and private/personal.

questions.question: The claim that everyday life is 'habitual in nature', which is what makes it feel so familiar, is attributed to:
questions.explanation: Felski (1999) characterised everyday life as habitual. The distractors are other theorists Scott cites for different points (Durkheim on deviance, Garfinkel on breaking rules, Foucault on discipline).

questions.question: Martin (2003) describes everyday phenomena as nebulous and ambiguous — 'obvious to the point of...':
questions.explanation: Martin's phrase is 'obvious to the point of elusiveness' — the everyday is so pervasive it slips from view.

questions.question: Everyday phenomena are called the 'connective tissue' that holds everything together by:
questions.explanation: Bennett (2004) called the everyday the 'connective tissue'; it forms the background against which concrete experiences are seen.

questions.question: Martin (2003) insists the everyday is NOT trivial because it is:
options: B. Infused with power, politics and historical significance
C. Beyond the reach of research
questions.explanation: Martin reminds us the everyday world is infused with power, politics and historical significance, so we must ask whose interests social practices serve.

questions.question: Before it was studied in its own right, Scott says everyday life had an:
questions.explanation: Everyday life had an 'absent presence' — implicitly addressed in earlier studies of poverty, kinship and deviance before being recognised as worthy of study on its own, like the sociology of the body (Turner 1996). The distractors are other real terms from the chapter.

questions.question: Which is one of Bennett and Watson's three reasons the sociology of everyday life emerged in the twentieth century?
options: A. A change in what counts as worthy of public representation
B. The invention of the internet and social media platforms
C. The gradual global spread of liberal democratic government
D. The steady decline of organised religion across the West
questions.explanation: Their three reasons: (1) ordinary lives became worthy of representation (photojournalism, diaries, reality TV); (2) the Foucauldian 'disciplinary society' of surveillance; (3) new social movements foregrounding identity.

questions.question: The argument that we live in a 'disciplinary society' where every move is subject to control, surveillance and regulation is:
questions.explanation: This is the Foucauldian strand of Bennett and Watson's account; the mass media (e.g. paparazzi) exemplify the surveillance of even mundane life.

questions.question: Scott names which trio as the most prominent early theorists of everyday life?
options: B. Lukács, Lefebvre and de Certeau
questions.explanation: The most prominent theorists in this mode were Georg Lukács, Henri Lefebvre and Michel de Certeau. The distractors are all real names from the chapter used for other points.

questions.question: Lukács warned that being too immersed in one's daily routines produces:
options: A. A 'false consciousness' produced by repetitive factory labour
B. A liberating grasp of the 'sociological imagination'
C. A defiant tactic of 'making do' against everyday authority
D. A 'pre-reflective acceptance' that stops people living authentically
questions.explanation: Lukács's 'pre-reflective acceptance' prevented people from realising their potential. Note the distractors are the neighbouring theorists' terms: false consciousness is Lefebvre's, making do is de Certeau's.

questions.question: Applying Marx to the working class, Lefebvre argued that dreary, repetitive capitalist workplaces kept people in:
options: A. A disciplinary society of surveillance
B. False consciousness, alienated from the true conditions of their existence
D. Pre-reflective acceptance of daily routine
questions.explanation: Lefebvre held that the factory's repetitive cycles alienated workers and sustained false consciousness; la vie quotidienne was routine and regular, broken only by occasional relief.

questions.question: de Certeau argued that people can subvert authority not by grand uprisings but by breaking minor rules in everyday life — a tactic he called:
questions.explanation: de Certeau (1984) stressed how people 'do' everyday life creatively and defiantly; resistance through minor rule-breaking he termed 'making do'.

questions.question: Berger and Luckmann (1967) famously argued that:
options: A. Reality is determined solely by economic class
B. Social reality is fixed permanently by institutions
C. We construct our own social reality through our everyday encounters with others
D. There is one objective reality waiting to be discovered
questions.explanation: For Berger and Luckmann there is no single objective reality but an infinite number of local, subjective realities we construct in daily interaction.

questions.question: The view that there is no single objective reality — only local subjective realities studied from the insider's perspective — is the central tenet of:
options: B. The sociology of the body
questions.explanation: This tenet informs interpretivist sociology — Symbolic Interactionists, phenomenologists, ethnomethodologists, ethnographers and action theorists.

questions.question: Cultural Studies theorists treat the places, images and artefacts of everyday life as:
options: A. Direct evidence of a single objective social reality
B. Neutral objects that carry no real social meaning
C. Purely economic commodities with a fixed market price
D. 'Texts' to be read critically for the ideologies they transmit
questions.explanation: Cultural Studies reads everyday places and artefacts as 'texts' conveying particular ideologies (Moran 2005).

questions.question: The phrase 'the anthropologist on Mars' — standing back to view familiar settings as if never seen before — is credited to:
questions.explanation: Sacks's 'anthropologist on Mars' captures the detached observer stance; Highmore's analogy is the detective story, Garfinkel's is challenging taken-for-granted assumptions.

questions.question: 'Making the familiar strange' requires the researcher to:
options: A. Rely almost exclusively on official government statistics
B. Focus only on the most dramatic instances of deviance
C. Decide which of the everyday behaviours observed are morally best
D. Bracket out prior assumptions and stay neutral and descriptive
questions.explanation: The first technique is descriptive and analytical, not evaluative — you suspend assumptions about what is normal or desirable and ask 'what is going on here?'

questions.question: Garfinkel's contribution to studying everyday life is the technique of:
options: A. Interview only powerful political elites and officials
B. Measure people's emotional responses in a laboratory
C. Challenge taken-for-granted assumptions by studying broken rules
D. Collect and carefully analyse large-scale official statistics
questions.explanation: Garfinkel (1967) urged us to challenge taken-for-granted assumptions; norm-breaking makes implicit rules visible.

questions.question: Durkheim argued that deviance is:
options: A. Purely destructive, eroding social order wherever it appears
B. Largely irrelevant to the question of social cohesion
C. Merely a symptom of individual psychological pathology
D. Functional: it unites 'us' against 'them' and reinforces shared values
questions.explanation: For Durkheim (1893) deviance is functional: identifying a rule-breaker as deviant safely contains the behaviour and makes the group more cohesive around common values.

questions.question: Scott notes some social rules 'only become visible when they are broken'. An example given is:
options: A. A subtle faux pas, such as misjudging a dress code
B. A violent crime prominently reported in the national news
C. A major, formal change to government legislation
D. A large and highly visible public protest movement
questions.explanation: Implicit rules surface through faux pas (dress codes, over-familiar address) or the noisy late-night neighbour — the breach reveals the norm.

questions.question: Scott discusses every topic through three themes: rituals and routines, challenges, and:
questions.explanation: The three organising themes are rituals and routines (specific practices), social order (underlying rules and expectations), and challenges (norm-breaking).

questions.question: In Scott's framework, the theme of 'challenges' refers to:
options: A. The routine habits that reproduce social life
B. The underlying structures of rules and expectations
C. Instances of norm-breaking — the 'exceptions that prove the rule'
D. The economic forces shaping consumption
questions.explanation: 'Challenges' are the norm-breaking cases that reveal a group's values and show who counts as deviant or conformist.

questions.question: Gracia's thesis is that we laugh at something because in it we see:
options: A. The insignificance of the significant
B. The absurdity of political authority
C. The triumph of heroic virtue
D. The significance of the insignificant
questions.explanation: Gracia proposes we laugh when we grasp the significance of the insignificant — and cry when we grasp the insignificance of the significant.

questions.question: By contrast, Gracia says we cry at something because through it we grasp:
options: A. The relativity of all cultures
B. The insignificance of the significant
C. The universal rules of etiquette
D. The significance of the insignificant
questions.explanation: Tragedy makes us see that what we hold to be significant and important is, in the larger scheme, insignificant — a shattering realisation.

questions.question: For Gracia, comedy focuses on what is ordinary and insignificant, whereas tragedy deals with subject matter that is:
options: A. Purely local and culturally specific
C. Trivial and everyday, like queuing or shopping
D. Momentous — love, death, betrayal, virtue, injustice and revenge
questions.explanation: Tragedy's subject matter is momentous — love, death, betrayal, vice, virtue, pain, injustice, cruelty, revenge — and its characters are 'larger than life'.

questions.question: Which everyday example does Gracia give as too insignificant ever to be the subject of a tragedy?
questions.explanation: Gracia's own examples are the sale of a van, mail delivery and non-fat yogurt. The distractors are genuine everyday examples — but from Scott's reading and the lecture, not Gracia — so recognition alone won't help.

questions.question: Gracia argues comedy 'dates more easily than tragedy' because:
options: A. Comedy is written down, whereas tragedy is performed live on stage
B. Tragedy, unlike comedy, deliberately strips out all emotion
C. Comedy simply becomes less popular with each new generation
D. Comedy leans on culture-specific customs; tragedy on a universal human core
questions.explanation: In tragedy (death, suffering, great vice and virtue) the shared core of human nature shows through, so it ages slowly; comedy's innocuous, culture-bound customs and idiosyncrasies date faster.

questions.question: The Seinfeld pitch 'it's a show about nothing' fits Gracia's argument because:
options: A. The show's significance lies precisely in bringing out overlooked everyday commonplaces
B. The characters are heroic figures larger than life
C. The show genuinely contains no social content
D. The show is really a tragedy in disguise
questions.explanation: Seinfeld's characters never think their doings are significant; the series draws out the commonplaces, underscoring their unnoticed relevance — comedy capturing the significance of the insignificant.

questions.question: Gracia stresses that his way of distinguishing the funny from the sad is:
options: A. A purely intellectual analysis carried out without feeling
B. A precise scientific formula that holds true universally
C. The single correct theory of humour, superseding all others
D. Just one way of seeing it — a matter of feeling, not scientific law
questions.explanation: Gracia explicitly disclaims perennial or scientific accuracy: laughing and crying are matters of emotion and feeling, of the heart, not of science and the intellect.

questions.question: The monobloc chair is manufactured by:
options: A. Building it up layer by layer with a 3D printer
C. Injection-moulding polypropylene heated to about 320 °C
D. Casting molten aluminium in a reusable sand mould
questions.explanation: The monobloc is injection-moulded from polypropylene granulate heated to ~320 °C and formed as one unbroken piece — hence 'mono-bloc'.

questions.question: Roughly how much does a single monobloc cost to manufacture?
questions.explanation: Each chair costs about US$3 to make and is usually sold for around US$10 — scalable production with little labour and low material cost.

questions.question: Ethan Zuckerman labelled the monobloc a:
questions.explanation: Zuckerman calls the monobloc a 'context-free object' — unlike most objects it gives no clue of time or place, marking it as a symbol of globalisation.

questions.question: Placing the chair in outdoor restaurant areas was for years forbidden by law in:
questions.explanation: In Basel, Switzerland the chair was banned from restaurants' outdoor areas because people said it destroyed the cityscape. (Denmark and Jerusalem are named as places the chair is found, not banned.)

questions.question: Defenders call the monobloc 'deeply democratic' because:
options: A. It can be fully recycled after use
B. Its affordability enables social equality and advancement
C. It is handmade by local craftspeople
D. It was created by a celebrated design studio
questions.explanation: The pro-monobloc argument is that its cheapness makes seating widely accessible, enabling social equality and economic advancement — 'deeply democratic'.

questions.question: The 1946 chair often credited as the first monobloc was designed by:
questions.explanation: Canadian designer D.C. Simpson made the arguable first monobloc in 1946, though moulding then wasn't suited to cheap mass production; Panton's stackable chair was the later technical predecessor.

questions.question: Regularly having breakfast at a set time with family is analysed sociologically as:
options: A. An example of quantitative research
B. A form of deviance from social norms
C. A purely biological need for morning energy
D. A ritual that builds a narrative of family life
questions.explanation: Done at a set time or with certain people, breakfast becomes a ritual/tradition that helps constitute family life and socialising.

questions.question: Choosing coffee or juice — not beer — with breakfast mainly shows that:
options: A. Breakfast has no social meaning at all
B. We are making a purely nutritional decision
C. Alcohol is banned everywhere in the morning
D. We follow social norms and avoid questionable choices
questions.explanation: Pairing breakfast with an 'acceptable' beverage shows we follow norms and avoid socially questionable choices — a beer at breakfast breaks the rule.

questions.question: In sociology, 'structure' refers to:
options: A. The social rules we largely conform to
B. An individual's freedom to act differently
C. A person's inherited biological traits
D. The physical buildings we occupy each day
questions.explanation: Structure is the social rules — from parents and teachers to the law — that most of us conform to most of the time.

questions.question: 'Agency' refers to:
options: A. The capacity to express individuality and challenge norms
B. A person's conformity to established tradition
