C. The social rules that constrain our behaviour
D. A branch of the federal government
questions.explanation: Agency is the individual's capacity to express individuality, think differently and challenge restrictive norms (within the law).

questions.question: Someone who refuses to conform to social structure is typically labelled:
questions.explanation: Those who don't conform to social rules are often seen as deviant.

questions.question: For Mills, blaming an unemployed person for 'laziness':
options: A. Mistakes a public issue for a private trouble
C. Correctly identifies the true cause
D. Is a good example of personal agency
questions.explanation: Unemployment is shaped by social forces (the job market, offshoring, AI); blaming the individual misreads a public issue as a purely private trouble.

questions.question: Participant observation, ethnography and focus groups are examples of:
questions.explanation: These are qualitative methods — they capture the depth and quality of participants' experience of the social world.

questions.question: The Australian census is used as an example of:
questions.explanation: The census is quantitative — a large-sample survey producing statistics, trends and snapshots of a changing society.

questions.question: The lecture argues that a person's class:
options: A. Is fixed entirely by their annual income
B. Is not just wealth but also taste and status
C. Has little bearing on everyday life
D. Is identical to their current job title
questions.explanation: The same income can carry very different tastes; class is not just wealth but also status and taste, so it needs more than a dollar figure.

questions.question: The idea that taste and lifestyle act as a marker of status is captured by the concept of:
questions.explanation: Taste as a status marker is the idea of cultural capital — the concept behind the sample quiz question 'who coined cultural capital?' (Bourdieu).

questions.question: The 'I love you return' and the search for the right gift in Seinfeld both illustrate:
options: A. The strengths of quantitative research
B. Reflexivity about unwritten social rules
D. Structural inequality in health care
questions.explanation: Both storylines make the characters monitor and question the unwritten rules of etiquette (reciprocation, gift-giving) — reflexivity.

questions.question: The unit's multiple-choice quiz is described as:
questions.explanation: The quiz is 60 multiple-choice questions, open book, testing attendance and the readings.

questions.question: Medicine's monopoly of expert knowledge over the human body is referred to as:
questions.explanation: The 'unseen dentist' joke introduces medicalisation — the way medicine holds a monopoly of knowledge over the body and health.

soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.title: SOCI1010 W2 · The Meaning of Everyday Life
soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.content: SOCI1010 Week 2 'The Meaning of Everyday Life' (A/Prof Selvaraj Velayutham) + essential reading Inglis, 'Modern Culture and Everyday Life' Ch.2. DEFINING: everyday life is NOT confined to important moments/events/festivities/holidays/the profane/'ordinary' people/private life; in its WIDE meaning it includes profane AND sacred, private AND public, all walks of life (COVID = a 'new normal'). SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS: (1) repetitive but punctuated by the unpredictable — repetition forms identity, 'we become who we are through acts of repetition' (Durkheim), and can enable creativity; (2) synonymous with habit — habit = action + attitude; Mauss 'techniques of the body' (squatting vs sitting mankind, people with/without chairs; bodily habits 'assembled by and for social authority'); Mauss coined HABITUS, developed by Bourdieu as 'durable dispositions' shaped by class & gender, taught by imitation; (3) spaces of familiarity — home as the privileged base; Giddens' ONTOLOGICAL SECURITY (trust in the world giving stability/continuity to identity); (4) the feel of 'normality'; (5) secular & democratic — no one escapes it, 'even the Queen'; (6) feels natural but is political (lecture room; gendered family home); (7) has a history — intellectual history (Goffman, Garfinkel, Durkheim, Simmel, Lefebvre, Bourdieu, Mauss, Douglas, Elias, Weber, Marx) and, per Lefebvre, emerges as a 'social category' with modernity (visible in 19th-c capitalism/industrialization; today exploded via social media). THE POLITICS OF WAITING: the bus stop as street furniture/corporate space (JCDecaux, Adshel)/social space; low-status, embodies social difference; unequal public spending (car-dependent Western Sydney); privatization/commercialization of public space; ads contested (Brandalism Project); counter-case = affordable/efficient/cuts congestion/climate. THE SOCIOLOGY OF THE QUEUE: an 'embryonic social system' (pattern of order, violation punishable); self-managed by the individual AND the queue-community; Goffman — the individual regulates their actions before others' eyes; a moral order / 'queue ethics'; types (physical, virtual, mobile, informal, regulated); Schwartz (1975); the Saarbrücken experiment — a single feeder line is faster and FEELS fairer than one-line-per-desk (fairness is designed). SITUATING THE EVERYDAY IN MODERNITY (Inglis): everyday activities are 'expressive of modernity'; method = DENATURALIZE the everyday ('a fish in its own cultural water'). Pre-modern (providence/religion/tradition) -> modern (progress/science/rationality); drivers = Enlightenment (17-18th c), industrialization, capitalism, the democratic state. MODERNIZATION (the process — weakening of traditional patterns) vs MODERNITY (the society born of industrialization/urbanization). Signature (Hall et al): rationality, routinization, market society, individualism. THE RATIONALIZATION OF EVERYDAY LIFE (Weber): modern West uniquely rational; ZWECKRATIONAL (efficient means to an end, e.g. business/profit) vs WERTRATIONAL (an ultimate moral/spiritual value). Protestant Ethic & the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) — capitalism's religious origins; the 'disenchantment of the world'. Authority: tradition/religion -> LEGAL-RATIONAL AUTHORITY (systematic application of rules) -> BUREAUCRACY ('control through regulations'); we obey the ROLE not the person (tax inspector, schoolteacher); officials as 'embodied rules'; bureaucracy colonizes everyday life. PROFESSIONALIZATION (only credentialed experts; the fake-doctor outrage). The IRON CAGE ('specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart'). Ritzer's McDonaldization: efficiency, predictability, calculability, dehumanization/control. RATIONALIZING EMOTIONS/MONEY/SPACE: Hochschild's FEELING RULES (airline staff drilled to be upbeat; emotion bureaucratized); Merton's ROLE AMBIVALENCE (doctor = detached scientist vs caring carer). Simmel's MONEY MENTALITY — money is impersonal & universalizing, judging by quantity not quality; relationships become monetary transactions (cashier, bank clerk); the 'have a nice day' veneer. Rationalizing space: Eichberg (pre-modern loose ball-games -> standardized rule-governed pitches for 'goal results'/'tension', commercialized); Lefebvre (car culture colonizes the city into 'geometric space'); Augé (motorways bypass places -> places become 'names/signs'). CULTURE & CHAOS (modernity is dualistic): Marx — 'all that is solid melts into air' (constant flux). Simmel — the metropolis bombards with stimuli, so the BLASÉ ATTITUDE blocks it out; the bigger the crowd the lonelier one feels; the 'leave me alone' city code. REVOLT INTO STYLE — rationalization (conform) vs individualization (cult of the unique self); style is a group-based 'individuality off the peg' (goths, subcultures, lifestyles); uniqueness is the flip side of sameness (the same designer dress). AUTHENTICITY & THE (POST/LATE) MODERN: INVENTED TRADITIONS (Hobsbawm & Ranger) — the Victorian 'traditional Christmas', 'timeless' Scottish tartan/bagpipes. TOURISM — the search for the authentic/exotic that destroys what it seeks (fishing village commodifies its culture); traveller vs tourist. The POST-TOURIST knowingly/ironically embraces the fake — post-modernity (Lyotard) / late modernity (Giddens); irony, knowingness, self-consciousness; pastiche/parody/bricolage (Jameson; Tarantino); Eco's 'As Barbara Cartland would put it, I love you madly'. Point: DENATURALIZE the everyday — our 'normal' is a peculiar, historically specific product of modernity (rationalization + chaos).

questions.question: In its wide meaning, everyday life includes:
options: A. Only mundane, profane and repetitive daily activities
B. Sacred and profane, private and public, and people of all kinds
C. Only major public events, festivities and holidays
D. Only the private routines of so-called ordinary people
questions.explanation: The wide definition refuses to confine the everyday to the trivial or private — it spans profane and sacred, private and public, and people from all walks of life.

questions.question: Which is offered as an example of a 'new everyday' or 'new normal'?
questions.explanation: Life under COVID becoming the 'new normal' shows how the everyday itself can be reshaped.

questions.question: The claim that 'we become who we are through acts of repetition' is credited to:
questions.explanation: For Durkheim, repetition is not mere boredom but key to the gradual formation of social identity — and can even enable creativity.

questions.question: Mauss's 'techniques of the body' (squatting vs sitting mankind) makes the point that:
options: A. Even bodily habits are learned and socially shaped
B. Ways of moving are the same in every society
C. The body is shaped by climate, not culture
D. Posture is determined by human genetics
questions.explanation: Mauss showed that how we hold and use our bodies is 'assembled by and for social authority' — bodily habits are cultural, not natural.

questions.question: The term 'habitus' was coined by Mauss and developed as 'durable dispositions' by:
questions.explanation: Bourdieu developed habitus as 'durable dispositions' — acquired, class- and gender-shaped ways of acting taught by imitation.

questions.question: For Bourdieu, our habitus (durable dispositions) is most strongly shaped by:
questions.explanation: Habitus is strongly influenced by class and gender and reaches into eating, home decoration and the TV we watch.

questions.question: Giddens's 'ontological security' refers to:
options: A. Complete certainty about religious and moral truth
B. Trust in the world that lends stability and continuity to identity
C. Having a home that is physically safe from crime
D. A comfortable level of financial security in old age
questions.explanation: Ontological security is the confidence/trust we have in the things and people we share our lives with — anchored in the home, it grounds a stable identity.

questions.question: Everyday life is called a 'democratic' concept because:
options: A. It treats everyone's tastes as equal
B. Everyone gets a vote on how it is run
C. No one escapes it — everyone eats and sleeps, 'even the Queen'
D. It is decided by majority rule
questions.explanation: In modernity the everyday is secular and democratic in the sense that all are anchored in the mundane world — no one is exempt.

questions.question: The everyday 'feels natural but is actually political' is best illustrated by:
options: A. The gendered spaces of the home and the layout of the lecture room
B. The basic human biology of hunger and sleep
C. The natural changing of the weather and the seasons
D. The physical laws that govern motion and gravity
questions.explanation: Spaces that feel neutral — the home, the lecture room — are in fact inhabited and shaped by power (gender hierarchies, teacher-student relations).

questions.question: According to Lefebvre, the everyday emerged as a 'social category' with:
questions.explanation: Lefebvre dates the visibility of the everyday to modernity: as bodies massed in cities under capitalism, new attention fell on the uniform, repetitive acts of life.

questions.question: Firms such as JCDecaux and Adshel, which build and own bus shelters, illustrate:
options: A. The rise of private car culture
B. The decline of the advertising industry
C. The privatization and commercialization of public space
D. The public funding of transport
questions.explanation: Advertising firms owning the shelters turns public space into commercialized private/public space — the privatization of public services.

questions.question: The bus stop is said to 'embody social difference' because:
options: A. Everyone in a city waits equally
B. Waiting for the bus is unequally distributed and low-status
C. Buses always run on strict timetables
D. Shelters are designed differently in each suburb
questions.explanation: Who waits, and where, is patterned by class and status; the bus stop is unglamorous and disempowering, tied to unequal public spending (e.g. car-dependent Western Sydney).

questions.question: The Brandalism Project, which subverts bus-shelter advertising, raises the question of:
questions.explanation: Altering corporate ads in public space poses the question of whether such acts are vandalism or a form of social activism.

questions.question: Sociologically, a queue is best described as:
options: A. An embryonic social system whose violation is punishable
D. A random collection of strangers
questions.explanation: A queue is a small but real pattern of social order; jumping it (violation) is punishable — yet no official enforces it.

questions.question: Goffman's point about the queue is that:
options: A. An official is needed to enforce the proper order
B. Queues are inherently unfair to those at the back
C. People in a queue act with no awareness of others
D. The individual must regulate their conduct before others' eyes
questions.explanation: For Goffman, members regulate themselves before others' eyes, which serve as an informal government of conduct.

questions.question: Order in a queue is maintained:
options: A. Only by written, posted rules
C. By no one at all
D. By the individual and collectively by the 'queue-community'
questions.explanation: The queue is self-managed at two levels — the individual and the collective queue-community — producing a moral order from within.

questions.question: The Saarbrücken queue experiment found that a single feeder line (versus one line per desk):
options: A. Is faster and feels fairer, so people are less grumpy
B. Is slower but more orderly
D. Is fairer but much slower
questions.explanation: A single serpentine queue feeding all desks saved ~half a minute per person and, crucially, felt fairer — fairness is designed.

questions.question: Inglis's method for studying the everyday is to:
options: A. Predict how it will change
B. Celebrate it as natural and universal
C. Denaturalize it — show our 'normal' is peculiar and specific
D. Quantify it with large surveys
questions.explanation: Inglis argues we live 'like a fish in our own cultural water'; the task is to denaturalize the everyday and see how strange our 'normal' really is.

questions.question: 'Modernization' refers to:
options: A. The process by which traditional patterns of living weaken
B. The spread of the internet
C. The society born of industrialization and urbanization
D. The growth of cities alone
questions.explanation: Modernization is the process (the weakening of traditional patterns and worldviews); modernity is the resulting society.

questions.question: 'Modernity' refers to:
options: A. A distinctive style of art and architecture
B. The philosophy developed during the Enlightenment
C. The gradual weakening of traditional patterns of living
D. The society that came into being with industrialization and urbanization
questions.explanation: Modernity is the society that emerged with industrialization and urbanization; modernization is the process that produced it.

questions.question: According to Hall et al, the cultural signature of the modern everyday is:
options: A. Leisure, festivity, sacredness and locality
B. Magic, ritual, kinship and myth
C. Rationality, routinization, market society and individualism
D. Tradition, religion, community and hierarchy
questions.explanation: As cities grew, culture and everyday life were altered by a growth in rationality, routinization, market society and individualism.

questions.question: The shift from pre-modern to modern society replaced providence and religion with:
options: B. Community, locality and the sacred
questions.explanation: Modernity substitutes progress, science and rationality for the older worldview of providence and religion.

questions.question: For Weber, what makes modern Western culture unique is:
options: C. Its exceptionally high level of rationality
questions.explanation: Weber held that no other society has been so organised around rational procedures — rationality is modernity's distinctive feature.

questions.question: Zweckrational action is oriented to:
options: A. The free expression of emotion
B. The most efficient means to a given end
C. An ultimate moral or spiritual value
questions.explanation: Zweckrational (instrumental) action calculates the most efficient means to a goal — the typical mode of the capitalist economy.

questions.question: Wertrational action is oriented to:
options: C. An ultimate value, moral or spiritual
D. The efficient means to an end
questions.explanation: Wertrational (value-rational) action works toward an ultimate value — like the devout believer acting to glorify God.

questions.question: In 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism', Weber located capitalism's origins in:
options: A. The protestant ethic and religious ideas
questions.explanation: Weber traced capitalism to religious ideas — the protestant valuing of hard work, all work as holy, and the disenchantment of the world.

questions.question: Weber's 'disenchantment of the world' means:
options: B. The loss of political freedom
C. The decline of the arts
D. The retreat of magic and miracle before science and rationality
questions.explanation: Disenchantment is the withdrawal of magical/miraculous belief as science and rational calculation take over.

questions.question: Weber's 'legal-rational authority' means people are governed by:
options: B. The systematic application of rules and procedures
C. The personal charisma of leaders
questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority replaces tradition and religion; power flows through impersonal rules and procedures, whose archetype is bureaucracy.

questions.question: The word 'bureaucracy' literally means:
options: A. Control through the use of regulations
B. Power exercised without any rules
D. Rule by officials' personal whims
questions.explanation: Bureaucracy is 'control through regulations' — the characteristic form domination takes in modernity.

questions.question: Weber's key insight about paying a tax inspector is that:
options: A. We obey the person's personal charisma
B. We obey out of religious duty
C. We obey the role and its rules, not the person
D. We obey out of long-standing tradition
questions.explanation: In a bureaucratic culture it is the role (tax inspector, schoolteacher) and its rules that command authority, not the individual occupying it.

questions.question: The horror provoked by an unqualified 'fake doctor' reflects:
options: A. The spread of the money mentality
C. The deep professionalization of modern work
questions.explanation: Only credentialed 'experts' are deemed competent; the outrage at a fake doctor shows how deeply professionalization runs in modern work culture.

questions.question: Weber's 'iron cage' describes modernity as:
options: A. A society of constant, dizzying change
B. A nostalgic return to tradition
C. A bloodless, over-rationalized world stripped of spiritual meaning
D. A prison created by mass poverty
questions.explanation: The iron cage is Weber's pessimistic image of a hyper-rational, bureaucratized world — 'specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart'.

questions.question: Hochschild's 'feeling rules' refer to:
options: A. Personal moral principles about feelings
B. The private feelings of managers
C. Workplace prescriptions for which emotions staff must display
questions.explanation: Feeling rules are the prescribed, predictable emotions demanded of workers (e.g. cabin crew's friendliness) — emotion itself bureaucratized.

questions.question: The doctor's 'role ambivalence' (Merton) is the tension between:
options: A. Being a detached scientist and a caring carer
B. Earning money and helping people
C. Following rules and breaking them
questions.explanation: Role ambivalence is the contradiction between the detached, dispassionate diagnostician and the warm, caring functionary — both demanded by the medical bureaucracy.

questions.question: For Simmel, money reshapes social relations because it is:
options: A. Rooted in tradition and kinship
B. Personal and exclusive, based on trust
C. Impersonal and universalizing, breeding calculation by quantity
D. Irrational and driven by emotion
questions.explanation: Money is impersonal and universalizing; it makes us judge things and people by quantity, not quality, turning encounters into monetary transactions.

questions.question: Eichberg's account of modern sport shows that:
options: A. Sport became steadily less commercial over time
B. Pitches shrank for no particular reason
C. Games gradually lost all of their rules
D. Loose pre-modern games became standardized, rule-governed pitches
questions.explanation: Pre-modern ball-games played across open land became demarcated, standardized pitches engineered for 'goal results' and 'tension' — a rationalization of space.

questions.question: Augé argues that motorway travel makes places:
options: A. Slower and harder to reach than before
B. Centres of local community life
C. Mere names and signs flashing by, bypassed for speed
D. Richer and more vivid to experience
questions.explanation: Motorways bypass the towns they name for the sake of speed, so places become abstract signs — space is flattened and depersonalized (Augé, extending Lefebvre).

questions.question: 'All that is solid melts into air' is Marx's image for:
options: A. The slow decline of organised traditional religion
B. The steady rise of rational modern bureaucracy
C. Modernity's constant flux, destroying what once seemed solid
D. The choking pollution of the new industrial cities
questions.explanation: Marx captured modernity's ceaseless upheaval — capitalist society lets nothing remain stable or secure for long.

questions.question: Simmel's 'blasé attitude' is:
options: A. An aggressive, fearful hostility toward all strangers
B. A protective detachment that screens out the city's stimuli
C. A deep sense of religious calm and peace
D. A naive, wide-eyed excitement at big-city life
questions.explanation: The blasé attitude is the 'seen it all' detachment that lets the city dweller cope with a bombardment of stimuli.

questions.question: Simmel's paradox of the metropolis is that:
options: A. The bigger the crowd, the lonelier one can feel
B. Isolation only happens in the countryside
C. Cities are always friendlier than villages
D. Crowds make people more sociable
questions.explanation: Confronted with a vast array of strangers, the individual withdraws into themselves — hence loneliness amid the crowd, and the 'leave me alone' city code.

questions.question: Style is called 'individuality off the peg' because:
options: A. A subculture lets you look distinctive while belonging to a group
B. It rejects all group membership
C. It is entirely unique to each single person
D. Fashionable clothes are cheap to buy
questions.explanation: Subcultures and lifestyles let you appear distinctive without inventing yourself from scratch — different enough to stand out, similar enough to belong.

questions.question: The horror of two women arriving in the same designer dress illustrates that:
options: C. Uniqueness is the other side of the coin from sameness
D. Fashion has no social meaning
questions.explanation: Taste and style make us different from some others but uncomfortably like others — a central paradox of modern individuality.

questions.question: An 'invented tradition' (Hobsbawm and Ranger) is:
options: A. A custom imported from another country
B. A recent practice presented as if it were ancient
C. An old custom that has died out
D. A law passed by parliament
questions.explanation: Invented traditions are quite recent inventions dressed up as timeless — offered to a public craving stability amid change.

questions.question: Which is given as an example of an invented tradition?
questions.explanation: The 'traditional family Christmas' of trees, cards and Santa is a Victorian invention, little more than 150 years old; 'timeless' Scottish tartan is likewise 19th-century.

questions.question: The paradox of mass tourism is that:
options: A. Tourism is too expensive for most people
B. Tourists prefer to stay in their own culture
C. Travel never changes anyone at all
D. Tourists destroy the authentic culture they come to find
questions.explanation: Seeking 'unspoiled' authenticity, tourists remake places around the tourist dollar, commodifying the very culture they came for.

questions.question: The 'post-tourist':
options: A. Knowingly and ironically embraces the fake, pre-packaged experience
B. Refuses to travel at all
C. Insists on finding the truly authentic
D. Travels only to unspoilt places
questions.explanation: The post-tourist accepts that no uncommodified 'reality' is left and enjoys the ironies of the fabricated experience — emblematic of post/late modernity.

questions.question: Eco's line 'As Barbara Cartland would put it, I love you madly' illustrates:
options: A. Sincerity smuggled back through self-conscious irony
C. The persuasive power of advertising
D. The sincerity of traditional romance
questions.explanation: When plain words sound like clichés, one recovers sincerity by ironically flagging the cliché — the knowing self-consciousness of late/post-modern culture.

questions.question: Post-modernity (Lyotard) and late modernity (Giddens) both describe a culture of:
questions.explanation: Whether called post-modern or late modern, the culture is marked by irony, knowingness and self-consciousness — pastiche, parody and bricolage (Jameson).

soci1010_wk3_not_so_mundane.html.title: SOCI1010 W3 · Not So Mundane — Theorising the Everyday
soci1010_wk3_not_so_mundane.html.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk3_not_so_mundane.html.content: SOCI1010 Week 3 'Not So Mundane' (A/Prof Selvaraj Velayutham) + readings (Susie Scott 2009 'Re-clothing the Emperor: The Swimming Pool as a Negotiated Order'; Goffman 1959). WHY THEORISE THE EVERYDAY: Highmore ('what's going on when nothing much is happening?'), Finkelstein (the taken-for-granted is the most interesting thing about us); Scott's warning — routine/familiar sites are NOT devoid of political interests, ideologies, subtle social control. Reasons: Durkheim's MORAL CONSENSUS (society's smooth functioning), hidden rules, the everyday as a site of conflict (class/gender/race/sexuality), the sociological imagination. REFLEXIVITY: people are shaped by interaction AND shape it (workplace-dress example). SZTOMPKA'S 5 POINTS to analyse a social event: (1) participants & roles — co-presence (direct face-to-face vs distant/mediated: phone/internet/social media), number of participants matters (dyad vs crowd, turn-taking); (2) the immediate situation — bystanders/witnesses distinguish PUBLIC from PRIVATE (lower our voice among strangers; crowds inflame conduct); (3) the wider social context (family/work/consumption/education/religion/leisure/sport — each demands different behaviour); (4) locales/arenas (similar content — library=read, worship=pray, street=walk/shop); (5) complex configurations following procedures (wedding, funeral, surgery, lecture). RITES OF PASSAGE mark context transitions (slippers at home, logging on at work; 'how's it going?'/'see you later'). RITUAL = when HOW something is done matters more than WHAT; Billig's BANAL NATIONALISM (flag-raising). PROJECTS = multi-step everyday journeys (a degree, a career). THE FOOTPATH: Nicholas Blomley 'Rights of Passage: Sidewalks and the Regulation of Public Flow'; footpaths historically recent (Melbourne 1863; proliferated with the car). PEDESTRIANISM = the unspoken logic prioritising smooth movement (A to B) over democratic assembly; sidewalk = finite public resource / transport corridor. Consequences: loiterers moved on ('visual clutter'/obstruction), cafés need permits for chairs, no cycling; protest that halts flow treated like stalled traffic. Never neutral: JIM CROW etiquette (1877-1950s) required Black pedestrians to step off the walk / 'give whites the wall'. LSE 'Ordinary Streets' study of Rye Lane, Peckham — URBAN MUTUALISM (a shop subdivided into tiny units; a migrant starts at a 1-metre table and ends up owning the building) vs GENTRIFICATION. MAX WEBER (1864-1920): The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism — Calvinist values (hard work, discipline, self-control, frugality, duty/calling) ALIGNED WITH (did NOT cause) capitalism. RATIONALISATION = modern life organised around calculation/efficiency/rules; four dimensions — EFFICIENCY, PREDICTABILITY, CALCULABILITY, DEHUMANISATION/CONTROL. BUREAUCRACY = rationalisation's highest form; five features — (1) formal rules & procedures, (2) hierarchy of authority, (3) specialisation, (4) impersonality (universal rules, no favouritism, often not even a person), (5) records/documentation; we obey the ROLE not the person. THE IRON CAGE = the 'irrationality of rationality'; over-rationalisation imprisons (bank-card runaround). Rationalisation of space (home, stadium vs pre-modern church). ARLIE HOCHSCHILD: The Managed Heart (1983); EMOTIONAL LABOUR = 'the management of feeling to create a publicly observable facial and bodily display; sold for a wage and therefore has exchange value' — workers manage their emotions to produce a desired state in customers/clients/patients. DISPLAY RULES (organisationally prescribed) vs FEELING RULES (broader societal norms). SURFACE ACTING (outward expression only — smile over annoyance) vs DEEP ACTING (try to actually feel it). Why it matters: work intensification, the AUTHENTICITY DILEMMA (genuine self vs work self), occupational health (emotional exhaustion, burnout, depersonalisation — esp. care work). GEORG SIMMEL (1858-1918): study the FORMS (kinds) of interaction not content ('only specific kinds of interaction'); bottom-up; the NUMBER of parties matters (dyad vs triad). Three studies — THE STRANGER (near and far at once); METROPOLIS AND MENTAL LIFE (overstimulation forces the BLASÉ ATTITUDE & reserve; anonymity frees individuality/subcultures yet makes standing out hard and isolates); THE PHILOSOPHY OF MONEY (money makes ties instrumental/calculable, reduces QUALITY TO QUANTITY, freedom at the cost of fragmentation/alienation). HENRI LEFEBVRE (1901-1991, Marxist): the everyday dismissed as trivial since the Enlightenment (which prized 'higher' reason). THE PRODUCTION OF SPACE (1974) — space is socially PRODUCED, not neutral. SPATIAL TRIAD: spatial practice (materially produced), representations of space (abstractly conceived/planned by engineers), representational spaces (lived/phenomenological). Capitalism produces ABSTRACT SPACE dominated by planners & privatisation (the drive-through), organised for productive consumption over community. MICHEL FOUCAULT (1926-1984): genealogy; Discipline and Punish — power shifts from VISIBLE public torture (power outside the body, the king's spectacle) to the PRISON/PANOPTICON (a central watchtower from which one MIGHT be seen). Because you never know if you're watched, you INTERNALISE the gaze and SELF-DISCIPLINE; power becomes invisible & productive not merely repressive (the classroom). Also discourse, biopower, governmentality. HAROLD GARFINKEL: ETHNOMETHODOLOGY (Studies in Ethnomethodology, 1967) — ethno=people, method=means, ology=study of; how people make sense of the potential chaos of social life; order APPEARS given but is continually created & re-created; reflexivity & agency. BREACHING EXPERIMENTS = deliberately break a rule of interaction to expose it (Case 6: over-answering 'How are you?'; standing too close in a queue; sitting beside a stranger on a half-empty bus; slamming a door). FORMAL norms (written) vs INFORMAL norms (unwritten). SYMBOLIC INTERACTIONISM (Chicago School, 1960s): people act toward things on the basis of MEANINGS, which arise from INTERACTION and are modified through INTERPRETATION; rely on SYMBOLS; reflect on themselves to shape action. ERVING GOFFMAN (1922-1982): DRAMATURGY — The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959); social life as theatre, performance of ROLES on STAGES. FRONT STAGE (perform to an audience — attentive waiter) vs BACK STAGE (out of role — the kitchen); IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT; the INTERACTION ORDER (face-to-face co-presence, studied by micro-analysis). INTERACTIVE RITUALS — extending Durkheim (Elementary Forms; sacred/profane), Goffman treats ALL interaction as ritual (greetings repeat & have explicit rules; the Curb 'dismissive bow' — wrong depth = 'not sorry at all'). READING — Susie Scott (2009) 'Re-clothing the Emperor': the swimming pool as a NEGOTIATED ORDER (Strauss) / POLITE FICTION nobody names; three tacit norms — respect for personal space, respect for individuals' disciplinary regimes ('body projects'/lane discipline), and the DESEXUALISATION of encounters; like the emperor's subjects, swimmers can't consciously attend to the precarious reality they co-construct yet stay poised to defend it. THEME: the world is not natural/inevitable but socially constructed — theory makes it visible.

questions.question: Susie Scott's Week-3 warning about everyday sites is that:
options: A. They are essentially identical across every human culture
B. They are governed purely by unconstrained individual choice
C. Routine and familiarity do not free them from power or control
D. They are far too trivial to reward any serious study
questions.explanation: Scott warns that although everyday sites are marked by repetition, routine and familiarity, they still carry political interests, ideologies and subtle forms of social control.

questions.question: The shared norms essential to society's smooth functioning were called 'moral consensus' by:
questions.explanation: Understanding how society functions draws on Durkheim's idea of moral consensus. The distractors are other Week-3 theorists used for different concepts.

questions.question: 'Reflexivity', as used in the lecture, means that:
options: A. People simply obey the rules society hands them
B. People are shaped by interaction and also shape it in turn
C. Society is fixed and cannot be changed by individuals
D. Individuals act entirely free of any social influence
questions.explanation: Reflexivity is the two-way loop: interaction shapes people's thoughts and identities, and their thoughts and actions reshape the interaction (the workplace-dress example).

questions.question: Which is one of Sztompka's five points for analysing a social event?
options: A. The economic cost of the event
B. The historical century in which it occurs
C. The personality type of each participant
D. The presence of bystanders, which distinguishes public from private
questions.explanation: Sztompka's five: participants/roles; the immediate situation (bystanders → public vs private); wider social context; locales/arenas; complex configurations.

questions.question: A face-to-face conversation and an exchange over social media differ mainly in that the latter is:
options: A. Never governed by any social rules
B. Distant and mediated rather than co-present
questions.explanation: Sztompka's first point distinguishes direct face-to-face co-presence from distant, mediated interaction (phone, internet, social media).

questions.question: Putting on slippers when you get home and logging on when you reach work are examples of:
options: B. Instances of paid emotional labour
C. Rites of passage that mark a change of context
D. Formal steps in a bureaucratic procedure
questions.explanation: Small daily rituals mark transitions between one context and another; entry/exit phrases ('how's it going?' / 'see you later') do similar work.

questions.question: Michael Billig's 'banal nationalism' refers to:
options: A. An aggressive, militant nationalist political movement
B. The heroic founding myths taught to schoolchildren
C. The everyday, unnoticed reproduction of national belonging
D. Official government national economic policy
questions.explanation: Banal nationalism is the routine, taken-for-granted marking of the nation in everyday life — e.g. the raising of a flag.

questions.question: Nicholas Blomley's term 'pedestrianism' describes the sidewalk's governing logic as:
options: A. A privately owned commercial zone
B. Prioritising smooth movement over democratic assembly
C. A space of free political expression
D. A purely decorative civic feature
questions.explanation: Pedestrianism treats the sidewalk as a finite public resource / transport corridor whose golden rule is unhindered passage from A to B, over assembly or protest.

questions.question: Under 'pedestrianism', people standing around on the footpath are likely to be:
options: A. Given priority over moving pedestrians
B. Charged a fee to remain
C. Moved on as obstruction or 'visual clutter'
D. Encouraged to gather and protest
questions.explanation: Because the golden rule is unhindered flow, loiterers 'without authorization' can be told to move on; cafés even need permits for chairs.

questions.question: Under Jim Crow segregation, the footpath encoded racial order by requiring Black pedestrians to:
options: A. Pay to use the footpath
C. Step off the sidewalk or 'give whites the wall'
questions.explanation: Jim Crow racial etiquette (1877–1950s) required Black pedestrians to give way — showing public space is never neutral.

questions.question: The 'urban mutualism' seen on Rye Lane, Peckham refers to:
options: B. A single shop subdivided into several small compatible units
questions.explanation: Urban mutualism = subdividing a shop into tiny compatible spaces (a migrant starts at a 1-metre table and grows), set against gentrification pressures.

questions.question: Weber's argument in 'The Protestant Ethic' is that Protestant values:
options: A. Aligned with and encouraged a mindset suited to capitalism
B. Actively opposed the rise of capitalism
C. Directly caused capitalism to appear
D. Had no relationship to economic life
questions.explanation: Weber does not claim Protestantism caused capitalism; its values (hard work, discipline, frugality, calling) fostered an attitude that aligned with capitalism's rise.

questions.question: Which is one of Weber's four dimensions of rationalisation?
options: B. Calculability — a concern with numerical data
D. Charisma — the pull of a leader
questions.explanation: The four dimensions are efficiency, predictability, calculability, and dehumanisation/control.

questions.question: In Weber's bureaucracy, we obey a tax official or clerk because of:
options: A. The remarkable personal charisma they happen to possess
B. The role they occupy and its rules, not the person
C. A binding sense of sacred religious duty
D. A long-standing and deeply inherited tradition
questions.explanation: Bureaucratic authority is impersonal: it attaches to the role and its formal rules, not to the individual.

questions.question: Which is one of the five features of bureaucracy?
options: A. An absence of written records
B. A clear hierarchy of authority
C. Decisions based on personal friendship
questions.explanation: The five features: formal rules/procedures, hierarchy of authority, specialisation, impersonality, and records/documentation.

questions.question: Weber's 'iron cage' names the danger that:
options: B. Over-rationalisation imprisons people — the irrationality of rationality
C. Society will return to tradition
D. Bureaucracy will collapse into chaos
questions.explanation: The iron cage is the 'irrationality of rationality' — rules meant to serve efficiency end up trapping the person (the bank-card runaround).

questions.question: Arlie Hochschild's 'emotional labour' is:
options: A. The unpaid domestic care work done at home
B. The private, unpaid management of personal grief
C. Managing one's feelings to create a required paid display
D. The sheer physical effort involved in manual work
questions.explanation: Emotional labour (The Managed Heart, 1983) is the management of feeling to create a publicly observable display, sold for a wage — so it has exchange value.

questions.question: The difference between 'display rules' and 'feeling rules' is that:
options: A. Display rules come from society; feeling rules from the worker
B. Display rules are set by the organisation; feeling rules by society
C. Display rules apply only when one is outside work
D. They are simply two different names for one thing
questions.explanation: Display rules are organisationally prescribed (how you must express emotion); feeling rules are broader societal norms about what one should feel.

questions.question: Plastering on a smile while feeling annoyed is Hochschild's:
questions.explanation: Surface acting modifies only the outward expression; deep acting is trying to actually feel the required emotion.

questions.question: The 'authenticity dilemma' of emotional labour is the tension between:
options: A. Surface acting and display rules
C. The genuine self and the work self
questions.explanation: Emotional labour can open a gap between one's genuine self and the self required by the job — alongside work intensification and burnout.

questions.question: Simmel argued sociology should study:
options: A. The natural laws governing society
B. The forms of interaction rather than their content
D. The economic base of society
questions.explanation: Simmel stressed studying the forms (kinds) of social relationship, working bottom-up from small-scale interaction.

questions.question: For Simmel, a two-person interaction (a dyad) differs from a three-person one because:
options: B. Only groups of three can have conflict
C. The content of talk is identical in both
D. The number of parties changes the nature of the interaction
questions.explanation: Simmel noticed the number of parties itself shapes interaction — a dyad differs from a triad or larger group.

questions.question: Simmel's figure of 'the Stranger' captures someone who is:
options: C. Both near and far at the same time
D. Permanently excluded from the group
questions.explanation: The Stranger combines distance and closeness — near and far at once — a distinct role in modern social life.

questions.question: Simmel's 'blasé attitude' is a response to:
options: B. The demands of emotional labour
C. The overstimulation of city life
D. The intimacy of village life
questions.explanation: In 'Metropolis and Mental Life', the city's bombardment of stimuli forces a protective, numbed detachment — the blasé attitude — and reserve.

questions.question: For Simmel, urban anonymity is double-edged because it:
options: A. Makes everyone in the city behave in identical ways
B. Frees individuality yet isolates and hides one in the crowd
C. Completely eliminates every social rule and norm
D. Guarantees strong and lasting local community ties
questions.explanation: Anonymity releases varied identities and subcultures, but if everyone is unusual it's hard to stand out — and reserve isolates people in the crowd.

questions.question: In 'The Philosophy of Money', Simmel argues money:
options: A. Makes ties instrumental, reducing quality to quantity
B. Strengthens deep personal and emotional bonds
C. Restores the lost intimacy of close village life
D. Leaves the way we relate to others quite unchanged
questions.explanation: Money makes ties calculable and instrumental (the 'hi, latte, bye'), reducing quality to quantity — freedom gained at the cost of fragmentation.

questions.question: In 'The Production of Space', Lefebvre's central claim is that space is:
options: A. Purely a matter of individual perception
D. Socially produced, not a neutral container
questions.explanation: Lefebvre argues space is socially produced through a triad of practices, and is shaped by capitalism and power — not neutral.

questions.question: In Lefebvre's spatial triad, the planners' and engineers' abstract conception of space is:
questions.explanation: The triad: spatial practice (materially produced), representations of space (abstractly conceived — the planners' view), representational spaces (lived experience).

questions.question: The drive-through is used to illustrate Lefebvre's idea of:
options: C. Abstract space produced for capitalist consumption over community
questions.explanation: The drive-through is single-purpose 'abstract space' — planner-dominated, privatised, organised for productive consumption rather than community.

questions.question: In 'Discipline and Punish', Foucault charts a shift from public torture to the prison, in which power becomes:
options: B. Held only by the monarch
D. Invisible and internalised, so we discipline ourselves
questions.explanation: Medieval torture put power outside the body and made it visible; the modern prison makes power invisible, so people internalise the gaze and self-discipline.

questions.question: The panopticon disciplines people because they:
options: A. Are rewarded for good behaviour
B. Are punished publicly for every error
C. Never know whether they are being watched, so they regulate themselves
D. Are physically restrained at all times
questions.explanation: The central watchtower means one might always be observed; uncertainty leads people to internalise the gaze and self-discipline (the classroom example).

questions.question: For Foucault, power in modern society is best described as:
options: A. Held only by the state
D. Everywhere and productive, not merely repressive
questions.explanation: Foucault sees power as diffuse and productive — shaping subjects and conduct through everyday routines, norms and institutions.

questions.question: Garfinkel's ethnomethodology studies:
options: A. How people make sense of and produce social order
B. The financial economics of the modern household
C. The underlying biology of all human behaviour
D. Large-scale patterns of historical social change
questions.explanation: Ethno (people) + method (means) + ology (study of): how people make sense of the potential chaos of social life; order is continually created and re-created.

questions.question: A 'breaching experiment' works by:
options: A. Observing social life without ever intervening
B. Deliberately breaking a tacit rule to expose it
C. Interviewing acknowledged experts about the rules
D. Surveying a large and random national sample
questions.explanation: Breaching experiments break an unwritten rule of interaction (e.g. over-answering 'How are you?') so the tacit rule becomes visible via the reaction.

questions.question: The difference between formal and informal norms is that formal norms are:
options: A. Enforced only by the police
B. Written rules, whereas informal norms are unwritten
D. Unwritten, whereas informal norms are written
questions.explanation: Formal norms are society's written rules; informal norms are the unwritten ones — the special focus of ethnomethodology and interactionism.

questions.question: The core premise of symbolic interactionism is that people:
options: A. People act toward things based on their meanings
B. People share fixed meanings that can never change
C. People are wholly determined by the social structure
D. People act purely from rational economic self-interest
questions.explanation: People act on meanings, which arise from interaction with others and can be modified through interpretation; we rely on symbols.

questions.question: In symbolic interactionism, the meanings people hold for things:
options: A. Arise from interaction and can be modified through interpretation
B. Are irrelevant to how they act
C. Come only from official institutions
questions.explanation: Meanings stem from interaction with others and are reworked through an interpretive process — the Chicago School premise.

questions.question: Goffman's 'dramaturgical' model treats social life as:
options: A. A battlefield of class conflict
B. Theatre — the performance of roles on stages
C. A machine governed by fixed laws
D. A marketplace of rational exchanges
questions.explanation: In 'The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life' (1959), interactions are performances of roles, and situations are the stages of social life.

questions.question: The difference between Goffman's 'front stage' and 'back stage' is:
options: A. Front stage performs to an audience; back stage is off-role
B. Front stage is private, whereas back stage is public
C. Front stage means at work; back stage means at home
D. They are simply two names for the very same thing
questions.explanation: Front stage is where we perform to an audience following the role's conventions (the attentive waiter); back stage is where the performance relaxes (the kitchen).

questions.question: Controlling the impression others form of us is Goffman's:
questions.explanation: Impression management is the everyday work of shaping how others perceive us within the interaction order.

questions.question: Goffman extends Durkheim's sacred/profane distinction by arguing that:
options: A. Only funerals count as rituals
B. Rituals have disappeared in modern life
C. Ritual belongs only to religion
D. All interaction, such as greetings, consists of 'interactive rituals'
questions.explanation: Where Durkheim tied ritual to the sacred, Goffman treats all interaction as ritualised — greetings repeat and carry explicit rules (the 'dismissive bow').

questions.question: The 'dismissive bow' from Curb Your Enthusiasm illustrates that in an interactive ritual:
options: A. Every apology offered is fundamentally sincere
B. In interaction only the spoken words really matter
C. Interactive rituals in fact have no rules at all
D. The ritual's precise form carries the actual meaning
questions.explanation: A bow of the wrong depth reads as 'not sorry at all' — the ritual's exact form, not just the words, conveys sincerity.

questions.question: Susie Scott analyses the swimming pool as a 'negotiated order', meaning:
options: A. An order imposed entirely by lifeguards
B. An order precariously upheld by participants through a polite fiction
D. A space with no rules at all
questions.explanation: Scott (2009) shows the pool's orderliness is a negotiated order (Strauss) sustained by a polite fiction nobody names — like the emperor's new clothes.

questions.question: Which is one of the three swimming-pool norms Scott identifies?
questions.explanation: Scott's three tacit norms: respect for personal space, respect for individuals' disciplinary regimes, and the desexualisation of encounters.

questions.question: Scott titles her study 'Re-clothing the Emperor' to make the point that swimmers:
options: A. They follow only the pool's posted written regulations
B. They openly and freely discuss the pool's near-nakedness
C. They are entirely unaware that any rules exist at all
D. They can't consciously attend to the reality they build, yet defend it
questions.explanation: Like the emperor's subjects who dare not admit they see nothing, swimmers can't consciously attend to the reality they co-construct, yet stay poised to defend it.

questions.question: Which pairing of theorist and concept is correct?
questions.explanation: Hochschild gave us emotional labour; the panopticon is Foucault, the blasé attitude is Simmel, and rationalisation/bureaucracy is Weber.

questions.question: Which pairing of theorist and concept is correct?
options: D. Lefebvre — front and back stage
questions.explanation: Garfinkel devised breaching experiments; the spatial triad is Lefebvre, front/back stage is Goffman, and the iron cage is Weber.

muscle_physiology_3_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W5 · Muscle Physiology III — Reflexes
muscle_physiology_3_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
muscle_physiology_3_mhhs2401.html.content: MHHS2401 Week 5 Muscle Physiology III — Reflexes (Dr Linda Ban). A REFLEX = a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by sensory input to and motor output from the SPINAL CORD; function = maintain homeostasis by rapid adjustments in position/function. Can be modulated by voluntary (conscious) brain control, EXCEPT if a spinal cord lesion sits above the arc (voluntary control lost, but the reflex arc still exists and fires). THE REFLEX ARC (5 components in order): receptor -> sensory (afferent) neuron -> integration center (CNS synapse, may include an interneuron) -> motor (efferent) neuron -> effector (muscle). Afferent=in, efferent=out. The integration center sets the reflex type. MUSCLE PROPRIOCEPTORS (report body position/movement), 2 types: MUSCLE SPINDLE = muscle belly, senses STRETCH (length), 1a fibre, active in isotonic contraction & resting tone, causes CONTRACTION (the stretch/knee-jerk reflex; defends length); GOLGI TENDON ORGAN = tendon (muscle-tendon junction), senses TENSION (force), 1b fibre, active in isometric contraction, causes RELAXATION (protects muscle/tendon from over-load). MONOSYNAPTIC vs POLYSYNAPTIC: monosynaptic = one CNS synapse, no interneuron, fastest (stretch reflex); polysynaptic = >=2 synapses via interneuron(s) (withdrawal, reciprocal, crossed-extensor); interneurons add routing/inhibition/divergence. IPSILATERAL (same side) polysynaptic reflex -> RECIPROCAL INHIBITION: agonist contracts while antagonist is inhibited (relaxed) via an inhibitory interneuron -> unopposed efficient joint movement. CONTRALATERAL (opposite side) polysynaptic reflex -> CROSSED-EXTENSOR REFLEX: reciprocal inhibition in both limbs in opposite directions — stimulated side flexors contract/extensors inhibited (withdrawal); opposite side extensors contract/flexors inhibited (bears shifted weight); a sensory collateral also ascends to the brain for pain + postural adjustment; function = postural stability. RHYTHMIC MOVEMENT (locomotion, breathing) = reflex + voluntary combined: INVOLUNTARY/maintenance via CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATORS (CPGs) that spontaneously activate the reflexes once started; VOLUNTARY/modulation = brain initiates/terminates and changes rate/intensity.

questions.question: A reflex is best defined as:
options: A. A conscious decision to move a limb
B. A hormonal response to a stimulus
C. A slow, voluntary response controlled by the cortex
D. A rapid, involuntary response controlled by the spinal cord
questions.explanation: A reflex is a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, with sensory input to and motor output from the spinal cord.

questions.question: The primary function of a reflex is to:
options: D. Maintain homeostasis via rapid adjustments
questions.explanation: Reflexes maintain homeostasis by making rapid adjustments in the position or function of an organ.

questions.question: Reflexes are fast mainly because the signal:
options: A. The cord processes it without waiting for the brain
B. The signal bypasses every synapse in the loop
C. Hormones are used in place of the neurons
D. The signal travels along myelin-free axons
questions.explanation: Routing the loop through the cord removes the slow trip up to the brain and back, so the response is immediate; the brain is informed in parallel.

questions.question: After a spinal cord lesion above the level of a reflex arc, the reflex:
options: A. Is permanently and completely abolished
B. Still fires, but can no longer be voluntarily modulated
C. Is converted into a voluntary movement
D. Moves across to the opposite side of the body
questions.explanation: The brain can no longer reach the circuit, so voluntary control is lost, but the reflex arc itself remains intact and still fires.

questions.question: Can a reflex normally be overridden?
options: B. No — reflexes are never modifiable
C. Yes — by voluntary conscious control from the brain
questions.explanation: Reflexes can be modulated by voluntary (conscious) control from the brain, except when a cord lesion sits above the arc.

questions.question: Which lists the components of the reflex arc in the correct order?
options: A. Receptor → motor neuron → integration center → sensory neuron → effector
B. Sensory neuron → receptor → effector → motor neuron → integration center
C. Receptor → sensory neuron → integration center → motor neuron → effector
D. Effector → motor neuron → integration center → sensory neuron → receptor
questions.explanation: The five links run receptor → sensory (afferent) → integration center → motor (efferent) → effector.

questions.question: In a reflex arc, the afferent limb is the:
options: B. Sensory neuron carrying signals into the cord
C. Motor neuron carrying signals out of the cord
questions.explanation: Afferent = in: the sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord; efferent (motor) carries it out.

questions.question: The component of the reflex arc that determines a reflex's character (simple vs complex) is the:
questions.explanation: The integration center (the CNS synapses, possibly via interneurons) sets whether a reflex is monosynaptic or polysynaptic.

questions.question: The effector in a somatic reflex arc is typically a:
questions.explanation: The effector is the muscle (or gland) that produces the response — a skeletal muscle in somatic reflexes.

questions.question: Muscle proprioceptors provide information about:
options: D. The position and movement of the body
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle proprioceptors report body position and movement; the two types are the muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ.

questions.question: The muscle spindle detects:
options: A. The blood flow to the muscle
B. The temperature of the muscle
C. Tension, the force in the tendon
D. Stretch, a change in muscle length
questions.explanation: The spindle lies in the muscle belly and senses stretch/length; the Golgi tendon organ senses tension/force.

questions.question: The Golgi tendon organ detects ___ and produces ___ of the muscle:
questions.explanation: The GTO senses tension (force) and causes the muscle to relax, protecting the muscle and tendon from excessive load.

questions.question: The muscle spindle is located in the:
questions.explanation: The spindle sits in the muscle belly; the Golgi tendon organ sits at the muscle–tendon junction.

questions.question: Which afferent fibre carries signals from the Golgi tendon organ?
questions.explanation: 1b fibres carry Golgi tendon organ signals; 1a fibres carry muscle spindle signals.

questions.question: During an isometric contraction (force rises, length constant), the more strongly activated proprioceptor is the:
questions.explanation: Isometric contraction raises tension without changing length, so it drives the tension-sensing Golgi tendon organ; the spindle is more tied to length/isotonic contraction.

questions.question: Stretching a muscle activates its spindle, which reflexively causes the muscle to:
options: A. Contract, as in the stretch reflex
questions.explanation: The spindle's stretch reflex contracts the muscle to resist being lengthened — the basis of the knee-jerk.

questions.question: A monosynaptic reflex has:
options: C. A single CNS synapse between sensory and motor neurons
questions.explanation: Monosynaptic = one synapse directly between the sensory and motor neuron, with no interneuron — the fastest reflex.

questions.question: Polysynaptic reflexes differ from monosynaptic reflexes in that they:
options: D. Include one or more interneurons
questions.explanation: Polysynaptic reflexes have two or more synapses via interneuron(s), which slows them slightly but allows routing, inhibition and divergence.

questions.question: The stretch (knee-jerk) reflex is an example of a ___ reflex:
questions.explanation: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic (one synapse, no interneuron); withdrawal and crossed-extensor reflexes are polysynaptic.

questions.question: Adding an interneuron to a reflex circuit allows the sensory signal to:
options: D. Be routed, inhibited and copied to other targets
questions.explanation: Interneurons add computation — routing, inverting excitation to inhibition, and diverging the signal to antagonists, the other limb and the brain.

questions.question: 'Ipsilateral' refers to a reflex acting on the:
options: C. Same side as the stimulus
D. Opposite side to the stimulus
questions.explanation: Ipsilateral = same side; contralateral = opposite side.

questions.question: Reciprocal inhibition means that when the agonist contracts, the antagonist is:
options: A. Stretched hard by the spindle
C. Contracted at the same time
D. Disconnected from the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition relaxes the antagonist as the agonist contracts, via an inhibitory interneuron.

questions.question: The purpose of reciprocal inhibition is to:
options: A. Contract both muscle groups at once
C. Lock the joint in place
D. Allow unopposed, efficient movement of the joint
questions.explanation: By switching off the antagonist, reciprocal inhibition lets the joint move without the two muscle groups fighting each other.

questions.question: Reciprocal inhibition requires a polysynaptic circuit because:
options: A. Two receptors must be stimulated
B. Two effectors share one synapse
C. An interneuron is needed to inhibit the antagonist's motor neuron
D. The signal must reach the brain first
questions.explanation: Only an inhibitory interneuron can convert the excitatory sensory input into inhibition of the antagonist — impossible in a single-synapse circuit.

questions.question: A contralateral reflex produces its effect on the:
options: C. Opposite side of the body
D. Same side of the body
questions.explanation: Contralateral = opposite side; the crossed-extensor reflex acts on the limb opposite the stimulus.

questions.question: In the crossed-extensor reflex, the limb OPPOSITE the painful stimulus:
options: A. Extends to bear the shifted weight
questions.explanation: The stimulated limb withdraws (flexors contract); the opposite limb extends (extensors contract) to support the body's shifted weight.

questions.question: The function of the crossed-extensor reflex is:
questions.explanation: By bracing the opposite limb as one limb withdraws, the crossed-extensor reflex maintains postural stability and prevents a fall.

questions.question: In the crossed-extensor reflex, the side receiving the painful stimulus shows:
options: A. Extensor contraction with flexor inhibition
B. Flexor contraction with extensor inhibition
C. Contraction of both flexors and extensors
D. Complete relaxation of all its muscles
questions.explanation: On the stimulated (ipsilateral) side the flexors contract and extensors are inhibited to withdraw the limb; the opposite side does the reverse.

questions.question: In the crossed-extensor circuit, one collateral of the sensory neuron ascends to the brain to provide:
options: B. The motor command to the effector
C. Pain sensation and postural adjustment
questions.explanation: A collateral ascends for conscious pain sensation and postural adjustment (shift in centre of gravity), in parallel with the spinal reflex.

questions.question: Rhythmic movements such as locomotion and breathing are:
options: C. Purely reflex with no voluntary input
D. A combination of reflex/involuntary and voluntary movement
questions.explanation: Rhythmic movements combine an involuntary (reflex) component with a voluntary one.

questions.question: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide the ___ component of rhythmic movement:
questions.explanation: Once the activity is initiated, CPGs in the CNS spontaneously activate the reflexes that maintain the rhythm — the involuntary/maintenance component.

questions.question: In rhythmic movement, conscious brain control is chiefly needed to:
options: A. Initiate/terminate the activity and change its rate or intensity
C. Generate each individual step automatically
questions.explanation: The voluntary component initiates or terminates the activity and changes its rate or intensity; the CPG handles the repetitive pattern in between.

upper_limb_blood_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.title: MHHS2401 W5 · Upper Limb Blood Supply & Lymphatics
upper_limb_blood_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
upper_limb_blood_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.content: MHHS2401 Week 5 Blood Vessels & Lymphatics of the Upper Limb (Dr Strkalj). ARTERIAL HIGHWAY (one artery renamed at landmarks): subclavian -> AXILLARY (at lateral margin of rib 1) -> BRACHIAL (at inferior margin of teres major) -> splits into RADIAL & ULNAR (in the cubital fossa, opposite neck of radius) -> superficial & deep PALMAR ARCHES. Anastomoses at scapula, elbow, hand = collateral routes. AXILLA = pyramidal space (arm-thorax junction); walls: anterior = pectoralis major & minor; posterior = scapula/subscapularis (posterior fold = teres major + latissimus dorsi); medial = thoracic wall + serratus anterior; lateral = humerus; apex = entrance from neck; base = skin/fascia; contents = axillary artery+vein, brachial plexus cords, axillary nodes. AXILLARY ARTERY: PECTORALIS MINOR divides it into 3 parts giving 1,2,3 branches — 1st (proximal): superior thoracic; 2nd (posterior): thoraco-acromial + lateral thoracic; 3rd (distal): anterior & posterior circumflex humeral + subscapular. Posterior circumflex humeral winds around the surgical neck with the axillary nerve (both injured in surgical-neck fracture/dislocation). Scapular anastomosis = collateral around shoulder. BRACHIAL ARTERY = main supply to the arm (teres major -> cubital fossa); branches profunda brachii + superior & inferior ulnar collateral (elbow anastomosis); lies medial to biceps tendon (BP auscultation/brachial pulse). CUBITAL FOSSA (triangular, anterior elbow): superior = intercondylar line; medial = pronator teres; lateral = brachioradialis. RADIAL (lateral) & ULNAR (medial) arteries: recurrent branches (radial recurrent, ant/post ulnar recurrent, interosseous recurrent) feed the elbow anastomosis; common interosseous -> anterior & posterior interosseous along the interosseous membrane. Radial artery at wrist = pulse/arterial sampling; ALLEN'S TEST checks ulnar supply via arches first. PALMAR ARCHES: SUPERFICIAL = mainly ULNAR (more distal) -> common -> proper palmar digital arteries; DEEP = mainly RADIAL (more proximal) -> princeps pollicis, radial a. of index. Cross-connection = one artery can supply the whole hand. VENOUS DRAINAGE (2 sets): SUPERFICIAL (superficial fascia, variable, don't accompany arteries, fewer valves) = cephalic (lateral, deltopectoral groove), basilic (medial), median cubital (connects them, venepuncture site); DEEP (deep to deep fascia, accompany arteries as paired VENAE COMITANTES, more valves — arterial pulse aids venous return). LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE: superficial + deep lymphatics -> AXILLARY NODES, 5 groups: 1 pectoral/anterior (breast + anterior thoracic wall), 2 subscapular/posterior (posterior wall + scapula), 3 humeral/lateral (most of upper limb), 4 central (receives 1-3, deep to pec minor), 5 apical (receives central + cephalic-vein vessels). Sequence: pectoral/subscapular/humeral -> central -> apical -> SUBCLAVIAN LYMPHATIC TRUNK -> right lymphatic duct (right) / thoracic duct (left). Palpate nodes: cervical, axillary, inguinal. Pectoral group drains breast (breast-cancer staging).

questions.question: Which sequence correctly names the main artery of the upper limb from trunk to hand?
options: A. Axillary → subclavian → brachial → radial & ulnar
B. Brachial → axillary → subclavian → radial & ulnar
C. Subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial & ulnar
D. Subclavian → brachial → axillary → radial & ulnar
questions.explanation: One artery is renamed at landmarks: subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial & ulnar → palmar arches.

questions.question: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the:
options: C. Inferior margin of teres major
questions.explanation: Subclavian → axillary at the lateral margin of rib 1; axillary → brachial at the inferior margin of teres major.

questions.question: The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the:
options: C. Inferior margin of teres major
D. Superior margin of pectoralis minor
questions.explanation: The axillary artery becomes brachial at the inferior margin of teres major.

questions.question: The main purpose of the arterial anastomoses at the scapula, elbow and hand is to:
options: A. Increase blood pressure in the limb
B. Provide collateral routes when the main vessel is kinked or blocked
C. Drain lymph from the limb
questions.explanation: Anastomoses give bypass routes so the distal limb stays perfused across joint movement or occlusion.

questions.question: The axilla is best described as a:
options: A. Flat sheet of fascia over the shoulder
C. Pyramidal space between the arm and thorax
D. Bony canal in the humerus
questions.explanation: The axilla is a pyramidal passageway carrying vessels, nerves and lymphatics to the upper limb.

questions.question: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by:
questions.explanation: Anterior: pectoralis major & minor; posterior: scapula/subscapularis; medial: serratus anterior; lateral: humerus.

questions.question: The medial wall of the axilla is formed by the thoracic wall and:
questions.explanation: The medial wall is the thoracic wall and serratus anterior.

questions.question: The posterior axillary fold is formed by:
options: C. Teres major and latissimus dorsi
questions.explanation: The posterior wall is scapula/subscapularis; its fold is formed by teres major and latissimus dorsi.

questions.question: The axillary artery is divided into its three parts by which muscle?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into 1st (proximal), 2nd (posterior) and 3rd (distal) parts.

questions.question: How many branches arise from the 1st, 2nd and 3rd parts of the axillary artery respectively?
questions.explanation: The three parts give 1, 2 and 3 branches — a handy count that matches the part number.

questions.question: The single branch of the 1st part of the axillary artery is the:
questions.explanation: 1st part: superior thoracic artery. 2nd part: thoraco-acromial & lateral thoracic. 3rd part: circumflex humerals & subscapular.

questions.question: Which branch arises from the 3rd part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: 3rd part: anterior & posterior circumflex humeral and subscapular arteries; superior/lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial are 1st/2nd.

questions.question: The posterior circumflex humeral artery is vulnerable because it winds around the:
options: D. Surgical neck of the humerus (with the axillary nerve)
questions.explanation: It winds around the surgical neck through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve, so both are injured in surgical-neck fractures/dislocations.

questions.question: The brachial artery provides the main blood supply to the:
questions.explanation: The brachial artery is the main supply to the arm, running from teres major to the cubital fossa.

questions.question: A main branch of the brachial artery is the:
options: D. Profunda brachii (deep artery of the arm)
questions.explanation: Its branches are the profunda brachii and the superior & inferior ulnar collateral arteries (elbow anastomosis).

questions.question: The brachial artery ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries in the:
questions.explanation: It divides in the cubital fossa, opposite the neck of the radius.

questions.question: The medial boundary of the cubital fossa is the:
questions.explanation: Cubital fossa: superior = intercondylar line; medial = pronator teres; lateral = brachioradialis.

questions.question: The lateral boundary of the cubital fossa is the:
questions.explanation: The lateral boundary is brachioradialis; the medial is pronator teres.

questions.question: When measuring blood pressure, the artery auscultated in the cubital fossa is the:
questions.explanation: The brachial artery, medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa, is auscultated for Korotkoff sounds.

questions.question: In the forearm, the radial and ulnar arteries run, respectively, on the ___ and ___ sides:
questions.explanation: The radial artery runs laterally; the ulnar artery runs medially.

questions.question: The anterior and posterior interosseous arteries run along the:
options: B. Surface of the biceps tendon
D. Interosseous membrane between radius and ulna
questions.explanation: The common interosseous artery gives anterior and posterior interosseous branches along the interosseous membrane.

questions.question: The classic site for arterial blood sampling and pulse in the distal upper limb is the:
options: A. Radial artery at the wrist
B. Axillary artery in the axilla
C. Brachial artery in the arm
questions.explanation: The radial artery at the wrist is the standard pulse and arterial-sampling site.

questions.question: Allen's test is performed before radial artery cannulation to confirm that the:
options: A. Cephalic vein is not thrombosed
B. Ulnar artery can supply the hand via the palmar arches
D. Radial artery is fully patent
questions.explanation: Allen's test checks the ulnar/palmar-arch supply so the hand stays perfused if the radial artery is used.

questions.question: The superficial palmar arch is formed mainly by the:
questions.explanation: The superficial arch is mainly ulnar; the deep arch is mainly radial.

questions.question: The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the:
questions.explanation: The deep arch is mainly the radial artery; the superficial arch is mainly ulnar.

questions.question: The fingers are supplied by proper palmar digital arteries that arise from:
options: B. Common palmar digital arteries off the arches
questions.explanation: The arches give common palmar digital arteries, which divide into proper palmar digital arteries to the digits.

questions.question: Which vein ascends on the lateral (radial) side of the limb in the deltopectoral groove?
questions.explanation: The cephalic vein runs laterally into the deltopectoral groove; the basilic vein runs medially.

questions.question: Compared with superficial veins, deep veins characteristically:
options: A. Have no valves at all
B. Do not accompany any arteries
C. Accompany arteries as paired venae comitantes and have more valves
D. Lie in the superficial fascia
questions.explanation: Deep veins accompany arteries as paired venae comitantes with more valves; superficial veins are variable, don't follow arteries and have fewer valves.

questions.question: A vena comitans aids venous return because the:
options: A. Vein has no valves to slow flow
B. Vein is warmed by the artery
C. Adjacent arterial pulse squeezes the paired veins toward the heart
D. Vein actively contracts like a muscle
questions.explanation: The pulse of the paired artery compresses the veins, and their valves make the squeeze pump blood toward the heart.

questions.question: The standard superficial vein used for venepuncture in the cubital fossa is the:
options: A. Cephalic vein at the wrist
questions.explanation: The median cubital vein connects cephalic and basilic veins across the cubital fossa and is the usual venepuncture site.

questions.question: Both the superficial and deep lymphatics of the upper limb converge on the:
questions.explanation: Superficial (skin) and deep lymphatics both drain to the axillary lymph nodes.

questions.question: Which axillary node group principally drains the breast and anterior thoracic wall?
questions.explanation: The pectoral (anterior) group drains the anterior thoracic wall and breast — key to breast-cancer staging.

questions.question: Lymph from the pectoral, subscapular and humeral node groups passes next into the:
options: A. Apical nodes, then central nodes
D. Central nodes, then apical nodes
questions.explanation: The three peripheral groups drain into the central nodes, then the apical nodes, then the subclavian trunk.

questions.question: The apical axillary nodes ultimately drain via the subclavian lymphatic trunk into the:
options: C. Right lymphatic duct (right side) or thoracic duct (left side)
questions.explanation: Apical → subclavian trunk → right lymphatic duct on the right, or the thoracic duct on the left, then into the venous system.

questions.question: The three main sites for palpating lymph nodes are cervical, inguinal and:
questions.explanation: The three main palpation sites are cervical, axillary and inguinal.

upper_limb_nerve_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.title: Upper Limb Nerve Supply
upper_limb_nerve_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
upper_limb_nerve_supply_mhhs2401_wk5.htm.content: The brachial plexus (C5-T1): roots, trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches; the course, motor and sensory territory of the musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, axillary and radial nerves; dermatomes and cutaneous maps; intrinsic hand supply and testing; and the classic plexus and peripheral nerve lesions (Erb's, Klumpke's, carpal tunnel, wrist drop, claw hand).

questions.question: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus arises from the anterior (ventral) rami of C5 through T1. C3-C4 form the cervical plexus, and T2 supplies the axilla but does not enter the brachial plexus.

questions.question: What is the correct proximal-to-distal order of the levels of the brachial plexus?
options: A. Roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches
B. Roots, cords, divisions, trunks, branches
C. Roots, divisions, trunks, cords, branches
D. Roots, trunks, cords, divisions, branches
questions.explanation: Roots -> Trunks -> Divisions -> Cords -> Branches, remembered as 'Read That Damn Cadaver Book'. Divisions always sit between trunks and cords.

questions.question: Which roots combine to form the superior trunk of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: Superior trunk = C5 + C6; the middle trunk is C7 alone; the inferior trunk = C8 + T1.

questions.question: The musculocutaneous nerve continues into the forearm as which cutaneous nerve?
options: A. Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
B. Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm
C. Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
D. Superficial branch of the radial nerve
questions.explanation: After supplying the anterior arm flexors, the musculocutaneous nerve emerges laterally at the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The medial and posterior cutaneous nerves and the superficial radial branch come from other nerves.

questions.question: The axillary nerve provides motor supply to which pair of muscles?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor. Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve, and supra/infraspinatus by the suprascapular nerve.

questions.question: Which bony feature does the radial nerve travel along in the arm?
options: A. The surgical neck of the humerus
B. The spiral (radial) groove of the humerus
C. The bicipital groove of the humerus
D. The medial epicondyle of the humerus
