questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove with the profunda brachii artery. The surgical neck relates to the axillary nerve, the bicipital groove to the brachial artery/median nerve, and the medial epicondyle to the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: The palmar skin of the lateral three and a half digits is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies the palmar surface of the lateral 3.5 digits (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring). The ulnar covers the medial 1.5 digits, and the radial supplies the dorsolateral hand.

questions.question: The long thoracic nerve supplies which muscle?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior; its loss causes a winged scapula. The rhomboids are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and latissimus dorsi by the thoracodorsal nerve.

questions.question: Which nerve roots are injured in Erb's palsy?
questions.explanation: Erb's palsy is an upper-trunk lesion of C5-C6, producing the waiter's-tip posture. C8-T1 (lower trunk) injury is Klumpke's palsy.

questions.question: The three cords of the brachial plexus are named according to their relationship to which structure?
options: A. The first rib and clavicle
C. The second part of the axillary artery
D. The coracoid process of the scapula
questions.explanation: The lateral, medial and posterior cords are named for their position relative to the second part of the axillary artery. The other structures are landmarks nearby but are not what the cords are named for.

questions.question: In the forearm the median nerve supplies all the flexor muscles EXCEPT which of the following?
options: A. Flexor carpi radialis and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus
B. Flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus
C. Flexor pollicis longus and pronator teres
D. Palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies all forearm flexors except the '1.5 muscles' taken by the ulnar nerve: flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus. FCR, FPL, pronator teres, palmaris longus and FDS are all median.

questions.question: Which two terminal nerves both arise from the posterior cord?
questions.explanation: The posterior cord (formed by all posterior divisions) gives the axillary and radial nerves - the extensor/abductor nerves. Musculocutaneous is from the lateral cord, ulnar from the medial cord, and median from both lateral and medial cords.

questions.question: The ulnar nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except which group?
options: A. The hypothenar muscles and the two medial lumbricals
B. The interossei and adductor pollicis
C. The two lateral lumbricals and palmaris brevis
D. The thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all intrinsic hand muscles except the thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals (the median 'LOAF' group). The interossei, medial lumbricals, hypothenars, adductor pollicis and palmaris brevis are all ulnar.

questions.question: Which vessel accompanies the axillary nerve as it passes through the quadrangular space?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery traverse the quadrangular space together and wind around the surgical neck. The profunda brachii accompanies the radial nerve, and the suprascapular artery runs with the suprascapular nerve.

questions.question: In carpal tunnel syndrome the central palm often retains sensation. Why?
options: A. The palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum
B. The recurrent motor branch carries the palmar sensory fibres round the tunnel
C. The ulnar nerve takes over palmar sensation once the median is compressed
D. The palmar digital branches all arise distal to the compressed segment
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the wrist and runs over (superficial to) the flexor retinaculum, so it escapes compression in the tunnel and the central palm keeps its sensation. The recurrent branch is purely motor to the thenar muscles.

questions.question: A mid-shaft humeral fracture injures the radial nerve. Why is elbow extension usually preserved?
options: A. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial head of triceps
B. Triceps is supplied by the axillary nerve at the shoulder
C. The branches to triceps leave the nerve before it enters the spiral groove
D. The deep radial branch to triceps is protected within supinator
questions.explanation: Triceps receives its radial branches high in the arm, before the nerve reaches the spiral groove; a mid-shaft fracture at the groove therefore spares elbow extension but paralyses the wrist and finger extensors (wrist drop). Triceps is radial, not ulnar or axillary.

questions.question: The suprascapular nerve, a branch of the superior trunk, supplies which muscles?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Teres minor and deltoid are axillary, and teres major is lower subscapular. Because it is a trunk branch, it is lost in Erb's palsy.

questions.question: The anterior divisions of the brachial plexus are destined to supply which compartment?
options: B. The intrinsic muscles of the hand only
D. The skin of the limb only
questions.explanation: Anterior divisions supply the flexor (anterior) compartment; posterior divisions supply the extensor (posterior) compartment. This flexor/extensor sorting is the whole purpose of the division stage.

questions.question: Which dermatome corresponds to the skin of the middle finger?
questions.explanation: C7 covers the middle finger. C6 corresponds to the thumb, C8 to the little finger, and T1 to the medial forearm.

questions.question: A patient's wrist and fingers hang flexed and cannot be extended after a humeral shaft fracture. Which deformity and nerve does this indicate?
options: B. Hand of benediction - median nerve
questions.explanation: Paralysed wrist/finger extensors with unopposed flexors produce wrist drop, the signature of a radial nerve lesion. Claw hand is ulnar, and the hand of benediction is a median-nerve sign seen on attempting to make a fist.

questions.question: The median nerve is unusual among the terminal branches because it forms from contributions of which cords?
options: A. The lateral and medial cords
B. The lateral and posterior cords
C. The medial and posterior cords
questions.explanation: The median nerve has two heads, one from the lateral cord and one from the medial cord, which clasp the axillary artery like the letter M. Musculocutaneous is lateral-cord only; axillary and radial are posterior-cord.

questions.question: Why does an ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist produce more obvious clawing of the medial fingers than a lesion at the elbow?
options: A. At the wrist the medial lumbricals are spared, exaggerating the interosseous deficit and deepening the claw
B. At the elbow the medial flexor digitorum profundus is paralysed too, so those fingers cannot flex at the DIP joints
C. At the elbow the median nerve compensates by re-innervating the deprived intrinsic hand muscles
D. At the wrist the dorsal cutaneous branch is preserved, and its intact sensation worsens the deformity
questions.explanation: This is the ulnar paradox. A wrist lesion leaves the medial FDP working, so the DIP joints of the ring and little fingers flex fully and the claw looks worse. An elbow lesion also knocks out the medial FDP, so those fingers cannot curl as tightly - a less dramatic claw despite the more proximal injury.

questions.question: The claw-hand deformity of an ulnar lesion arises because the lost muscles normally perform which combined action?
options: A. Extend the metacarpophalangeal joints and flex the interphalangeal joints
B. Flex both the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
C. Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
D. Abduct the fingers and flex the wrist
questions.explanation: The lumbricals and interossei flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints. Without them the long extensors hyperextend the MCPs and the long flexors flex the IPs, curling the fingers into a claw - most marked in the ulnar (ring and little) fingers.

questions.question: An isolated posterior interosseous nerve lesion gives finger drop but the wrist can still be extended, and there is no sensory loss. Which feature of the radial nerve's branching explains this?
options: A. The superficial radial branch is purely motor here, while the deep branch is purely sensory
B. It is the deep motor branch, arising after the sensory branch and after the wrist extensors
C. It supplies extensor carpi radialis longus and the sensory skin before it enters supinator
D. The wrist extensors draw their supply from the axillary nerve, sparing them in a radial lesion
questions.explanation: Near the elbow the radial nerve splits into a superficial (sensory) branch and a deep branch that becomes the posterior interosseous nerve (motor). Because the deep branch supplies finger extensors after the radial wrist extensors are already innervated, a posterior interosseous lesion drops the fingers while wrist extension and skin sensation are preserved.

questions.question: The 'waiter's-tip' posture of Erb's palsy features a pronated forearm. Which loss most directly causes the pronation?
options: A. Loss of supinator, which is by far the strongest supinator of the whole forearm
B. Sparing of pronator quadratus by C8-T1, letting it overpower the weakened supinators
C. Loss of brachioradialis, which normally acts as the main supinator of the forearm
D. Loss of biceps, removing a strong supinator so the pronators act unopposed
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is a powerful supinator and is paralysed in Erb's (musculocutaneous, C5-C6), so the intact pronators (pronator teres/quadratus, from C6-T1) act unopposed and the forearm rests pronated. Supinator contributes to supination but its loss alone would not dominate; brachioradialis is not the main supinator.

questions.question: The lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (to the index and middle fingers) receives its motor supply from which nerve?
options: A. The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve
B. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve
C. The posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve
D. The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve
questions.explanation: The lateral (radial) half of FDP is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median. The medial half is ulnar. The recurrent median branch is motor to the thenar muscles, not FDP.

questions.question: A patient has numbness confined to a compact patch over the little finger and the ulnar border of the hand, front and back, with normal sensation elsewhere. This pattern best fits a lesion of what?
options: A. The C8 dermatome (a single spinal segment)
B. The T1 dermatome (a single spinal segment)
C. The ulnar nerve (a peripheral cutaneous territory)
D. The medial cord affecting all its cutaneous branches
questions.explanation: A discrete patch matching the medial 1.5 digits and hypothenar skin, both palmar and dorsal, is the ulnar nerve's cutaneous territory. A C8 or T1 dermatome would form a longitudinal strip extending up the forearm, not a hand patch, and a medial-cord lesion would add forearm/arm skin loss and intrinsic weakness beyond the ulnar field.

questions.question: Striking the 'funny bone' shoots tingling to the little finger. Which anatomical fact makes the ulnar nerve so exposed there?
options: A. It passes through the quadrangular space against the humeral neck
B. It runs superficially in a bony groove behind the medial epicondyle
C. It lies deep to pronator teres at the elbow
D. It travels within the cubital fossa alongside the brachial artery
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes superficially through the cubital tunnel in a groove behind the medial epicondyle, directly against bone, so a knock compresses it and refers tingling to its little-finger territory. The quadrangular space relates to the axillary nerve, and the median nerve lies with the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.

questions.question: To specifically test the palmar interossei at the bedside, you would ask the patient to do what?
options: A. Grip a card between adducted fingers while you try to pull it out
B. Spread the fingers apart against your resistance
C. Oppose the thumb to the little finger
D. Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while keeping the fingers straight
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei ADduct the fingers (PAD), so gripping a card between the fingers tests them. Spreading the fingers tests the dorsal interossei (DAB, ABduct). Thumb opposition tests the median-supplied opponens pollicis. All interossei are ulnar.

questions.question: Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1) is classically produced by which mechanism, in contrast to the shoulder-down force of Erb's?
options: A. A direct downward blow to the point of the shoulder that drives it away from the neck
B. Sudden upward traction on an abducted arm, as in grabbing to break a fall
C. Slowly progressive compression of the cords by an axillary artery aneurysm
D. A penetrating knife wound into the posterior triangle of the neck above the clavicle
questions.explanation: Klumpke's follows a sudden superior pull on the abducted limb (e.g. clutching an object to arrest a fall, or excess traction on a baby's arm at delivery), stretching or avulsing the lower trunk. Erb's is the opposite force - a widening of the neck-shoulder angle from a fall onto the shoulder.

questions.question: In the arm, the median nerve can be located at the surface by tracing which structure?
options: A. The cephalic vein in the deltopectoral groove
B. The basilic vein along the medial forearm
C. The profunda brachii artery in the spiral groove
D. The brachial artery in the medial bicipital groove
questions.explanation: The median nerve runs alongside the brachial artery in the medial bicipital groove, so palpating the brachial pulse locates the nerve - useful for nerve blocks and predicting combined injury. The profunda brachii/spiral groove marks the radial nerve.

drug_targets_medi2004_wk5.html.title: Drug Targets — Enzymes, Receptors & Transporters
drug_targets_medi2004_wk5.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
drug_targets_medi2004_wk5.html.content: The four protein target classes (receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters) and the three actions drugs exert; enzymes as targets (reversible/irreversible anticholinesterases, false substrates, antifolates); the four receptor superfamilies with their location, effector, coupling, structure and timescale; and transporters as targets (SLC vs ABC, reuptake inhibitors).

questions.question: Which set lists the four main protein classes that account for almost all drug targets?
options: A. Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters
C. Receptors, ion channels, ribosomes, transporters
D. Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, structural proteins
questions.explanation: The four druggable classes are receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers). Antibodies, ribosomes and structural proteins are not the standard target classes taught here — structural/bulk proteins make poor targets because binding them changes little downstream.

questions.question: A drug can do which three things to any of its targets?
options: A. Synthesise, transport or degrade it
B. Absorb, distribute or excrete it
C. Phosphorylate, cleave or oxidise it
D. Activate, inhibit/block or modulate it
questions.explanation: On any target a drug activates, inhibits/blocks, or modulates it. Absorb/distribute/excrete are pharmacokinetic processes; the others describe biochemical reactions, not the pharmacological actions on a target.

questions.question: Which enzyme's inhibition raises acetylcholine levels in the synapse?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase degrades ACh; inhibiting it lets ACh linger, boosting cholinergic transmission. Choline acetyltransferase makes ACh, monoamine oxidase degrades monoamines, and adenylyl cyclase is a GPCR effector.

questions.question: Which receptor superfamily controls the fastest (millisecond) synaptic events?
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated (ionotropic) receptors are the fastest because the effector is the ion channel itself (direct coupling). GPCRs act in seconds; kinase-linked and nuclear receptors take hours because they depend on gene transcription.

questions.question: How many transmembrane helices define a G-protein-coupled receptor?
questions.explanation: GPCRs are 7-transmembrane receptors. A single TM helix is typical of kinase-linked receptors; ion-channel subunits often cross four times (M1–M4); twelve is common for many transporters.

questions.question: Nuclear receptors produce their effects by acting as:
options: A. Ligand-gated ion channels at the surface
questions.explanation: Nuclear receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors that bind hormone-response elements to regulate gene expression, giving a slow effect. The other options describe the three membrane-based superfamilies.

questions.question: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin by inhibiting which transporter?
questions.explanation: SSRIs block SERT, the serotonin reuptake transporter, so released 5-HT stays in the synapse. NET carries noradrenaline, DAT dopamine, and VMAT packages monoamines into vesicles.

questions.question: Why does the body need transporters (carriers) for many solutes?
options: A. The solutes are too lipid-soluble to stay dissolved in blood
B. The solutes are too large to fit through any membrane protein
C. The solutes are too poorly lipid-soluble to cross membranes alone
D. The solutes are electrically neutral so they cannot move at all
questions.explanation: Carriers move molecules that are insufficiently lipid-soluble to penetrate membranes on their own, across barriers like the renal tubule, gut epithelium and blood-brain barrier. Lipid-soluble molecules cross unaided; size and charge are not the defining reason given.

questions.question: A patient recovers cholinergic function only after about two days despite the offending chemical being cleared from blood within hours. This best fits:
options: A. An irreversible organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitor
B. A reversible cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil
C. A competitive muscarinic receptor antagonist like atropine
D. A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor such as fluoxetine
questions.explanation: Irreversible organophosphates destroy the enzyme, so recovery depends on synthesising new AChE, not on clearing the drug — hence the days-long lag. A reversible inhibitor's effect tracks drug levels and fades within hours; the other options do not act on AChE.

questions.question: Which pairing of antifolate drug and its target enzyme is correct?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR); fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthetase. Options A and B swap the two enzymes, and choline acetyltransferase is unrelated to folate metabolism.

questions.question: In the G-protein cycle, which event switches the signal OFF?
options: A. Binding of the agonist to the receptor's orthosteric site
B. Exchange of GDP for GTP on the α subunit
C. Dissociation of the Gα subunit from the βγ dimer
D. Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP by the α subunit
questions.explanation: The α subunit's intrinsic GTPase hydrolyses GTP to GDP, letting the subunits re-associate and terminating signalling — the built-in off-switch. Options A–C are all steps that turn the signal on.

questions.question: Which coupling correctly matches a G-protein subunit to its effect?
questions.explanation: Gαq activates phospholipase C, generating IP3 and DAG. Gαs stimulates and Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (cAMP), so A reverses Gαs, and C and D misassign the PLC effect.

questions.question: On the GABA_A receptor, benzodiazepines bind at which site?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines bind an allosteric (BZ) site distinct from the GABA site and enhance GABA's action rather than opening the channel themselves. GABA_A has no glutamate site (that is NMDA), and benzodiazepines do not plug the pore.

questions.question: The first structural change when a growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase is:
options: A. Release of a βγ subunit
B. Opening of an ion channel
D. Translocation of the receptor to the nucleus
questions.explanation: Ligand binding brings two RTKs together (dimerisation) so their kinase domains phosphorylate each other's tyrosines. βγ release is a GPCR event, ion-channel opening is ionotropic, and nuclear translocation belongs to nuclear receptors.

questions.question: Where does a class I nuclear receptor reside before its ligand binds?
options: A. In the cytoplasm, held inactive by heat-shock protein
B. In the nucleus, already bound to its response element
C. Spanning the plasma membrane as a surface receptor
D. Inside the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Class I receptors sit in the cytoplasm held by heat-shock protein; ligand binding releases HSP and the complex translocates to the nucleus. Class II receptors are already nuclear, and nuclear receptors are not membrane-spanning.

questions.question: A symporter moving glucose into a cell using the sodium gradient is an example of:
options: A. Primary active transport using ATP directly
B. Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
C. Facilitated diffusion of a single solute
D. Secondary active transport using an ion gradient
questions.explanation: Symport uses an existing ion (Na+) gradient rather than ATP directly, making it secondary active transport. Primary active transport hydrolyses ATP itself (e.g. Na+/K+ pump); diffusion moves solutes down their gradient without carrying a second solute uphill.

questions.question: P-glycoprotein moves drugs out of cells. To which transporter family and energy source does it belong?
options: A. SLC family, driven by an ion gradient
B. SLC family, driven by ATP hydrolysis
C. ABC family, driven by ATP hydrolysis
D. ABC family, driven by an ion gradient
questions.explanation: P-glycoprotein is an ABC (ATP-Binding Cassette) transporter that pumps substrate against its gradient using ATP hydrolysis at its nucleotide-binding domains. SLC carriers instead facilitate movement down the electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: An MAOI differs from an SSRI in that its primary target is:
options: A. The serotonin reuptake transporter SERT
B. The noradrenaline reuptake transporter NET
C. A monoamine-degrading enzyme in the terminal
questions.explanation: MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks down monoamines — an enzyme target, not a transporter. SSRIs and SNRIs target the reuptake transporters SERT/NET; neither class primarily blocks postsynaptic receptors.

questions.question: Two receptor types both act over hours. The shared reason is that both:
options: A. Require dissociation of a βγ subunit before acting
B. Depend on gene transcription and protein synthesis
C. Must first be phosphorylated by a G-protein-coupled receptor kinase
D. Open an ion channel only after a delay
questions.explanation: Kinase-linked and nuclear receptors are both slow because their outputs require transcription and new protein synthesis. βγ dissociation and GRK phosphorylation are GPCR-specific events, and neither slow type acts by opening an ion channel.

questions.question: Memantine acts on the NMDA receptor at the same location as which of the following?
options: A. Glutamate at the agonist site
B. Glycine at a modulatory site
C. Mg2+ blocking the open pore
D. A benzodiazepine at an allosteric site
questions.explanation: Memantine is a channel blocker that sits inside the open pore, the same region where Mg2+ produces its voltage-dependent block. Glutamate and glycine act at binding sites on the receptor, and benzodiazepines act on GABA_A, not NMDA.

questions.question: The rationale for developing a G-protein-biased μ-opioid agonist rests on the idea that:
options: A. Analgesia and respiratory depression run through different downstream pathways
B. G-protein signalling is precisely what produces the dangerous respiratory depression
C. β-arrestin recruitment is strictly required for producing the analgesic effect
D. The μ-opioid receptor couples to only a single downstream signalling transducer
questions.explanation: Biased agonism exploits a receptor coupling to more than one pathway; if analgesia runs mainly through G-protein and harm through β-arrestin, favouring one arm can separate benefit from side effect. B and C invert the proposed roles, and D contradicts the premise of multiple transducers.

questions.question: Opioid tolerance from receptor down-regulation is best explained by which sequence?
options: A. GRK phosphorylation → β-arrestin binding → internalisation → degradation
B. GTP hydrolysis → βγ subunit release → inhibition of adenylyl cyclase
C. Receptor dimerisation → tyrosine autophosphorylation → Ras activation
D. Lipophilic ligand entry → heat-shock-protein release → nuclear translocation
questions.explanation: Sustained agonism drives GRK phosphorylation, β-arrestin recruitment, clathrin-mediated internalisation and lysosomal degradation, reducing surface receptors and causing tolerance. B is a normal signalling step, C is an RTK cascade, and D is nuclear-receptor activation.

questions.question: How does a false substrate differ mechanistically from a simple competitive inhibitor?
options: A. It binds an allosteric site located well away from the active site
B. It permanently and covalently destroys the enzyme molecule it binds
C. It raises the enzyme's binding affinity for its normal true substrate
D. It is chemically transformed by the enzyme into an abnormal product
questions.explanation: A false substrate is actually processed by the enzyme into an abnormal product while also competing with the true substrate, whereas a competitive inhibitor merely occupies the active site without being converted. It is not allosteric, not necessarily destructive, and does not raise substrate affinity.

questions.question: A β1-selective antagonist is safer in a patient with asthma than a non-selective one because:
options: A. It spares β2 receptors that mediate bronchodilation
B. It also blocks α1 receptors in the airway
C. It activates β2 receptors to open the airway
D. It prevents noradrenaline release from nerve terminals
questions.explanation: Receptor subtypes are mostly separate genes with distinct pharmacology, so a β1-selective drug largely leaves airway β2 receptors (which drive bronchodilation) untouched. It is an antagonist so it does not activate β2, does not target airway α1, and its selectivity is not about blocking transmitter release.

questions.question: A cytokine receptor with no intrinsic kinase activity transmits its signal to the nucleus mainly through:
options: A. Ras, Raf, MEK and MAPK
D. Phospholipase C generating IP3 and DAG
questions.explanation: Cytokine receptors lack their own kinase and recruit associated Janus kinases (JAK) that phosphorylate STAT transcription factors (opposed by SOCS). The Ras/MAPK cascade is typical of receptor tyrosine kinases, while cAMP and IP3/DAG are GPCR second-messenger routes.

questions.question: Which statement about allosteric modulators is most accurate?
options: A. They bind at the orthosteric site and fully activate the receptor by themselves
B. They can act on G-protein-coupled receptors but on no other receptor superfamily
C. They tune the response to the endogenous ligand and offer a ceiling effect
D. They bind irreversibly and then destroy the receptor a short time afterwards
questions.explanation: An allosteric modulator binds away from the orthosteric site and shifts the response to the natural ligand, giving a built-in ceiling and often better selectivity. All four superfamilies can be allosterically modulated, they do not occupy the orthosteric site, and they do not destroy the receptor.

questions.question: Cocaine, amphetamine and MDMA all raise synaptic monoamines, but which best captures their transporter action?
options: A. Cocaine blocks only serotonin reuptake, and amphetamine blocks only dopamine reuptake
B. All three raise synaptic monoamines solely by inhibiting the enzyme monoamine oxidase
C. Cocaine blocks dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake; MDMA chiefly serotonin
D. MDMA blocks dopamine and noradrenaline uptake, and cocaine blocks only dopamine uptake
questions.explanation: Cocaine inhibits reuptake of dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline; amphetamines inhibit dopamine and noradrenaline uptake; MDMA chiefly inhibits serotonin uptake (all have additional mechanisms). The other options misassign or oversimplify these carrier actions.

questions.question: A new drug produces its full effect within a few milliseconds. Its target is most likely a(n):
questions.explanation: A millisecond effect points to a ligand-gated ion channel, where the channel is the direct effector. GPCRs act over seconds, and kinase-linked and nuclear receptors act over hours because they depend on transcription.

questions.question: Combining an SSRI with an MAOI is dangerous mainly because:
options: A. Both block the same reuptake transporter, halving serotonin
B. Both raise synaptic serotonin, risking serotonin syndrome
C. Both inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing a cholinergic crisis
D. Both antagonise dopamine receptors, causing parkinsonism
questions.explanation: An SSRI blocks serotonin reuptake and an MAOI blocks its breakdown, so together they push synaptic serotonin dangerously high (serotonin syndrome). They act on different targets (transporter vs enzyme), neither touches AChE, and the risk is excess serotonin, not dopamine blockade.

cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.title: Anatomy of the Heart & Blood Vessels
cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.content: Cardiovascular anatomy for MHHS2402 Week 5: mediastinum and pericardium, the four chambers and valves, the fibrous skeleton, coronary vessels, the conduction system and nerve supply, systemic vs pulmonary circulation, foetal circulation, the great vessels, and surface anatomy with valve auscultation.

questions.question: The sternal angle lies at the level where the costal cartilage of which rib articulates with the sternum?
questions.explanation: The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) marks the articulation of the 2nd costal cartilage — the standard rib-counting landmark, and the level of the carina, aortic-arch origin and the superior/inferior mediastinal divide.

questions.question: Which mediastinal subdivision contains the heart, pericardium and the roots of the great vessels?
questions.explanation: The middle mediastinum houses the pericardium, heart and great-vessel roots. The anterior holds thymic remnants, the posterior holds the oesophagus/sympathetic chain/azygos, and the superior sits above the T4/T5 plane.

questions.question: The apex of the heart is formed by which chamber?
questions.explanation: The apex is the tip of the left ventricle, projected to the left 5th intercostal space. The right atrium forms the right border and the left atrium forms the base.

questions.question: How many cusps does the tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve have?
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve has three cusps ('Tri before you Bi'); the left AV (bicuspid/mitral) valve has two. The two semilunar valves each have three cup-shaped cusps.

questions.question: The coronary sinus returns the heart's venous blood directly into which chamber?
questions.explanation: The coronary sinus lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove and empties into the right atrium, alongside the openings of the SVC and IVC.

questions.question: Which structure is the normal pacemaker of the heart?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node in the right atrium sets the rate and depolarises the atria first. The AV node relays and delays; the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres distribute the impulse to the ventricles.

questions.question: Which layer of a vessel wall is a thin endothelium sitting on a basement membrane?
questions.explanation: The tunica intima is the innermost endothelial layer that reduces friction. The media is smooth muscle/elastic tissue; the externa (adventitia) is the outer connective-tissue coat.

questions.question: After birth, the foramen ovale becomes which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale seals to leave the fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, the umbilical vein the ligamentum teres, and the ductus venosus the ligamentum venosum.

questions.question: Which is the first branch of the aortic arch?
questions.explanation: The arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk first, then the left common carotid, then the left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk itself splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian.

questions.question: The crista terminalis of the right atrium separates which two regions?
options: A. The smooth-walled sinus venarum from the rough pectinate atrial wall
B. The right atrial cavity from the inflow of the right ventricle beyond it
C. The dimple of the fossa ovalis from the opening of the coronary sinus
D. The muscular auricle from the entering mouth of the superior vena cava
questions.explanation: The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge marking the developmental junction between the smooth-walled sinus venarum (venous inflow) and the rough, pectinate-muscled part derived from the primitive atrium.

questions.question: The moderator band of the right ventricle carries which structure to the anterior papillary muscle?
questions.explanation: The moderator band is a muscular bridge conveying the right bundle branch across the ventricular cavity to the anterior papillary muscle, so it contracts on time and the tricuspid valve shuts promptly.

questions.question: Why do the atrioventricular valves have chordae tendineae whereas the semilunar valves do not?
options: A. AV valves are simply larger and heavier, so they require some extra structural support
B. AV valves must resist high ventricular pressure without everting back into the atria
C. Semilunar valves are instead held shut by the surrounding arterial pulse pressure
D. Semilunar valves anchor onto the fibrous skeleton and therefore need no free cusps
questions.explanation: AV cusps face the huge pressure a contracting ventricle generates and would invert into the atrium without the chordae/papillary tethers. Semilunar cusps are pockets that self-seal under downstream pressure, so they need no chordae.

questions.question: In a right-dominant circulation (about 80–85% of people), the posterior interventricular artery arises from the:
questions.explanation: Right dominance is defined by the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery arising from the right coronary artery. In the 15–20% who are left-dominant it comes off the circumflex.

questions.question: The roughly 0.1-second delay imposed at the atrioventricular node serves mainly to:
options: A. Let the ventricles finish filling with atrial blood before they contract
B. Slow the resting heart rate down toward a steadier baseline rhythm
C. Let the atria fully repolarise before the ventricles begin to depolarise
D. Give the relaxing coronary arteries the time they need to fill up
questions.explanation: The AV delay lets atrial contraction complete ventricular filling before the ventricles squeeze, maximising stroke volume. It is a timing device, not a rate control or a repolarisation window.

questions.question: The left ventricular wall is far thicker than the right ventricular wall primarily because it must:
options: A. Hold a larger stroke volume than the right ventricle
B. Overcome the high resistance of the systemic circuit
C. Resist the high pressure of the pulmonary veins entering nearby
D. Contract more times per minute than the right ventricle
questions.explanation: Both ventricles eject the same volume per beat, but the LV drives blood through the long, narrow, high-resistance systemic circuit (~120/80 mmHg) versus the RV's short, low-resistance pulmonary circuit (~25/10 mmHg), so the LV wall is about three times thicker.

questions.question: Which capillary type is found in bone marrow, where whole blood cells must cross the wall?
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal capillaries have large pores and an incomplete basement membrane, permitting passage of large proteins and whole cells — suiting bone marrow, liver and spleen. Continuous capillaries have no pores; fenestrated have only small pores.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches location and function at the carotid bifurcation?
options: A. Carotid sinus at the bifurcation — chemoreceptor for O2/CO2/pH
B. Carotid body just below the bifurcation — baroreceptor for pressure
C. Carotid body at the bifurcation — chemoreceptor for O2/CO2/pH
D. Carotid sinus above the bifurcation — chemoreceptor for stretch
questions.explanation: The carotid body sits at the bifurcation and is a chemoreceptor (O2, CO2, pH); the carotid sinus is a dilatation just before the bifurcation acting as a baroreceptor (stretch/pressure). 'Body at Bifurcation, Basic; Sinus Sooner, Stretch.'

questions.question: Sensory innervation of the fibrous and parietal serous pericardium is supplied by the:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) carries somatic sensation from the pericardium and runs along its lateral edges. The vagus and sympathetic trunks contribute autonomic fibres; this C3–5 route underlies referral of cardiac pain to the shoulder.

questions.question: Coronary arterial inflow peaks during ventricular diastole. Which best explains why systole restricts it?
options: A. Aortic diastolic pressure is far too low to force blood into the coronary ostia
B. The coronary arteries lack the elastic recoil that the great veins depend upon
C. Myocardial compression and the open aortic cusps together shroud the coronary ostia
D. The closing pulmonary valve blocks retrograde flow back into the coronary sinus
questions.explanation: In systole the contracting myocardium squeezes its intramural vessels and the open aortic cusps partly cover the coronary ostia; in diastole the myocardium relaxes and aortic recoil drives the 'back-splash' into the ostia. This is why a very fast heart rate (short diastole) can ischaemically starve the heart.

questions.question: Which consequence follows directly from the fibrous skeleton acting as an electrical insulator between atria and ventricles?
options: A. The impulse can only reach the ventricles by way of the AV node and bundle of His
B. The semilunar valves are forced to close before the atrioventricular valves each beat
C. The SA node is compelled to fire faster than any subsidiary ventricular pacemaker
D. The Purkinje fibres are made to depolarise the atria from the cardiac apex upward
questions.explanation: The non-conducting fibrous rings wall atrial muscle off from ventricular muscle, so the only surviving electrical route is the AV node and bundle of His piercing the skeleton — which is exactly what lets the AV node impose its delay and coordinate the beat.

questions.question: Cardiac pain is felt in the left shoulder and jaw. The best mechanistic explanation is that:
options: A. The vagus nerve carries sharp pain fibres directly from the heart up to the neck
B. The pericardium is in physical contact with the capsule of the shoulder joint
C. Sympathetic fibres actively project the pain signals outward onto the overlying skin
D. Cardiac and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal second-order neurons
questions.explanation: Convergence: visceral afferents from the heart (T1–T5 sympathetics, and C3–5 via the phrenic-supplied pericardium) enter the cord with somatic afferents from those dermatomes and synapse on the same second-order neurons, so the brain mislocalises the pain to the body surface.

questions.question: On an unlabelled coronal section, which single feature most reliably identifies the left ventricle?
options: A. The presence of a moderator band
B. Three papillary muscles arising from the wall
C. A markedly thicker myocardial wall
D. Coarser trabeculae carneae lining the cavity
questions.explanation: The LV myocardium is about three times thicker than the RV — the single most reliable clue. The moderator band and coarser trabeculae belong to the right ventricle; the LV typically has two papillary muscles, not three.

questions.question: What defines a portal venous system such as the hepatic portal vein?
options: A. A vein that carries oxygenated blood back toward the heart rather than deoxygenated
B. A vein that runs alongside its analogous artery as a set of venae comitantes
C. A vein equipped with one-way valves that resist backflow against gravity
D. A vein that links two capillary beds instead of returning straight to the heart
questions.explanation: A portal system interposes a second capillary bed before the blood returns to the heart, delivering cargo at high concentration to a target (gut nutrients to the liver; hypothalamic hormones to the pituitary). It is not defined by oxygenation, companion arteries or valves.

questions.question: Which foetal shunt allows blood to bypass the liver, and where does it deliver that blood?
options: A. Foramen ovale — passing from the right atrium into the left atrium
B. Ductus arteriosus — passing from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta
C. Umbilical arteries — passing from the foetal aorta back to the placenta
D. Ductus venosus — passing from the umbilical vein into the inferior vena cava
questions.explanation: The ductus venosus shunts oxygenated umbilical-vein blood past the liver into the IVC. The foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs; the umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

questions.question: The aortic valve sits behind the sternum yet is auscultated at the right 2nd intercostal space. Why is it heard away from its surface projection?
options: A. Bone conducts the closure sound rightward through the manubrium of the sternum
B. The right lung resonates and amplifies the right-sided heart sounds preferentially
C. The aortic valve in fact lies directly beneath the right 2nd intercostal space
D. Ejected blood carries the valve sound downstream in the direction of its flow
questions.explanation: Valve sounds travel with the blood in the direction of flow, so a valve is heard where its ejected stream lies closest to the chest wall. Aortic ejection is directed up-and-right, so it is loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space — not over the valve itself.

questions.question: An inferior myocardial infarction frequently causes heart block. Which anatomical relationship best explains this?
options: A. The right coronary artery usually supplies both the SA and the AV nodes
B. The circumflex artery usually supplies the bundle of His and its branches
C. The left anterior descending artery is the main supply to both cardiac nodes
D. The moderator band conveys the nodal artery across to the AV node itself
questions.explanation: The right coronary artery typically supplies the SA and AV nodes, so an inferior/RCA-territory infarct can compromise the AV node and produce heart block. The LAD supplies the anterior wall and septum, not usually the nodes.

questions.question: The azygos venous system chiefly provides a collateral connection between which two vessels?
options: A. The superior and inferior venae cavae
B. The pulmonary veins and the left atrium
C. The hepatic portal vein and the IVC
D. The subclavian vein and the internal jugular vein
questions.explanation: The azygos, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins form a collateral channel linking the SVC and IVC along the posterior thoracic wall — a vital bypass if either cava is obstructed.

questions.question: Which of these arteries is a branch of the external carotid artery?
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid is the first external carotid branch (Some Anatomists Love Freaking Out Poor Med Students). The ophthalmic and anterior cerebral arise from the internal carotid, and the vertebral from the subclavian.

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the thoracic inlet?
questions.explanation: The inlet is bounded by the T1 vertebra posteriorly, the first ribs and costal cartilages laterally, and the superior border of the manubrium anteriorly.

questions.question: Which vessel is an artery that carries deoxygenated blood?
questions.explanation: All systemic arteries — the aorta, coronary and carotid arteries — carry oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery (like the fetal umbilical artery) is the exception that carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart. 'Artery' denotes direction (away from the heart), not oxygen content.

questions.question: Stimulating the vagus nerve to the heart produces which combination of effects?
options: A. Decreased heart rate and slowed AV-node conduction
B. Increased heart rate and increased contractile force
C. Increased AV-node conduction velocity and decreased rate
D. Decreased rate but markedly increased contractile force
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic (vagal, CN X) supply slows the SA node and AV-node conduction with only minimal effect on force. The sympathetic cardiac nerves (T1–T5) do the opposite: up-rate, up-force and faster AV conduction.

dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.title: DNA Replication
dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.content: Eukaryotic DNA replication: structure, semi-conservative principle, the four steps, and the polymerases/proofreading (MEDI2200 Wk5, Parts I-III).

questions.question: How does the sugar in DNA differ from the sugar in RNA?
options: A. It lacks a hydroxyl at the 3′ carbon
B. It lacks a hydroxyl at the 2′ carbon
C. It carries an extra phosphate group
D. It forms a six-membered ring
questions.explanation: DNA's sugar is 2′-deoxyribose — it lacks the 2′-OH that ribose has, which makes DNA chemically more stable and suited to being the archival copy.

questions.question: In DNA, adenine base-pairs with:
questions.explanation: A pairs T (two hydrogen bonds). Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, not DNA — a common trap.

questions.question: New DNA strands are synthesised in which direction?
options: C. Either, depending on the strand
questions.explanation: Nucleotides can only be added to a free 3′-OH, so synthesis is always 5′→3′ on both strands — the constraint behind the leading/lagging split.

questions.question: 'Semi-conservative' replication means each new double helix contains:
options: B. One original strand and one new strand
D. A patchwork of old and new within each strand
questions.explanation: Each parental strand is kept as a template, so every daughter duplex is half old, half new. A patchwork within each strand would be 'dispersive' — not what happens.

questions.question: Okazaki fragments are made on the:
questions.explanation: The lagging strand runs opposite to fork movement, so it is built discontinuously in short Okazaki fragments; the leading strand is continuous.

questions.question: The primer that starts each new DNA strand is made of:
questions.explanation: Primase (an RNA polymerase) lays a short RNA primer, providing the 3′-OH that DNA polymerase needs to begin.

questions.question: The short arm of a chromosome is designated:
questions.explanation: Short arm = p, long arm = q; they meet at the centromere. Bands are numbered outward from the centromere.

questions.question: Which enzyme unwinds the double helix at the replication fork?
questions.explanation: MCM2-7 is the replicative helicase. Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling (a tempting distractor) but does not unwind the strands at the fork.

questions.question: DNA replication takes place during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation: Replication is confined to S phase (~8 hours), keeping it coupled to cell-cycle control.

questions.question: DNA ligase acts to:
questions.explanation: Ligase seals the nick between fragments by forming a phosphodiester bond between a 3′-OH and a 5′-phosphate.

questions.question: The lagging strand is made discontinuously because:
options: A. Its template is more tightly wound than the leading one
B. Only it can be copied by RNA primase
C. It accumulates more errors than the leading strand
D. Its template runs opposite to fork movement
questions.explanation: Synthesis is 5′→3′ only; on the lagging template that direction points away from the fork, so it must be copied backward in Okazaki fragments.

questions.question: The 3′ exonuclease activity of a DNA polymerase:
options: A. Adds nucleotides to the 5′ end
B. Synthesises the short RNA primer
C. Removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide
D. Unwinds the parental duplex ahead
questions.explanation: Proofreading backs up over a wrongly inserted base and excises it, cutting the error rate ~100-1000×.

questions.question: Which polymerase synthesises the leading strand?
questions.explanation: Pol ε (epsilon) makes the leading strand; Pol δ (delta) makes the lagging strand; Pol α primes.

questions.question: The lagging strand is synthesised mainly by:
questions.explanation: Pol δ (delta) extends the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand; Pol ε handles the leading strand.

questions.question: PCNA raises replication efficiency by:
options: A. Removing RNA primers from the strand
B. Relaxing supercoils ahead of the fork
C. Selecting the correct incoming nucleotide
D. Clamping the polymerase onto the DNA
questions.explanation: PCNA is a ring around the DNA that tethers the polymerase so it stays on — giving high processivity.

questions.question: Replication protein A (RPA) functions to:
options: A. Coat the exposed single strand
C. Add the first RNA primer
questions.explanation: RPA binds single-stranded DNA to protect it and stop the strands re-annealing until they are copied.

questions.question: Roughly how many origins of replication fire per eukaryotic cell cycle?
questions.explanation: Thousands of origins are needed because forks move only ~2-3 kb/min; they also fire in a staggered fashion, not all at once.

questions.question: Topoisomerases are required during replication to:
options: A. Proofread the newly synthesised strand
B. Join the two daughter helices together
C. Relieve over-winding ahead of the fork
D. Load the sliding clamp onto DNA
questions.explanation: Unwinding over-winds the DNA ahead of the fork; topoisomerases nick, let the strain unwind, then reseal.

questions.question: Primase is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Primase makes RNA de novo, so it is an RNA polymerase — the only replication enzyme that can start a strand from nothing.

questions.question: During lagging-strand maturation, FEN1 endonuclease:
options: A. Seals the final phosphodiester bond
questions.explanation: As Pol δ displaces the downstream fragment into a flap, FEN1 cuts it off; DNA ligase then seals the nick.

questions.question: A tumour with a Pol ε (POLE) proofreading mutation becomes 'ultra-mutated' because loss of 3′ exonuclease activity:
options: A. Halts all DNA synthesis at the replication fork
B. Prevents removal of every RNA primer
C. Removes proofreading, so errors rise about 100-fold
D. Blocks the MCM helicase at each origin
questions.explanation: Proofreading normally cuts the error rate ~100×; without it, mutations accumulate genome-wide (the fidelity 'layers' run in reverse).

questions.question: Why are RNA primers removed and replaced with DNA before ligation?
options: A. RNA cannot base-pair with the DNA template
B. RNA primers are built in the 3′→5′ direction
C. Ligase can only join RNA to other RNA
D. RNA is less stable and was made with low fidelity
questions.explanation: The finished genome must be all DNA: the temporary primers (and Pol α's error-prone DNA) are excised and rebuilt accurately, then sealed.

questions.question: A fully heavy-labelled DNA duplex replicates once in light medium. Each daughter duplex is:
options: A. Entirely heavy in both strands
B. Entirely light in both strands
C. One all-heavy duplex plus one all-light duplex
D. A hybrid: one heavy strand, one light strand
questions.explanation: Semi-conservative replication keeps each old (heavy) strand and pairs it with a new (light) one — the classic Meselson-Stahl result. Option D describes conservative replication.

questions.question: Pol δ is slightly less accurate than Pol ε. Overall lagging-strand fidelity is kept high by:
options: A. Pol ε proofreading the lagging strand as well
B. Extra mismatch repair on the lagging strand
C. Primase correcting errors as it primes
D. PCNA excising mismatched bases directly
questions.explanation: The lecture notes the lower fidelity of Pol δ is counterbalanced by more active mismatch repair on that strand.

questions.question: Replication licensing ensures each origin fires only once per cycle by:
options: A. Degrading each origin sequence once it is used
B. Firing all origins together at the G1/S boundary
C. Separating helicase loading (G1) from firing (S)
D. Requiring two rounds of firing per origin
questions.explanation: MCM helicases are loaded in G1 but can only fire in S, and firing blocks any reloading — so a fired origin can't restart until the next cycle.

questions.question: What supplies the energy for adding each nucleotide during DNA synthesis?
options: A. Hydrolysis of ATP by the polymerase
B. Cleavage of the incoming dNTP to dNMP + PPi
C. A conformational change in the sliding clamp
D. A proton gradient across the nuclear envelope
questions.explanation: Each incoming dNTP is hydrolysed to a dNMP plus pyrophosphate; that release of pyrophosphate drives the addition — no separate ATP is needed.

questions.question: Most of the DNA initially laid down by Pol α is later replaced because:
options: A. Pol α cannot proofread, so its DNA is error-prone
B. Pol α synthesises only RNA primers, never DNA
C. Pol α works solely on the leading strand
D. Pol α is completely blocked by the PCNA clamp
questions.explanation: Pol α lacks 3′ exonuclease proofreading, so its stretch is relatively inaccurate and Pol δ replaces most of it.

questions.question: 'Strand-displacement synthesis' by Pol δ means Pol δ:
options: A. Runs into the next fragment, lifting a 5′ flap
B. Hands the lagging strand over to Pol ε
C. Evicts the MCM helicase from the fork
D. Unwinds the parental duplex ahead of itself
questions.explanation: On reaching the previous Okazaki fragment, Pol δ pushes into it and displaces its 5′ end as a flap, which FEN1 then removes.

questions.question: Given forks move only ~2-3 kb/min, firing tens of thousands of origins is needed mainly to:
options: A. Finish the genome within one S phase
B. Raise the overall accuracy of the copy
C. Remove the need for any topoisomerase
questions.explanation: One fork would take far too long to copy a chromosome; thousands of origins provide the throughput to finish in a single ~8-hour S phase.

questions.question: Compared with an AT-rich region, a GC-rich region will:
options: A. Melt apart more easily at lower temperature
B. Have fewer hydrogen bonds per base pair
C. Require more energy to separate into single strands
D. Pair adenine directly with cytosine
questions.explanation: C-G pairs have three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, so GC-rich DNA is more stable and harder to melt apart.

soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.title: Researching Everyday Life — Ethnography & the Go-Along
soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.content: SOCI1010 Week 4 on the methods of studying everyday life: wrapping up Garfinkel's ethnomethodology and Goffman's dramaturgy, the self-checkout as Weber's rationalisation, research design (deductive/inductive, quant/qual/mixed), ethnography (thick description, the two components, emic/etic, the positioned subject) and its history (Malinowski, the Chicago School), four case studies (Goffman's total institution, Willis, Wacquant, Venkatesh), and the week's reading — Kusenbach's go-along and its five themes.

questions.question: Which sociologist coined the term 'ethnomethodology' and used breaching experiments?
questions.explanation: Garfinkel introduced ethnomethodology in Studies in Ethnomethodology (1967) and pioneered breaching experiments. Goffman is dramaturgy; Weber is rationalisation; Willis studied the 'lads'.

questions.question: A breaching experiment works by:
options: A. surveying a large representative sample to find a statistical trend
B. living abroad for years to learn a community's language and customs
C. measuring observed behaviour against a clearly stated prior hypothesis
D. deliberately breaking a tacit rule to expose it through the reaction
questions.explanation: Breaking an unwritten rule (e.g. over-answering 'How are you?') makes it visible via the discomfort it provokes. The other options describe surveys, Malinowski-style fieldwork, and deductive testing.

questions.question: In Goffman's dramaturgy, a waiter relaxing out of role in the kitchen is on the:
questions.explanation: Back stage is where the performance relaxes; front stage is performing to the diners. Emic/etic and macro/micro belong to other parts of the lecture.

questions.question: The word 'ethnography' breaks down to mean, roughly:
questions.explanation: Ethno = people/culture, graphy = writing. 'Study of methods' loosely fits ethno-methodology; measuring trends is quantitative; production of space is Lefebvre (Week 3).

questions.question: Which method is best suited to capturing people's subjective, lived experience of everyday life?
questions.explanation: Qualitative research prioritises meaning and lived experience; the census, polls and statistics are quantitative tools for measuring and generalising trends.

questions.question: Bronisław Malinowski's foundational ethnographic fieldwork was conducted in the:
questions.explanation: Malinowski studied the Trobriand Islands (1915–19). Goffman's PhD was in the Shetlands; the Robert Taylor Homes were Venkatesh's site; Hammertown was Willis's.

questions.question: The 'go-along' method, as Kusenbach defines it, means the researcher:
options: A. mails a questionnaire to residents of an area
B. observes a street from a fixed hidden vantage point
C. accompanies an informant on a natural everyday outing
D. interviews the informant in a quiet office
questions.explanation: A go-along walks or rides with the informant on their own routine trip, asking and observing in situ. The others are a survey, static observation and a sit-down interview.

questions.question: Which of these is one of Kusenbach's five themes the go-along is suited to explore?
questions.explanation: Her five are perception, spatial practices, biographies, social architecture and social realms. Surface acting is Hochschild, the iron cage is Weber, and banal nationalism is Billig (Week 3).

questions.question: The lecture frames the self-checkout mainly through which Weberian idea?
questions.explanation: Self-checkouts illustrate rationalisation, the iron cage, and the irrationality of rationality. Emotional labour is Hochschild; production of space is Lefebvre; symbolic interactionism is a separate micro tradition.

questions.question: A researcher wanders into a classroom with no prior hypothesis, watches what students do with their phones, and only afterwards forms a general conclusion. This reasoning is:
questions.explanation: Building a general conclusion up from specific observations is inductive; starting from a hypothesis to test would be deductive. Quantitative and etic name a data type and a viewpoint, not the direction of reasoning.

questions.question: Knowing that a 'wink' carries a coded insider meaning while a 'blink' is just dust in the eye is an example of grasping the:
questions.explanation: The emic perspective is the insider's point of view that distinguishes a meaningful wink from a mere blink; the etic is the outsider's/sociologist's view. Macro structure and front-stage scripts are different concepts.

questions.question: Ethnography is said to have two components. Alongside participant observation, the second is:
options: D. coding a large survey dataset
questions.explanation: The two components are (1) participant observation and (2) recording/documenting what one sees and hears — 'he writes' (Geertz). Sampling, experiments and survey coding belong to other methods.

questions.question: Describing ethnographers as 'positioned subjects' captures the claim that they:
options: A. must remain detached, neutral observers of social reality
B. rely mainly on numerical data to stay unbiased
C. impose a fixed hypothesis on the field before entering
D. do not try to be objective but become part of the world they study
questions.explanation: Ethnographers are the research tool; the work is experiential, subjective and dialogical, and meaning is negotiated. Detachment, numerical neutrality and a fixed prior hypothesis describe the opposite stance.

questions.question: The Chicago School's approach to studying the city is best summarised as:
options: A. deductive survey research designed to test a set of fixed prior hypotheses
B. treating the city as a 'social experiment' studied by participant observation
C. armchair analysis of second-hand reports sent back by traders and explorers
D. purely statistical modelling of the city's shifting crime and poverty rates
questions.explanation: Dissatisfied with the survey method, they treated the city as a living social experiment and used inductive participant observation. Armchair analysis is what Malinowski rejected; the survey/statistical options are the very approach they moved away from.

questions.question: Which practice was central to Malinowski's method?
options: A. Running brief structured interviews with a large representative sample
B. Keeping daily diary entries while living long-term among the people studied
C. Analysing traders' and explorers' second-hand reports from back home
D. Timing and measuring informants' regular walking routes with an odometer
questions.explanation: Malinowski kept daily diaries, learned the language and stayed long in the field. Second-hand reports are 'armchair anthropology' he rejected; timing walking routes is Kusenbach's informant Tony, not Malinowski.

questions.question: Goffman's 'total institution' is defined by which feature?
options: A. A voluntary open space that people freely enter and leave again each day
B. An enclosed, formally administered life cut off from the wider community
C. A market arena where transactions are purely instrumental and calculable
D. A public street governed by the unspoken logic of smooth pedestrian flow
questions.explanation: A total institution (asylum, prison, monastery, army camp) encloses similarly-situated people under one administered regime, stripping identity. The other options describe an ordinary workplace, Simmel's money relations, and Blomley's sidewalk.

questions.question: Willis's central explanation for why working-class 'lads' end up in working-class jobs is that they:
options: A. are passively processed by schools into docile, compliant future workers
B. are formally barred from better jobs by examination and testing hurdles alone
C. actively 'let themselves' through a counter-school culture of resistance
D. simply lack the cognitive ability that the school curriculum sets out to measure
questions.explanation: Willis argued the lads consciously reject school via a culture of resistance and choose manual work — 'why they let themselves' — reproducing class. The passive-processing view is exactly the Marxist account he revised.

questions.question: Wacquant joined a boxing gym and trained himself in order to honour Bourdieu's claim that:
questions.explanation: Bourdieu's 'we learn by body' warrants embodied participation — the sociologist submits to 'the fire of action in situ'. The other phrases are Lefebvre, Durkheim and Goffman respectively.

questions.question: How did Venkatesh's Robert Taylor Homes research change after his first encounter with the gang?
options: A. He abandoned fieldwork altogether for a large-scale door-to-door survey
B. He relocated the whole study to an inner-city boxing gym across town
C. He shifted from studying poverty generally to studying the gang and its leader
D. He switched to covert observation inside a psychiatric mental asylum
questions.explanation: Held at first, then invited to 'live with people', he refocused on the gang, shadowing JT for years. The survey, boxing gym and asylum belong to other studies in the lecture.

questions.question: For authenticity, Kusenbach argues a go-along should ideally be:
options: A. natural, following a trip the informant would take anyway
B. contrived, steering the informant into unfamiliar territory
C. replaced by a static sit-down interview
D. conducted only with total strangers to reduce bias
questions.explanation: Natural go-alongs track routine trips (same day/time/route), preserving authentic practice; contrived ones into unfamiliar territory yield less authentic data. She favours the go-along over the static interview.

questions.question: A key limit of the sit-down interview that the go-along overcomes is that the interview:
options: A. cannot record any of the informant's subjective meanings or interpretations at all
B. is only usable with very large, statistically representative random samples
C. structurally prevents the researcher from asking the informant any questions
D. removes people from the environment the talk is about, hiding pre-reflective detail
questions.explanation: Interviews are static and pull informants out of place, so trivial, pre-reflective environmental detail never surfaces; the go-along keeps them in situ. Interviews do access meaning and do allow questions, so those options are false.

questions.question: In the self-checkout example, replacing 10 staffed lanes with 20 self-service machines is described as the:
questions.explanation: Reconfiguring the shop floor around the machines is the 'rationalisation of space'. Desexualisation is Scott's pool study, mortification is Goffman's asylum, and the dramaturgical loop is impression management.

questions.question: Ross calls an overgrown house a 'jungle' meaning an eyesore, while Jill calls the same house a 'jungle' meaning an exotic treasure. Kusenbach uses this mainly to show that:
options: A. pre-existing 'relevances' (tastes/values) filter perception before the seeing
B. informants unconsciously copy each other's vocabulary over time
C. the aesthetic judgment is formed on the spot as a reaction to seeing the house
D. spatial practices thicken with meaning as routines are repeated
questions.explanation: The shared word with opposite meanings shows perception is filtered by relevances that were in place long before — not formed on seeing (B is the trap). Copying vocabulary is not the point, and 'thickening routines' is theme 2 (spatial practices), not perception.

questions.question: Tony times and measures his walk and buys a lottery ticket for 'fun'. Under which theme, and why is a go-along needed to see it?
options: A. Biographies — because the timed walk recalls memories of his late wife's death
B. Spatial practices — because such 'thickening' is unobservable and missed in interview
C. Social realms — because the walking route crosses from public into private space
D. Social architecture — because the route maps out his social ties to the neighbours
questions.explanation: Reframing a routine as fun/competition is a spatial practice ('thickening'); it can't be observed from outside and didn't come up when interviewed — it emerged only during the walk. The other themes describe different examples.

questions.question: Tony passing a bungalow (now behind a strip club) and recalling his post-war home and a pet duck illustrates which theme?
questions.explanation: A personal landmark triggering memory is the 'biographies' theme — the environment as a personal biographer. Social architecture is the web of relationships (Jill's front-yard status map), not landmark-triggered memory.

questions.question: Jill reads a messy 'rental' and a top model's 'wonderful' house as a status map and places her own home near the top. Kusenbach names the two operations at work as:
options: A. surface acting and deep acting
questions.explanation: Locals assess their own standing by comparing other places and positioning themselves relative to them — the social-architecture theme. Surface/deep acting is Hochschild; mortification is Goffman; emic/etic is a viewpoint pair.

questions.question: Kusenbach argues the lone, transient observer suits the PUBLIC realm, whereas the walk-along has the edge in communal and private realms. The reason is that public space is governed by:
options: A. personal, biographical knowing between familiar intimates
B. the deductive testing of pre-formed research hypotheses
C. categoric (anonymous) knowing rather than personal knowing
D. formal written norms enforced by uniformed officials
questions.explanation: In public space anonymity reigns and conduct rests on categoric (not personal) knowing, which a detached observer can access; personal/parochial realms need the grounded walk-along. Personal knowing is precisely what public space lacks.

questions.question: The lecture contrasts anthropology and sociology by saying ethnography makes the:
options: A. 'familiar unfamiliar' for anthropology and the 'unfamiliar familiar' for sociology
B. 'sacred profane' for both disciplines equally
C. 'unfamiliar familiar' for anthropology and the 'familiar unfamiliar' for sociology
D. 'front stage back stage' distinction for both
questions.explanation: Anthropology abroad makes the unfamiliar familiar; sociology at home makes the familiar unfamiliar (de-familiarising the taken-for-granted). Option B reverses it; sacred/profane and front/back stage are Durkheim and Goffman.

questions.question: A student answers 'How are you?' with 'In regard to what — my health, my finances...?' and the other person gets angry. This best demonstrates ethnomethodology's claim that:
options: A. social order only appears orderly and is recreated moment to moment
B. society rests on a durable moral consensus imposed from above
C. money reduces relationships to calculation
D. space is produced by planners and capital
questions.explanation: The breach shows order is a fragile achievement, continually re-created by actors filling in the taken-for-granted — Garfinkel's core claim. Moral consensus (Durkheim), money relations (Simmel) and produced space (Lefebvre) are other theorists' arguments.

questions.question: Goffman entered the asylum posing as an assistant so he could observe covertly. What did this position let him recover?
options: A. The 'unofficial reality' seen from the patients' point of view
B. A statistically representative sample of diagnoses
C. The managers' official account of treatment
D. A quantified measure of recovery rates
questions.explanation: Covert immersion gave him the 'unofficial reality' from the patients' standpoint, rather than the psychiatric categories imposed on them — showing behaviour that looks insane outside is rational in context. The other options are quantitative or the official view he looked past.

questions.question: Kusenbach's overall argument about the go-along relative to observation and interviewing is that it is:
options: A. a hybrid whose strengths accumulate best when the three are combined
B. strictly superior and should replace both
C. only a way to recruit people for later formal interviews
D. unable to access meaning because the researcher intrudes
questions.explanation: She argues not for superiority but for combining methods to gather 'many kinds of evidence' (Becker); the go-along is a hybrid of observation and interviewing. It does access meaning and does more than mere recruitment, so C and D are wrong.

soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.title: Class, Gender & Bodies — The Sociology of the Body
soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.content: Week 5 of Introduction to Sociology: the sociology of the body. Opens with a history of the toilet, then covers class (Marx, Weber, Bourdieu), embodiment (Foucault, Bourdieu, Goffman, Young), the sex-gender system and contemporary bodies (neoliberal self, Hockey's trainers/material culture, ageing and non-human bodies), integrating the Archer, Young and Hockey readings.

questions.question: Why does the lecturer open a lecture on class, gender and bodies by discussing the history of the toilet?
options: A. To prove that bodily functions are ultimately biological, not social
B. To argue that plumbing technology created the modern class system
C. To show a mundane object reveals the social organisation of the body
D. To demonstrate that toilet design is identical across all cultures
questions.explanation: It is the lecturer's trademark 'sociology of the banal': a bizarre everyday object exposes how the body is socially organised (nature/culture, class, gender, privacy). A, B and D each contradict the lecture's point that the body's organisation is social and culturally variable.

questions.question: In Elizabeth Shove's practice theory, the learned ability to squat comfortably at a squat toilet counts as which element of the practice?
options: A. A material — the physical technology the practice relies on
B. A competence — the bodily skill and know-how it demands
C. A meaning — the taboo or value attached to the practice
D. A discourse — the authoritative knowledge that governs it
questions.explanation: Competences are the skills and bodily know-how a practice needs; squatting is a learned competence 'inscribed on the body' (Mauss). Materials are the technologies (the toilet itself), meanings are the taboos/values, and 'discourse' is Foucault's term, not one of Shove's three elements.

questions.question: The lecture calls elimination a 'human leveller' yet insists the toilet is socially differentiated. Which statement best captures this dual claim?
options: A. Because toilets differ by wealth, the biological need itself differs by class
B. Elimination is universal, which proves class differences are imaginary
C. Only in the West is elimination treated as a private, individual act
D. All must eliminate, yet the technology and meanings are class-shaped
questions.explanation: The universal act ('bodily democracy') is exactly what makes the layered differences — a luxury Japanese toilet vs a pit latrine, gendered vs unisex rooms — legible as social, not natural. A and B misread the leveller claim; C overstates the modern/Western privatization point.

questions.question: For Marx, the two great classes of capitalist society are distinguished by which single criterion?
options: A. Whether they make profits or earn wages
B. The social honour and prestige they command
C. The amount of cultural taste they display
D. The size of the social networks they hold
questions.explanation: Marx bases class on the split between those who make profits (bourgeoisie, who own the means of production) and those who earn wages (proletariat). Social honour is Weber's status; cultural taste and networks are Bourdieu's cultural and social capital.

questions.question: Marx's concept of 'surplus value' most precisely refers to which of the following?
options: A. The total revenue a company earns before it deducts any costs
B. The value a worker creates beyond the wage they are paid
C. The personal savings a worker accumulates across a career
D. The prestige a worker gains from holding a skilled job
questions.explanation: Surplus value is the value workers create over and above their wage, which the owner appropriates as profit (the iPhone made for ~$200 selling for ~$1700). A confuses it with gross revenue; C is personal saving; D is Weber's status.

questions.question: The lecture stresses that Marxian exploitation is 'structural, not personal.' What does this mean?
options: A. It happens only in factories, never in cafes or in retail
B. It is the feeling of disconnection a worker has from their product
C. It is built into the relationship, whatever the boss's manner
D. It occurs only where an employer deliberately mistreats staff
questions.explanation: Exploitation is the systemic appropriation of surplus value, so it operates even if the employer is personally decent — a property of the relationship, not a moral failing. A is false (the barista example is used); B describes alienation; D inverts the claim.

questions.question: Which everyday parallel does the lecturer use to explain Marx's concept of alienation?
options: A. Feeling proud of a chair you built and bartered with a neighbour
B. Feeling out of place at a formal dinner with many cutleries
C. Feeling certain that a doctor's diagnosis must be correct
D. Feeling that an essay handed to GPT is not really yours
questions.explanation: Alienation is losing a meaningful connection to what you produce; the GPT-essay that doesn't feel like yours captures it. A is the pre-alienation craftsman (the contrast case); B illustrates Bourdieu's habitus; C illustrates the medical gaze/biopower.

questions.question: Weber defines the 'class' dimension of stratification chiefly in terms of which of the following?
options: A. Internalised bodily dispositions acquired in childhood
B. Ownership of the means of production, and nothing else
C. The performance of a role in front of an audience
D. Market-determined life chances from property and skills
questions.explanation: For Weber, class is market-determined life chances resting on property (assets) and skills/education (credentials). A is Bourdieu's habitus; B is Marx's single criterion, which Weber broadens; C is Goffman's dramaturgy.

questions.question: Weber adds a dimension Marx omits: social honour granted for group membership, based on lifestyle and consumption. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Status is Weber's honour/prestige dimension, based on consumption, lifestyle and the 'us vs them' distinction. Class is the market dimension (broadly shared with Marx); capital and habitus are both Bourdieu's terms.

questions.question: The lecturer contrasts King Charles ('high status, little power') with the Pope ('high status and power') in order to show that:
options: A. Status and power are separate axes that need not align
B. Economic ownership ultimately determines everything else
C. Charismatic authority always outranks traditional authority
D. Cultural capital can be converted into economic capital
questions.explanation: The point is Weberian: because prestige (status) and authority (party/power) can come apart, stratification needs more than one axis. B is Marx (and contradicts the example); C is not the lesson drawn; D is a Bourdieusian claim about a different theorist.

questions.question: Which statement best defines Bourdieu's concept of 'habitus'?
options: A. The honour conferred by membership of a recognised status group
B. Internalised, embodied structures shaping how we perceive
C. A structured social arena organised around types of capital
D. The surplus value that owners appropriate from their workers
