questions.explanation: Habitus is the internalised, 'embodied' social structures that shape what feels normal or 'for people like us.' A is Weber's status; C defines Bourdieu's field (not habitus); D is Marx's surplus value.

questions.question: A violinist who is not wealthy and has few connections is nonetheless widely revered as world-class. In Bourdieu's terms this person is richest in:
options: A. Economic capital and surplus value
B. Social capital and party power
C. Cultural capital and symbolic capital
D. Property capital and life chances
questions.explanation: Mastery of the instrument is embodied cultural capital, and the reverence it earns is symbolic capital — you can be rich in these while poor in economic and social capital. The other options pair a Bourdieu term with a Marx (surplus value) or Weber (party, life chances) term.

questions.question: The lecturer's shorthand 'who you know' corresponds to which of Bourdieu's four capitals?
questions.explanation: Social capital = networks of influence/support ('who you know', e.g. LinkedIn, an influencer's following). Cultural = 'what you know' (taste/credentials), symbolic = prestige/honour, economic = 'what you have' (money).

questions.question: Two students of equal ability differ: A assumes she should apply to the top university; B feels 'people like me don't belong there.' This best illustrates:
options: A. Bourdieu's habitus, a felt sense of one's place
B. Weber's concept of party, or power over others
C. Marx's reserve army of surplus, cheap labour
D. Goffman's back-stage region of the performance
questions.explanation: Same test scores, different disposition: habitus shapes what feels possible or comfortable, steering real choices. B concerns authority over others; C concerns labour supply; D is the off-stage region in dramaturgy, not a sense of one's social place.

questions.question: The week's class reading, Archer's 'Class and Class Relations,' deploys Marx, Weber and Bourdieu mainly to challenge which idea?
options: A. That gender is a purely biological phenomenon
B. That Australia is a classless 'fair-go' society
C. That the medical gaze depersonalises the patient
D. That trainers can be used to resist gender norms
questions.explanation: Archer marshals the three class theorists against the Australian myth of an egalitarian society where 'class' is a 'dirty word.' A belongs to §3 (sex-gender), C to Foucault, and D to the Hockey reading.

questions.question: In The Birth of the Clinic, Foucault's 'medical gaze' does what to the patient?
options: A. Rewards the patient with social status for being ill
B. Turns the patient into a performer managing impressions
C. Treats the patient as a whole person with a relationship
D. Separates the body from the person as a 'text to read'
questions.explanation: Under the medical gaze the person becomes 'a site of observable phenomena' — the body is abstracted from the person and diagnosed, which is depersonalising. A confuses illness with Weber's status; B is Goffman; C is the gaze's opposite.

questions.question: Foucault would classify public-health messages like 'don't sit in the sun more than 20 minutes' as an example of:
options: A. Biopower — medical knowledge as control of the body
B. Alienation — a lost connection to one's own labour
C. Symbolic capital — prestige recognised by others
D. Impression management — controlling how one appears
questions.explanation: Because medical discourse is authoritative, its rules regulate everyday conduct — biopower welds knowledge of life/the body to power (defining normal vs pathological = medicalization). B is Marx, C is Bourdieu, D is Goffman.

questions.question: Foucault's Panopticon produces disciplined conduct primarily because:
options: A. Guards physically punish every prisoner who steps out of line
B. Prisoners, unsure if watched, come to police themselves
C. Prisoners are granted high status for good behaviour
D. The prison converts prisoners' labour into surplus value
questions.explanation: The watchtower design means the possibility of being watched is internalised, so power is exercised from within ('you do it yourself') without constant external force. A is the pre-modern model Foucault contrasts; C and D import Weber and Marx.

questions.question: Bourdieu calls habitus 'history transformed into nature' and a 'conductorless orchestration.' The deeper point is that:
options: A. Society appoints a conductor to coordinate everyone's conduct
B. Bodily habits are fixed at birth and can never be altered
C. Class dispositions feel innate though they were learned
D. Only the wealthy classes actually possess a habitus
questions.explanation: Habitus is powerful because it is 'forgotten history' — socially learned dispositions that feel biological, so coordinated conduct appears without any conductor. A misreads 'conductorless'; B is false (habitus is 'changeable' via reflexivity); D is false (everyone has a habitus).

questions.question: In Goffman's dramaturgical metaphor, the 'back stage' is where:
options: A. We are out of role and the performance relaxes
B. We perform a role to an audience by the scene's rules
C. The medical gaze is applied to the patient's body
D. Surplus value is extracted from a worker's labour
questions.explanation: Back stage (e.g. the kitchen) is where the performer drops the mask; front stage (the dining room) is where the role is performed. C is Foucault and D is Marx — different theorists entirely.

questions.question: The lecturer says someone 'standing upright, looking at you straight in the eyes' is presenting the body. Which pairing best fits this?
options: A. Marx's alienation and Weber's dimension of party power
B. Foucault's biopower and Young's restricted motility
C. Goffman's impression management and Bourdieu's habitus
D. Kopytoff's commoditisation and informal singularisation
questions.explanation: Bearing is both a managed performance (Goffman) and a class disposition inscribed in the body (Bourdieu) — the lecture explicitly links the two. The other pairs name real concepts that do not describe posture-as-self-presentation.

questions.question: Iris Marion Young argues that 'throwing like a girl' is best understood as:
options: A. A biological difference that is present from birth
B. A socially produced, restricted style of movement
C. A form of Goffmanian impression management
D. A type of Bourdieusian cultural capital
questions.explanation: Young rejects the biological explanation (Straus) and argues the inhibited style is socially produced through gendered socialisation. A is the view she refutes; C is Goffman's; D is Bourdieu's.

questions.question: Which description best fits Young's 'restricted' or 'inhibited' modalities of feminine movement?
options: A. The body is a transparent medium fully mastering its world
B. The body is performed differently front stage and back stage
C. The whole body flows in fluid, directed motion at the target
D. Motion sits in one part and does not reach or follow through
questions.explanation: Young's modalities describe motion concentrated in one part (e.g. the arm), not reaching/extending/following through in the direction of intention. A describes Merleau-Ponty's unproblematic 'I can'; B is Goffman; C is the un-inhibited (masculine-coded) style.

questions.question: Young builds her phenomenology on the 'lived body' and the immanence/transcendence tension. These derive respectively from:
options: A. Michel Foucault and Karl Marx
B. Max Weber and Emile Durkheim
C. Merleau-Ponty and Simone de Beauvoir
D. Pierre Bourdieu and Erving Goffman
questions.explanation: Merleau-Ponty supplies the lived body (the 'I can'); de Beauvoir supplies woman-as-Other and the immanence/transcendence tension. Young adds the feminine 'I cannot.' The other pairings are theorists from elsewhere in the unit.

questions.question: The 'sex-gender system' argues that:
options: A. Biological sex differences make men more capable than women
B. A biological difference is tied to an unequal social order
C. Gender and sexuality are one and the same phenomenon
D. Nature favours one sex over the other for social success
questions.explanation: The system 'translates' a biological difference into an 'order of value' in which men are treated as primary — the inequality lives in the social arrangement, not the biology. A naturalises inequality (the opposite of the argument); C collapses distinct axes; D inverts the claim that nature favours neither.

questions.question: In the lecture's definitions, which axis does 'intersex' belong to, and which does 'nonbinary' belong to?
options: A. Intersex under sex; nonbinary under gender
B. Intersex under gender; nonbinary under sex
C. Intersex under sexuality; nonbinary under sex
D. Both intersex and nonbinary under sexuality
questions.explanation: Intersex describes biological sex (reproductive anatomy/chromosomes/hormones); nonbinary describes gender (identity outside the man/woman categories). Sexuality (straight/gay/lesbian/bisexual) is a third, separate axis, so B, C and D misassign the terms.

questions.question: Which athlete does the lecture use for the sex-verification and testosterone scrutiny an intersex woman faced in athletics?
questions.explanation: Caster Semenya, an intersex woman, was subjected to sex-verification and testosterone rules by the IAAF. Hubbard is the transgender weightlifter; Wendy Davis is the pink-trainers filibuster (Hockey reading); Kate Winslet refused digital slimming (Kilbourne).

questions.question: The Norwegian handball team was fined for wearing shorts instead of the required bikini bottoms. Sociologically this is best read as:
options: A. Gatekeeping that polices the binary for a male audience
B. Proof that women lack the skill to play elite handball
C. An instance of the medical gaze operating within sport
D. A case of informal singularisation of a commodity
questions.explanation: The uniform rule enforces gendered display 'for the male audience' — a gatekeeping intervention that polices the binary. B is not a sociological reading; C is Foucault's clinic concept; D is Kopytoff/Hockey applied to objects, not uniforms.

questions.question: The 'toned body as cultural icon' is tied most directly to which logic?
options: A. The logic of Durkheim's collective conscience
B. The logic of Weber's charismatic authority
C. The logic of neoliberal capitalism and self-work
D. The logic of Marxist proletarian revolution
questions.explanation: The firm body signals willpower and 'caring' about oneself; neoliberalism shifts responsibility for self-improvement onto the individual (you fund the gym, coaching, yoga). A, B and D name real frameworks not used for the toned body here.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches the early- and late-capitalist body?
options: A. Early = the body as a project; late = the human leveller
B. Early = consumption and leisure; late = the work ethic
C. Early = hedonism and desire; late = discipline, asceticism
D. Early = discipline, asceticism; late = hedonism, the project
questions.explanation: Early capitalism links the body to discipline, asceticism and production (the work ethic); late capitalism emphasises hedonism, desire, consumption and the body as a 'project.' C reverses the eras; A and B misassign both.

questions.question: What is the central question of Hockey et al.'s study of trainers?
options: A. How individuals design and manufacture better trainers
B. How trainers 'make' the individual as a body prosthetic
C. How wearing trainers causes repetitive strain injuries
D. How the price of trainers is set by supply and demand
questions.explanation: Hockey et al. reverse the usual question to ask how the trainer 'makes' the wearer — a body prosthetic entangled with embodied identity. A is the conventional question they set aside; C and D are not the paper's focus.

questions.question: A generic 1970s trainer that consumers begin to prize and re-classify as a 'vintage collectible' illustrates Kopytoff's concept of:
questions.explanation: Singularisation is the process by which private meanings make an object special and differentiated (a collectible), as opposed to commoditisation (an object reduced to exchange value among identical units). Alienation is Marx; medicalization is Foucault.

questions.question: Senator Wendy Davis's 'hot pink' trainers, worn for an 11-hour filibuster, are used by Hockey et al. to show that trainers can:
options: A. Only ever reproduce conventional gender and class norms
B. Depersonalise the wearer under the clinical medical gaze
C. Resist and subvert gender, class and sexuality norms
D. Serve as economic capital that converts into status
questions.explanation: Through singularisation, the same object that usually signals gender/class norms can subvert them — Davis's pink running shoes politicise the trainer. A ignores the reading's 'resistance' argument; B is Foucault; D borrows Bourdieu/Weber for something the example is not about.

questions.question: Which of the following is the lecture's example of 'non-human bodies' in everyday life?
options: A. Cadavers dissected in the early modern clinic
B. Athletes' bodies used as professional tools
C. Women's bodies represented in advertising
D. Socially-assistive robots in Japanese aged-care
questions.explanation: Socially-assistive robots (aged-care carers that converse and 'express emotion', robot teachers) are the 'non-human bodies' frontier. A relates to Foucault's clinic, B to the toned/athletic body, and C to Kilbourne — all human bodies.

questions.question: The conclusion frames the body through three lenses. Which lens is paired with the correct theorist?
options: A. 'Lived experience' paired with Michel Foucault
B. 'Social phenomenon' paired with Bourdieu and Goffman
C. 'Political subject' paired with Iris Marion Young
D. 'Lived experience' paired with Erving Goffman
questions.explanation: The body as social phenomenon = Bourdieu's habitus and Goffman's dramaturgy. Lived experience pairs with Young (phenomenology) and political subject with Foucault (gaze/biopower) — so A, C and D swap the theorist onto the wrong lens.

questions.question: An 'intersectional' understanding of the body, as the lecture uses it, means:
options: A. Studying only the single most important axis for a body
B. Studying the body purely as a biological organism
C. Studying class, gender, race and ability as overlapping
D. Studying bodies only where two physical roads intersect
questions.explanation: Intersectionality treats class, gender, race and ability as overlapping and mutually constituting, applied via the sociological imagination. A reduces it to one axis, B strips out the social, and D takes 'intersection' literally.

pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.title: Pelvis, Hip Joint & the Lower Limb
pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.content: General organisation of the lower limb (regions, fascia, compartments, nerves, line of gravity); osteology of the hip bone, sacrum and proximal femur; the pelvic joints and their ligaments; the hip joint (articular surfaces, capsule, ligaments, blood supply, movements); and the clinical anatomy of hip dislocations and femoral fractures.

questions.question: In anatomical terminology, the 'leg' refers to which segment of the lower limb?
options: A. The knee to the ankle only
B. The whole limb below the hip
C. The hip to the knee
D. The ankle and the foot
questions.explanation: The 'leg' is strictly the knee-to-ankle segment (tibia and fibula); the hip-to-knee segment is the thigh.

questions.question: Which bone is the pelvic girdle of the lower limb?
questions.explanation: The hip bone (os coxae) is the pelvic girdle, joining the free limb to the axial skeleton at the sacrum and pubic symphysis.

questions.question: What is the deep fascia of the thigh called?
questions.explanation: The fascia lata is the deep fascia of the thigh; the crural fascia is that of the leg.

questions.question: Which three bones fuse to form the mature hip bone?
questions.explanation: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the acetabulum to form the os coxae.

questions.question: Which bony landmark is the 'sitting bone' and the origin of the hamstrings?
questions.explanation: The ischial tuberosity bears weight in sitting and gives origin to the hamstrings.

questions.question: The hip joint is classified as which type of synovial joint?
options: A. Hinge, uniaxial like the elbow
C. Plane, gliding like the facets
questions.explanation: The hip is a ball-and-socket (multiaxial) joint between the femoral head and the acetabulum.

questions.question: The sacrum is formed by the fusion of how many vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The sacrum is five fused vertebrae forming a wedge in the pelvic ring.

questions.question: Which landmark on the femur receives the insertion of gluteus medius and minimus?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius and minimus (and the deep rotators) insert on the greater trochanter.

questions.question: Which ligament is the strongest reinforcement of the hip joint capsule?
questions.explanation: The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the body and prevents hyperextension.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists the three compartments of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The thigh has anterior, medial and posterior compartments; the leg has anterior, posterior and lateral.

questions.question: What structure passes through the saphenous opening in the fascia lata?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein dives through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein.

questions.question: In quiet standing, the line of gravity passes in which relation to the hip and knee?
options: A. Anterior to the hip, posterior to the knee
B. Through both the hip and the knee
C. Posterior to the hip, anterior to the knee
D. Posterior to both the hip and the knee
questions.explanation: It passes posterior to the hip and anterior to the knee/ankle, so ligament tension keeps the joints extended with little muscle work.

questions.question: In the anatomical position, which two landmarks lie in the same vertical plane?
options: A. ASIS and the ischial tuberosity
B. Iliac crest and the pubic tubercle
C. PSIS and the greater trochanter
D. ASIS and the superior pubic symphysis
questions.explanation: The ASIS and the top of the pubic symphysis lie in one vertical plane, defining the pelvic tilt.

questions.question: What type of joint is the sacroiliac joint, and which ligament restrains it most?
options: A. Plane synovial; interosseous sacroiliac ligament
questions.explanation: It is a weight-bearing plane synovial joint whose strongest restraint is the interosseous sacroiliac ligament.

questions.question: Which ligament converts the lesser sciatic notch into the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The sacrospinous ligament (to the ischial spine) forms the lesser foramen; the sacrotuberous forms the greater.

questions.question: A pathological decrease in the femoral neck-shaft angle is termed:
questions.explanation: A decreased angle of inclination is coxa vara; an increased angle is coxa valga.

questions.question: Which structure completes the acetabular rim inferiorly across the acetabular notch?
options: B. Ligament of the head of the femur
questions.explanation: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch, completing the socket rim below.

questions.question: The three capsular ligaments of the hip all become taut in which position?
questions.explanation: All three spiral ligaments tighten in extension, locking the head into the socket for energy-efficient standing.

questions.question: How does the pubic symphysis differ between the sexes?
options: A. It is a synovial joint in women only
B. It ossifies completely early in men
C. It lacks any interpubic disc in women
D. Its interpubic disc is thicker in women
questions.explanation: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint whose fibrocartilaginous interpubic disc is thicker in women.

questions.question: Which artery is the dominant blood supply to the head and neck of the femur in adults?
questions.explanation: The medial circumflex femoral artery supplies the head/neck via retinacular vessels; its disruption causes avascular necrosis.

questions.question: Posteriorly, the fibrous capsule of the hip attaches to which part of the femoral neck?
options: A. The full intertrochanteric crest ridge
B. The base of the lesser trochanter
C. The whole neck up to the trochanteric fossa
D. Only the proximal neck, sparing the crest
questions.explanation: Anteriorly the capsule reaches the intertrochanteric line, but posteriorly it stops at the proximal neck, leaving the posterolateral neck extracapsular.

questions.question: Why is a transcervical femoral neck fracture more dangerous to the femoral head than an intertrochanteric fracture?
options: A. It can tear the retinacular branches to the head
B. It is invariably far more displaced
C. It routinely shatters the acetabular rim
D. It transects the nearby sciatic nerve
questions.explanation: A neck (intracapsular) fracture can sever the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery supplying the head, risking avascular necrosis; intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular and usually spare that supply.

questions.question: After a dashboard injury with the hip flexed and adducted, the limb is held flexed, adducted and internally rotated. This indicates which dislocation?
questions.explanation: Posterior dislocation is commonest; the flexed, adducted, internally rotated (and shortened) limb is the classic presentation.

questions.question: The deep circular fibres of the hip capsule that collar the femoral neck are called the:
questions.explanation: The zona orbicularis (orbicular zone) grips the neck, resisting distraction of the head from the socket.

questions.question: On an AP pelvic radiograph, Shenton's line is a smooth curve joining the inferior femoral neck to which structure?
options: A. The highest point of the iliac crest
B. The line of the sacroiliac joint
C. Superior margin of the obturator foramen
D. The tip of the ischial spine
questions.explanation: Shenton's line runs from the inferior femoral neck onto the superior margin of the obturator foramen; a break signals fracture, dislocation or dysplasia.

questions.question: The artery within the ligament of the head of the femur is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: A small acetabular branch of the obturator artery runs in the ligament of the head; it is a minor supply in adults.

questions.question: Which pair best describes the two main causes of developmental (congenital) dislocation of the hip?
options: A. Femoral neck fracture and marked coxa valga
B. Sciatic nerve injury and gluteal muscle wasting
C. Avascular necrosis and an acetabular labral tear
D. Abnormal acetabular development and joint laxity
questions.explanation: DDH is more common in females and arises from abnormal acetabular development and (often inherited) generalised joint laxity.

questions.question: How do the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments stabilise the sacrum under body weight?
options: A. They permanently fuse the sacroiliac joint surfaces
B. They anchor the lower sacrum to the ischium against tilt
C. They pull the sacral promontory forward and down
D. They compress and tighten the pubic symphysis disc
questions.explanation: They anchor the lower sacrum to the ischial spine and tuberosity, so weight loading wedges rather than tips the sacrum — a self-locking keystone.

questions.question: Compared with the shoulder, the hip joint achieves greater stability chiefly because it has:
options: A. A deep socket with labrum and spiral ligaments
B. A shallower socket ringed by more muscles
C. No labrum and comparatively loose ligaments
D. A hinge-type articulation with a deep groove
questions.explanation: Both are ball-and-socket, but the hip's deep acetabulum, labrum and three strong spiral ligaments favour stability for weight-bearing, whereas the shoulder favours mobility.

gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.title: Gluteal Region & Posterior Thigh
gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.content: Muscles of the gluteal region (gluteus maximus/medius/minimus, TFL, and the deep lateral rotators — piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli, quadratus femoris); the gluteal vessels and sciatic nerve relative to piriformis; the safe quadrant for intramuscular injection; bony features of the femur, tibia and fibula; and the hamstrings of the posterior thigh with their actions and innervation.

questions.question: What is the main action of gluteus maximus at the hip?
options: B. Medial rotation of the thigh
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the powerful hip extensor, especially from a flexed position (e.g. rising from sitting or climbing).

questions.question: Which nerve supplies gluteus maximus?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve; medius, minimus and TFL are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

questions.question: Which muscles are the main abductors of the hip in the gluteal region?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius and minimus (with TFL) abduct and medially rotate the hip and keep the pelvis level in stance.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the three hamstring muscles?
questions.explanation: The hamstrings are semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris (long head); rectus femoris and sartorius are anterior-thigh muscles.

questions.question: From which bony landmark do most hamstrings take their origin?
questions.explanation: The hamstrings share a common origin from the ischial tuberosity; the short head of biceps femoris is the exception (linea aspera).

questions.question: The sciatic nerve usually exits the pelvis into the buttock in what relation to piriformis?
options: D. Through the lesser sciatic foramen
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve typically leaves the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.

questions.question: Which quadrant of the buttock is safe for an intramuscular injection?
options: A. Lower medial, near the sciatic nerve
B. Lower outer, below the muscle mass
C. Upper inner, toward the sacrum
D. Upper outer, over gluteus medius
questions.explanation: The upper outer quadrant lies over gluteus medius, away from the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal vessels.

questions.question: What is the shared action of the deep gluteal muscles (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli, quadratus femoris)?
options: B. Medial rotation of the thigh
D. Lateral rotation of the thigh
questions.explanation: The deep group are the lateral (external) rotators of the hip, running from pelvis to greater trochanter.

questions.question: Gluteus maximus and TFL both insert into which structure?
questions.explanation: Both feed the iliotibial tract; maximus also has deep fibres to the gluteal tuberosity.

questions.question: A patient's pelvis drops on the right when standing on the left leg. Which muscle is weak?
questions.explanation: The pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak muscle; standing on the left leg means the left gluteus medius (stance side) is failing.

questions.question: Gluteus medius inserts onto which surface of the greater trochanter?
questions.explanation: Medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter; minimus inserts on the anterior surface — a common exam distinction.

questions.question: Which structures leave the greater sciatic foramen ABOVE piriformis?
options: A. The sciatic nerve and its divisions
B. Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
C. Superior gluteal nerve and vessels
D. Inferior gluteal nerve and vessels
questions.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis; the sciatic, pudendal and inferior gluteal structures pass below.

questions.question: Where does piriformis originate?
options: C. Anterior surface of the sacrum
D. The outer lip of the iliac crest
questions.explanation: Piriformis arises from the anterior sacrum and inserts on the superior greater trochanter, dividing the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.question: Which hamstring does NOT arise from the ischial tuberosity and has a different nerve supply?
options: B. Short head of biceps femoris
D. Long head of biceps femoris
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris arises from the linea aspera and is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: Because the hamstrings cross both the hip and the knee, they produce which combined action?
options: A. Flex the hip and extend the knee
B. Extend both the hip and the knee
C. Abduct the hip and flex the knee
D. Extend the hip and flex the knee
questions.explanation: Spanning two joints, the hamstrings extend the thigh at the hip and flex the leg at the knee.

questions.question: Which three muscles form the 'triceps coxae' inserting together on the medial greater trochanter?
options: A. Superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus
B. Piriformis, obturator internus, quadratus femoris
D. Obturator externus, piriformis, quadratus femoris
questions.explanation: The two gemelli sandwich the obturator internus tendon, together called the triceps coxae.

questions.question: A gluteal injection placed too low and medial risks damaging which nerve?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve lies in the lower medial region beneath gluteus maximus; a low-medial needle can injure it, causing foot-drop.

questions.question: Quadratus femoris inserts onto which femoral landmark?
options: A. Gluteal tuberosity of the posterior femur
B. Lesser trochanter of the medial femur
C. Fovea capitis of the femoral head
D. Quadrate tubercle of the intertrochanteric crest
questions.explanation: Quadratus femoris runs from the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest; it is a pure lateral rotator.

questions.question: Which sciatic nerve variant most predisposes to piriformis syndrome?
options: A. The common fibular division piercing piriformis
B. The whole nerve passing below piriformis
C. The tibial division piercing obturator internus
D. The nerve passing through the lesser sciatic foramen
questions.explanation: When the common fibular division pierces piriformis, muscle contraction can compress those fibres, causing buttock pain radiating down the leg.

questions.question: Which hamstring contributes to the pes anserinus on the medial proximal tibia?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus; semimembranosus inserts on the medial tibial condyle instead.

questions.question: Why does the fibula bear almost no body weight?
options: A. It is completely fused to the tibia proximally
B. It articulates directly with the femoral condyle
C. Its head sits below the plateau, outside the knee
D. It has no distal articulation at the ankle at all
questions.explanation: The fibular head is not part of the knee joint, so femoral load passes into the tibia; the fibula mainly anchors muscles and forms the lateral malleolus.

questions.question: The common tendon of biceps femoris inserts onto which bone?
questions.explanation: Both heads of biceps femoris insert via a common tendon on the head of the fibula, forming the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve is functionally two nerves in one sheath. Which are they?
options: A. Tibial and common fibular divisions
D. Pudendal and posterior femoral cutaneous
questions.explanation: The tibial and common fibular (peroneal) divisions travel bundled in the thigh but supply different territories.

questions.question: During single-leg stance, how do the gluteus medius and minimus keep the pelvis level?
options: A. They actively lift the swinging leg's hip up on that same side
B. They forcefully extend the stance-limb hip to raise the trunk
C. Stance-side muscles pull the pelvis toward the fixed femur
D. They laterally rotate the swinging-limb femur outward in the air
questions.explanation: In a reverse-origin action, the stance-side abductors pull the pelvis down toward the planted femur, keeping the unsupported side level.

questions.question: The transverse plane through the highest points of the iliac crests crosses which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The supracristal plane crosses the L4 spinous process — the landmark used for a lumbar puncture.

questions.question: A misplaced gluteal injection injuring the common fibular fibres of the sciatic nerve would most likely produce:
options: A. Foot-drop from loss of ankle dorsiflexion
B. Loss of powerful hip extension strength
C. A Trendelenburg gait from abductor failure
D. Loss of active knee extension when walking
questions.explanation: The common fibular division supplies the dorsiflexors; its injury causes foot-drop, unlike superior gluteal injury which causes a Trendelenburg gait.

questions.question: How does obturator internus reach its insertion on the greater trochanter?
options: A. It passes above piriformis via the greater sciatic foramen
B. Its tendon hooks ~90° through the lesser sciatic foramen
C. It runs alongside the obturator nerve in the canal
D. It crosses the midline through the pubic symphysis
questions.explanation: Obturator internus arises inside the pelvis and its tendon bends ~90° through the lesser sciatic foramen (a bony pulley) to reach the medial greater trochanter.

questions.question: The visible gluteal fold (sulcus) is formed by what, rather than the muscle's edge?
options: A. A fat pad over the inferior border of gluteus maximus
B. The visible lower border of gluteus medius muscle
C. The taut lateral edge of the iliotibial tract
D. The underlying course of the sacrotuberous ligament
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus fibres run obliquely, so the horizontal fold is a fat-pad crease where the buttock meets the thigh, not the muscle's lower edge.

circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.title: MHHS2402 W7 · Circulation, Blood Pressure & Flow
circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.content: MHHS2402 Week 7 (Butlin): haemodynamics — systemic/pulmonary circuits, five vessel types, wall structure and compliance, the arterial pressure waveform, MAP/PP, Poiseuille flow=ΔP/R with resistance ∝ 1/r⁴, MAP = CO × TPR, and local (regional) autoregulation (four theories, hyperaemia, the L-arginine–NO pathway), with a pointer to the online blood-constituents module.

questions.question: Which side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body?
questions.explanation: Left = Lungs: the left atrium/ventricle receive oxygenated blood from the lungs and drive the high-pressure systemic circuit. The right heart takes deoxygenated blood from the Rest of the body to the lungs.

questions.question: Leaving the heart in either circuit, in what order does blood pass through the vessel types?
options: A. Arteries → venules → capillaries → arterioles → veins
B. Arterioles → arteries → capillaries → veins → venules
C. Veins → venules → capillaries → arterioles → arteries
D. Arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins
questions.explanation: The sequence away from the heart is arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins, in both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. Exchange happens in the middle, at the capillaries.

questions.question: The pulmonary arteries are correctly classified as arteries because they:
options: A. Carry blood away from the heart
C. Have the thickest walls in the body
D. Lie within the lung tissue
questions.explanation: An artery is defined by direction — carrying blood away from the heart — not by oxygen content. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs yet are still arteries.

questions.question: Which layer of a large vessel wall contains the smooth muscle and the load-bearing elastin and collagen?
questions.explanation: The tunica media is the middle coat holding smooth muscle plus elastin and collagen. The intima is the endothelial lining, the adventitia the outer connective sheath, and the lumen is the space (not a layer).

questions.question: At rest, roughly what proportion of the total blood volume sits in the systemic veins?
questions.explanation: Around 64% — close to two-thirds — of blood volume is held in the systemic veins, the body's capacitance reservoir, mobilised by sympathetic venoconstriction.

questions.question: The relationship flow = (P₁ − P₂) / resistance is the fluid analogue of which physical law?
questions.explanation: It mirrors Ohm's law I = V/R: pressure difference behaves like voltage, blood flow like current, and resistance like resistance.

questions.question: Which segment of the systemic circulation accounts for the steepest fall in mean pressure?
questions.explanation: The arterioles carry the greatest resistance, so mean pressure drops most steeply across them — which is exactly why they regulate regional flow.

questions.question: In which two circulations is autoregulation of blood flow strongest?
questions.explanation: Autoregulation exists everywhere but is strongest in the cerebral (brain) and coronary circulations — the beds that least tolerate any interruption of supply.

questions.question: Neglecting venous pressure, mean arterial pressure is the product of which two quantities?
options: A. Heart rate and the arterial pulse pressure
B. Cardiac output and total peripheral resistance
C. Stroke volume and the peak systolic pressure
D. Arterial compliance and the venous return
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ CO × TPR — the pump (cardiac output) times the pipes (total peripheral resistance). It is the lumped form of flow = ΔP/R applied to the whole systemic circuit.

questions.question: What structural feature defines a portal system, distinguishing it from a normal circulatory route?
options: A. An artery that carries deoxygenated blood
B. A vein that bypasses the heart entirely
C. Two capillary beds connected in series by a vein
D. A capillary bed fed directly by two arteries
questions.explanation: A portal system links two capillary beds in series via a portal vein (e.g. gut → hepatic portal vein → liver). Normal routes have a single capillary bed between artery and vein.

questions.question: Compared with an elastic (conducting) artery, a muscular (medium) artery is specialised mainly to:
options: A. Store part of each stroke volume and recoil to smooth the pulse
B. Permit the exchange of oxygen and nutrients with the tissue
C. Regulate the blood supply to a region by constricting or dilating
D. Act as a distensible low-pressure reservoir for blood volume
questions.explanation: Muscular arteries have a smooth-muscle-rich media that lets them constrict or dilate to distribute flow. Storing stroke volume is the elastic artery's job; exchange is the capillary's; the reservoir role is the vein's.

questions.question: Arterioles have by far the highest wall-thickness-to-radius ratio (~1.33). What does this best equip them to do?
options: A. Maximise surface area for exchange
C. Store the largest share of blood volume
D. Generate high wall tension to set resistance
questions.explanation: A thick wall on a narrow lumen lets arterioles develop the wall stress needed to clamp down on flow without tearing (Laplace: σ = P·r/h). That is what makes them the body's resistance vessels.

questions.question: Arterial compliance (the Windkessel effect) is important chiefly because it:
options: A. Converts pulsatile ejection into near-continuous capillary flow
B. Raises mean arterial pressure above systolic
C. Increases the resistance offered by the aorta
D. Prevents any pressure drop between aorta and capillaries
questions.explanation: The elastic aorta stores part of each stroke in systole and recoils in diastole, smoothing the heart's pulsatile output so that flow reaching the capillaries is nearly continuous.

questions.question: The incisura seen on the aortic pressure waveform is produced by:
options: A. Reflection of the pressure wave
B. Closure of the aortic valve
C. Opening of the mitral valve
D. Contraction of the left atrium
questions.explanation: The incisura marks aortic-valve closure. The peripheral dichrotic notch occurs at similar timing but is a wave-travel phenomenon, not valve closure — a common trap.

questions.question: For a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, the estimated mean arterial pressure is closest to:
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓·PP = 80 + ⅓(40) = 80 + 13.3 ≈ 93 mmHg. It sits nearer diastolic because diastole occupies about two-thirds of the cardiac cycle.

questions.question: If a vessel's radius is halved with the pressure gradient unchanged, flow through it falls to about:
questions.explanation: Since flow ∝ r⁴, halving the radius multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16 and cuts flow to 1/16 of its original value — the dramatic leverage that makes arterioles powerful flow controllers.

questions.question: Total peripheral resistance is best described as the combined resistance of:
options: A. All systemic arteries, arterioles and capillaries
B. The systemic veins and venae cavae
C. The pulmonary arteries and arterioles
D. The aorta and its first-order branches only
questions.explanation: TPR is the summed resistance of all the systemic arteries, arterioles and capillaries, altered mainly by combined regional changes in arteriolar and pre-capillary tone.

questions.question: Blood flow to a tissue is occluded for two minutes; on release, flow briefly overshoots well above baseline. This is:
questions.explanation: Reactive hyperaemia is the post-occlusion overshoot: accumulated vasodilatory metabolites (plus shear-induced NO on restored flow) leave the bed dilated, so a large compensatory surge passes through.

questions.question: During high oxygen demand, the large resting blood volume in the veins is mobilised mainly by:
options: A. Opening of the precapillary sphincters guarding the tissue capillary beds
B. Passive elastic recoil of the aorta driving blood back toward the veins
C. Increased sympathetic outflow contracting the venous smooth muscle
D. A rise in central venous compliance drawing more blood into the reservoir
questions.explanation: Sympathetic signals contract the smooth muscle in vein walls (venoconstriction), stiffening the compliant veins and shifting stored blood back toward the heart.

questions.question: Why does reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity (e.g. CO poisoning) raise local blood flow?
options: A. The lower oxygen content makes the blood more viscous and faster-flowing
B. Oxygen starvation thickens the arteriolar wall and widens its lumen
C. Falling oxygen directly raises the systemic arterial driving pressure
D. Raising flow is the only way to defend oxygen delivery when content falls
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery = flow × content. If content falls, the only way to keep delivery up is to increase flow, so the local vessels dilate — often enough to compensate for the shortfall.

questions.question: Harvey's decisive argument that blood circulates rather than being made and consumed rested on:
options: A. The volume ejected per hour far exceeding what ingested food could supply
B. Dissecting the venous valves to show one-way flow toward the heart
C. Directly observing red cells crossing capillaries under a microscope
D. Timing the pulse at several sites to prove a wave travelled outward
questions.explanation: Harvey's quantitative point: the volume pumped per beat and per hour vastly exceeds any possible intake, so by conservation of mass the same blood must be recirculated in a closed loop, not consumed.

questions.question: Systolic pressure measured at the brachial artery is typically higher than at the aorta because:
options: A. The brachial artery is stiffer yet wider in bore than the aorta itself
B. Cardiac output progressively rises as the blood is carried out peripherally
C. Reflected waves augment the peripheral systolic peak more than the aortic one
D. Mean arterial pressure climbs steadily with distance travelled from the heart
questions.explanation: Wave reflection off branch points and arterioles adds to the forward wave, and in the stiffer peripheral arteries this augmentation raises the systolic peak more than at the compliant aorta — even though mean pressure still falls downstream.

questions.question: In the myogenic theory of autoregulation, a rise in perfusion pressure ends up holding flow steady because the stretch:
options: A. Opens calcium channels, so Ca²⁺ influx contracts the muscle and narrows the lumen
B. Washes accumulated vasodilator metabolites out of the surrounding interstitium
C. Depletes the oxygen that the vascular smooth muscle needs in order to contract
D. Triggers endothelial nitric-oxide release that relaxes the muscle and widens it
questions.explanation: The myogenic mechanism is purely mechanical: wall stretch opens Ca²⁺ channels, Ca²⁺ influx contracts the smooth muscle, the vessel narrows and resistance rises — offsetting the pressure rise. Metabolite washout is the separate metabolic theory.

questions.question: Which set are all listed as vasodilator metabolites in the vasodilator theory of local autoregulation?
options: A. Adenosine, carbon dioxide, potassium ions, hydrogen ions
B. Adenosine, oxygen, sodium ions, calcium ions
C. Noradrenaline, angiotensin II, endothelin, calcium ions
D. Nitric oxide, oxygen, chloride ions, bicarbonate
questions.explanation: The vasodilators named are adenosine (from ATP breakdown), adenosine phosphates, carbon dioxide, potassium ions and hydrogen ions (lactic acid). Oxygen, noradrenaline, angiotensin II and endothelin are not in this dilator set.

questions.question: In the endothelial nitric-oxide pathway, the step immediately downstream of guanylate cyclase activation is:
options: A. Oxidation of L-arginine to nitric oxide
B. Conversion of GTP to cyclic GMP
C. Shear stress acting on the endothelial cell
D. Release of L-citrulline as a by-product
questions.explanation: Order: shear → NOS oxidises L-arginine to NO (+ L-citrulline) → NO activates guanylate cyclase → guanylate cyclase converts GTP to cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation. cGMP formation is the step right after guanylate cyclase.

questions.question: The extra flow boost that distinguishes reactive hyperaemia from simple active hyperaemia comes from:
options: A. A surge of sympathetic outflow that transiently raises the cardiac output
B. Shear from the restored flow surge releasing endothelial nitric oxide
C. Precapillary sphincters snapping firmly shut throughout the occlusion period
D. A direct myogenic contraction of the arterioles the moment flow returns
questions.explanation: On top of accumulated metabolites, the restored-flow surge shears the endothelium and triggers NO release, dilating the arteries further — an amplifier absent from ordinary activity-driven active hyperaemia.

questions.question: Arterioles constrict, raising TPR to 1.2× baseline, while a reflex lowers CO to 0.92× baseline. Mean arterial pressure will:
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ CO × TPR, so the MAP factor is 0.92 × 1.20 = 1.104 — about a 10% rise. The vasoconstriction wins the tug-of-war despite the small reflex fall in output.

questions.question: A histology slide shows an artery whose internal elastic lamina is thrown into deep wavy folds around a small lumen. This most likely indicates:
options: A. A muscular artery caught in active constriction
B. An elastic conducting artery at high pressure
D. A vein with a competent valve
questions.explanation: The crimped internal elastic lamina reflects smooth-muscle contraction narrowing the lumen — the signature of a muscular (distributing) artery constricting. Elastic arteries show a wide lumen and layered elastin, not this folding.

questions.question: A patient's arteries stiffen with age. Which blood-pressure change best reflects loss of the elastic-artery cushioning function?
options: C. A fall in mean arterial pressure
D. An unchanged systolic with lower diastolic only
questions.explanation: A stiff aorta cannot bank the stroke volume, so systolic rises and diastolic falls — a widened pulse pressure. A narrowed pulse pressure instead signals a low stroke volume (e.g. hypovolaemia).

questions.question: In carbon-monoxide poisoning a patient can have a normal blood pressure yet be tissue-hypoxic because CO:
options: A. Slashes the oxygen content carried on haemoglobin
B. Raises total peripheral resistance sharply
C. Blocks the arteriolar precapillary sphincters
D. Lowers cardiac output by depressing the heart
questions.explanation: Delivery = flow × content. CO binds haemoglobin far tighter than O₂, collapsing oxygen content while flow (and blood pressure) can look normal — the flow is fine, the cargo is not.

gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.title: Gene Expression — Transcription & Translation
gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.content: Gene expression from DNA to protein: RNA chemistry, gene structure, RNA polymerases, transcription initiation, RNA processing (cap/splice/poly-A), the genetic code, tRNA, and translation (MEDI2200 Wk6, Parts I-III).

questions.question: In which direction is a new RNA strand synthesised?
options: A. 3′ → 5′, by adding nucleotides to the free 5′ phosphate
B. 5′ → 3′, by adding nucleotides to the free 3′-OH
D. 5′ → 3′, by adding nucleotides to the free 5′ cap
questions.explanation: The only reactive site for chain growth is the free 3′-OH, so RNA is always extended 5′ → 3′.

questions.question: In RNA, adenine base-pairs with which base?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, so A pairs with U (and C pairs with G) — a purine with a pyrimidine.

questions.question: Which codon signals the start of translation, and which amino acid does it specify?
questions.explanation: AUG is the start/initiation codon and codes for methionine; it also sets the reading frame.

questions.question: Which set lists the three stop codons?
questions.explanation: UAA, UAG and UGA are the three termination codons; none specifies an amino acid.

questions.question: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase synthesises mRNA?
questions.explanation: RNA Pol II (in the nucleoplasm) makes mRNA (plus snRNA and miRNA). Pol I makes pre-rRNA; Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

questions.question: What molecule forms the 5′ cap added to eukaryotic mRNA?
options: B. A poly-A stretch of ~200 adenines
questions.explanation: A 7-methylguanosine is added to the 5′ end through an unusual 5′-to-5′ linkage once the transcript reaches ~25 nucleotides.

questions.question: Of the 64 codons, how many specify amino acids and how many are stop codons?
questions.explanation: There are 64 codons: 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons, which is why the code is redundant.

questions.question: Which ribosomal site binds the incoming charged tRNA carrying the next amino acid?
questions.explanation: The A site accepts the incoming charged tRNA; the P site holds the growing peptide; the E site is where spent tRNA exits.

questions.question: Which two subunits join to form the eukaryotic 80S ribosome?
questions.explanation: The small 40S and large 60S subunits, assembled in the nucleolus, join on the mRNA to form the 80S ribosome.

questions.question: What part of a tRNA base-pairs with the mRNA codon?
questions.explanation: The anticodon — three consecutive bases in the anticodon loop — pairs with the complementary codon; the amino acid attaches at the 3′ end.

questions.question: How does the 2′-OH group of ribose affect RNA compared with DNA?
options: A. It makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA
B. It makes RNA more stable, so it is the archival molecule
C. It allows RNA to form a double helix like DNA
D. It prevents RNA from base-pairing internally
questions.explanation: The reactive 2′-OH (absent in DNA) makes RNA less stable — why DNA is the archival copy and mRNA is a disposable working copy.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an exon and an intron?
options: A. Exons are transcribed; introns are not transcribed at all
B. Exons are retained in mature mRNA; introns are transcribed then spliced out
C. Introns are translated; exons are only regulatory
D. Exons are removed by the spliceosome; introns are joined together
questions.explanation: Both are transcribed, but introns are removed by splicing and the exons (expressed sequences) are joined to form the mature mRNA.

questions.question: Why is the non-template strand called the 'coding' strand?
options: A. Because the polymerase reads it directly to build the RNA
B. Because its sequence is the same as the new RNA (with T for U)
C. Because it always contains the promoter and enhancer
D. Because it is the strand that is spliced
questions.explanation: The template strand is read by the polymerase; the coding strand is named for matching the RNA sequence (T in place of U), so it can be read like the message.

questions.question: Compared with DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase…
options: A. requires a primer and proofreads tightly
B. needs no primer and has only modest proofreading
C. needs no primer and cannot make errors
D. requires a primer but has no proofreading at all
questions.explanation: RNA pol starts a chain without a primer and proofreads only modestly (~1 error per 10⁴ nt), acceptable because mRNA is a disposable copy.

questions.question: What is the conserved core of a Pol II pre-initiation complex?
options: A. RNA polymerase, DNA ligase and primase
B. RNA polymerase, TBP and the general transcription factors (TFIIA/B/D/E/F/H)
C. Poly-A polymerase, CPSF and CstF
questions.explanation: The PIC core is RNA Pol II + TATA-binding protein (TBP) + the general transcription factors; TBP is needed even at TATA-less promoters.

questions.question: In the first splicing reaction, what does the branch-point adenosine do?
options: A. It attacks the 5′ splice site, forming a lariat intron–3′ exon intermediate
B. It attacks the 3′ splice site, releasing the 5′ exon
C. It adds a 5′ cap to the exon
D. It ligates the two exons directly
questions.explanation: Branching: the branch-point A attacks the phosphodiester bond at the 5′ splice site, cleaving the 5′ exon and forming a lariat; exon ligation then follows.

questions.question: Which factor recognises the AAUAAA polyadenylation signal?
questions.explanation: CPSF binds the AAUAAA signal while CstF binds the downstream GU-rich sequence; after cleavage, poly-A polymerase adds ~200 adenines.

questions.question: At which codon position is 'wobble' (a tolerated mismatch) allowed?
options: D. Wobble is allowed at all three positions
questions.explanation: Pairing is strict at positions 1 and 2 but a purine–pyrimidine wobble is tolerated at the third position, letting one tRNA read several codons.

questions.question: How does the small ribosomal subunit locate the start codon during initiation?
options: A. It cleaves the mRNA at the poly-A tail and works backwards
B. It scans from the 5′ cap to the first AUG in a Kozak sequence (ACCAUGG)
C. It binds directly to the 3′ UTR and waits for eRF1
D. It is positioned by the spliceosome at the branch point
questions.explanation: The 40S + eIFs + initiator tRNA-Met scan from the 5′ cap to the first AUG embedded in a Kozak consensus, then the 60S joins to form the 80S.

questions.question: What powers each step of the translation elongation cycle, and roughly how fast is it?
options: A. ATP hydrolysis, about 2 amino acids per second
B. GTP hydrolysis, about 15 amino acids per second
C. The 5′ cap, about 200 amino acids per second
D. The proton gradient, about 15 amino acids per minute
questions.explanation: Elongation factors use GTP hydrolysis for each of the three steps; eukaryotic elongation runs at ~15 amino acids per second.

questions.question: When do DNA replication and most transcription occur in the cell cycle?
options: B. Replication in S-phase; most transcription in G1 (after division)
C. Replication in G1; transcription in M-phase
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated in S-phase (before division); transcription happens mainly in G1, after division, when the cell is expressing genes.

questions.question: Where does the energy for adding each nucleotide during transcription come from?
options: A. Hydrolysis of the incoming rNTP to rNMP + pyrophosphate
B. Hydrolysis of ATP by the polymerase's kinase domain
D. Breaking the hydrogen bonds of the DNA template
questions.explanation: Each incoming ribonucleotide triphosphate is hydrolysed (rNTP → rNMP + PPi); that release of pyrophosphate drives chain extension.

questions.question: The death-cap toxin α-amanitin is lethal chiefly because it inhibits…
options: A. RNA polymerase I, halting rRNA synthesis
B. RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA synthesis
C. the spliceosome, blocking intron removal
questions.explanation: α-amanitin specifically blocks RNA Pol II; with mRNA synthesis shut down, protein production collapses, causing fatal liver failure.

questions.question: Which two activities does TFIIH bring to transcription initiation?
options: A. Helicase/ATPase to open the DNA, and CDK7 kinase to phosphorylate Pol II
B. Poly-A polymerase and 3′ cleavage activity
C. Anticodon reading and peptide-bond formation
D. Branch-point recognition and lariat formation
questions.explanation: TFIIH's helicase/ATPase opens the DNA into the open complex, and its CDK7 kinase phosphorylates Pol II to release it from the promoter into elongation.

questions.question: Why is TATA-binding protein (TBP) still required at promoters that have no TATA box?
options: A. TBP is only needed to remove introns
B. TBP is a conserved core component of the PIC needed to position the polymerase at both TATA and TATA-less promoters
C. TBP replaces the missing enhancer
D. TBP adds the 5′ cap when a TATA box is absent
questions.explanation: TBP is part of the universal PIC core; it is required to nucleate the complex and position the polymerase whether or not a TATA box is present.

questions.question: What is the main functional consequence of alternative splicing?
options: A. It permanently deletes a gene from the genome
B. It lets a single gene produce several different RNA and protein species
C. It replaces the poly-A tail with a second 5′ cap
D. It converts introns into exons in the DNA
questions.explanation: By choosing which exons to keep, alternative splicing lets one DNA sequence encode multiple proteins — expanding the proteome without expanding the genome.

questions.question: What does it mean that the genetic code is 'redundant' (degenerate)?
options: A. Every codon specifies more than one amino acid
B. A single amino acid can be specified by 1–6 different codons
C. Each amino acid has exactly one codon
D. Stop codons also code for amino acids
questions.explanation: With 61 coding codons for 20 amino acids, most amino acids are specified by several codons (1–6 each) — the basis for wobble tolerance.

questions.question: How does an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase help drive later peptide-bond formation?
options: A. It links the amino acid to its tRNA by a high-energy bond, using ATP
B. It hydrolyses the mRNA to release energy
C. It phosphorylates the ribosome's A site
D. It adds a poly-A tail that stores energy
questions.explanation: Each of the 20 synthetases charges its tRNA using ATP, forming a high-energy amino-acid–tRNA bond whose energy later powers peptide-bond formation.

questions.question: Why does a stop codon end translation even though it enters the A site?
options: A. It is bound by a special tRNA that blocks the ribosome
B. No tRNA has an anticodon for a stop codon, so release factor eRF1 binds and releases the polypeptide
C. It triggers splicing of the mRNA
D. It recruits the 60S subunit to detach the 40S
questions.explanation: There is no tRNA complementary to a stop codon; instead eRF1 recognises it in the A site, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome separates.

questions.question: Why do a 40S and a 60S subunit combine into an 80S ribosome rather than a 100S one?
options: A. Some rRNA is lost when they join
B. S values are sedimentation rates (depending on mass and shape), so they are not additive
C. The subunits shrink on binding mRNA
D. 80S is simply an approximation of 100S
questions.explanation: The 'S' is a Svedberg (sedimentation) unit that reflects both mass and shape, so the values do not add arithmetically: 40S + 60S → 80S.

heart_physiology_mhhs2402_wk6.html.title: The Heart — Cardiac Cycle, Conduction & Output (MHHS2402 Wk6)
heart_physiology_mhhs2402_wk6.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
heart_physiology_mhhs2402_wk6.html.content: Cardiac physiology from Week 6: the heart as a double pump, the three myocardial cell types, cardiac action potentials and excitation-contraction coupling, the conduction pathway, the ECG and its 12 leads, and cardiac output with the pressure-volume loop. Tests reasoning about mechanism and consequence, not just recall.

questions.question: The pulmonary and systemic circuits are arranged in series. What does this force to be true over time?
options: A. Right and left ventricular outputs must be equal
B. The left ventricle must pump a larger volume than the right
C. The right ventricle must generate the higher pressure
D. The atria must contract at a faster rate than the ventricles
questions.explanation: In series, every millilitre the right ventricle sends to the lungs returns to the left ventricle to be ejected. If outputs differed for long, blood would dam up in one circuit, so on average they are equal. Pressures differ (left is higher), but volumes must match.

questions.question: Which pair of valves are the atrioventricular (AV) valves?
questions.explanation: The AV valves sit between each atrium and its ventricle: tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left. The pulmonary and aortic valves are the semilunar valves guarding the ventricular outflows.

questions.question: Which structure in the intercalated disc provides the electrical connection between cardiac cells?
questions.explanation: Gap junctions are low-resistance channels that let current pass cell-to-cell, making the myocardium a functional syncytium. Desmosomes in the same disc provide the mechanical anchor, not the electrical link.

questions.question: The long plateau of the cardiac contractile action potential is produced mainly by the influx of which ion?
questions.explanation: Sustained Ca2+ entry through L-type calcium channels holds the membrane depolarised during the plateau, a feature unique to cardiac muscle. Sodium drives the fast upstroke and potassium efflux repolarises.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the normal cardiac conduction pathway?
options: A. AV node, SA node, bundle branches, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
B. SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres
C. SA node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle branches
D. AV node, bundle of His, SA node, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres
questions.explanation: The signal starts at the SA node, is delayed at the AV node, travels down the bundle of His, splits into the left and right bundle branches, and spreads through the Purkinje fibres.

questions.question: Which ECG deflection corresponds to ventricular depolarisation?
questions.explanation: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, which triggers ventricular contraction. The P wave is atrial depolarisation and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation.

questions.question: Which expression correctly defines stroke volume?
options: A. End-systolic volume minus end-diastolic volume
B. End-diastolic volume divided by heart rate
C. Cardiac output multiplied by heart rate
D. End-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is what the ventricle held after filling (EDV) minus what remains after ejection (ESV): SV = EDV - ESV. Ejection fraction is SV/EDV, and cardiac output is SV x HR.

questions.question: During diastole, the ventricles are:
options: B. Contracting with all valves shut
C. Relaxed with the semilunar valves open
D. Relaxed and filling with blood
questions.explanation: Diastole is the filling phase: the ventricles relax and blood flows in through the open AV valves. Systole is the ejection phase, when the ventricles contract and blood leaves through the semilunar valves.

questions.question: Why must the deep myocardium be fed by the coronary arteries rather than by the blood inside the chambers?
options: A. Chamber blood is deoxygenated on both sides of the heart
B. The wall is too thick to be supplied by diffusion from chamber blood
C. The endocardium is impermeable to oxygen
D. The chambers are at too low a pressure to deliver oxygen
questions.explanation: Diffusion cannot reach the deep muscle of so thick a wall, so a dedicated arterial supply is needed. The coronaries branch from the aortic root and tap the most oxygenated blood available.

questions.question: Autorhythmic and conductive cells trigger and route every beat, yet they do not appear on the ECG. The best explanation is that:
options: A. Their action potentials are too brief to be recorded
B. They are electrically insulated from the recording electrodes
C. They are too few in mass to contribute much to the summed surface signal
D. They repolarise at the same instant that they depolarise
questions.explanation: The ECG reflects the summed activity of the heart, which scales with the mass of tissue depolarising together. These cells have little contractile bulk, so their signal is swamped by the large contractile mass, even though they set and carry the rhythm.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a cardiomyocyte sits near -90 mV rather than near E_Na (+81 mV) principally because:
options: A. The sodium-potassium pump directly holds the voltage at -90 mV
B. Intracellular sodium concentration exceeds extracellular sodium
C. Chloride is actively pumped out to set the resting voltage
D. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+
questions.explanation: The membrane potential is a permeability-weighted average of the ions' equilibrium potentials. At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+, so the voltage is pulled close to E_K (about -97 mV). The Na+/K+ pump maintains the gradients but is not what sets the resting voltage directly.

questions.question: The AV node conducts slowly, delaying the signal on its way to the ventricles. The physiological advantage of this delay is that it:
options: A. Lets the atria finish contracting and top up the ventricles before they eject
B. Prevents the ventricles from ever being re-excited during a beat
C. Speeds ventricular depolarisation so the ventricles contract as one
D. Allows the SA node to reset the atrial rhythm each cycle
questions.explanation: The pause gives the atria time to complete the atrial kick, maximising ventricular filling before contraction. Refractoriness (from the long action potential) is what prevents re-excitation, and the Purkinje fibres are what synchronise the ventricles.

questions.question: In cardiac calcium-induced calcium release, which best describes the trigger and the amplifier?
options: A. A large Ca2+ influx through L-type channels triggers a small release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
B. Na+ influx triggers Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through ryanodine receptors
C. A small Ca2+ influx through L-type channels triggers a larger Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
D. Ca2+ release from mitochondria triggers further influx through L-type channels
questions.explanation: A small trigger influx through L-type channels opens ryanodine receptors on the SR, releasing a much larger store of Ca2+ (the spark). This amplification is why cardiac contraction depends on extracellular calcium.

questions.question: The SA node, not the AV node, normally sets heart rate because:
options: A. It is the only region of the heart able to reach threshold spontaneously
B. It conducts action potentials faster than the Purkinje fibres
C. Its steep prepotential reaches threshold first
D. It has the most negative threshold of any pacemaker site
questions.explanation: All sites have prepotentials, but the SA node's is steepest, so it fires first and depolarises the others before their own slower drifts reach threshold (overdrive suppression). The slower sites are backups, not incapable of firing.

questions.question: Which ordering of conduction velocity (fastest to slowest) is correct?
options: A. Purkinje fibres, large nerve fibres, atrial muscle, ventricular muscle
B. Large nerve fibres, ventricular muscle, Purkinje fibres, atrial muscle
C. Large nerve fibres, Purkinje fibres, ventricular muscle, atrial muscle
D. Purkinje fibres, ventricular muscle, large nerve fibres, atrial muscle
questions.explanation: Approximate velocities: large nerve fibres 80-120 m/s, Purkinje fibres 4 m/s, ventricular muscle 0.5 m/s, atrial muscle 0.3 m/s. The Purkinje system is fast relative to muscle but still far slower than nerve.

questions.question: A standard 12-lead ECG is made up of:
options: A. 3 bipolar limb leads, 3 augmented unipolar limb leads, and 6 chest leads
B. 6 bipolar limb leads, 3 augmented limb leads, and 3 chest leads
C. 3 bipolar limb leads and 9 chest leads
D. 6 augmented unipolar limb leads and 6 chest leads
questions.explanation: The 12 leads are the bipolar limb leads I, II, III; the augmented unipolar limb leads aVR, aVL, aVF; and the six precordial chest leads V1-V6. Together they view the heart from many angles.

questions.question: On a Wiggers diagram the ECG deflections sit slightly ahead of the pressure changes they cause because:
options: A. Depolarisation precedes the contraction it triggers
B. Pressure sensors respond more slowly than ECG electrodes
C. The mechanical events occur in a different part of the heart
D. Repolarisation must complete before contraction can begin
questions.explanation: Depolarisation is the trigger; excitation-contraction coupling (calcium entry, release, troponin binding) takes a few milliseconds before force develops. So the electrical signal leads the mechanical event it produces.

questions.question: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 84 mL. Its ejection fraction is closest to:
questions.explanation: SV = 140 - 84 = 56 mL; EF = SV/EDV = 56/140 = 0.40, i.e. 40%. (56 mL is the stroke volume, a distractor; 84 mL is the ESV.)

questions.question: At a fixed end-diastolic volume, an increase in contractility raises stroke volume by:
options: A. Lowering end-systolic volume so more is ejected
B. Raising end-diastolic volume through greater filling
C. Increasing heart rate so more beats occur per minute
D. Prolonging diastole to allow more complete filling
questions.explanation: Contractility acts on the ESV term of SV = EDV - ESV: a stronger squeeze empties the ventricle more completely, lowering ESV and widening the gap. It does not depend on extra filling or a faster rate.

questions.question: During which two phases of the pressure-volume loop does ventricular volume stay constant?
questions.explanation: In both isovolumic phases all four valves are shut, so no blood can enter or leave while pressure changes; these are the two vertical limbs of the loop. Ejection and filling are when a valve is open and volume changes.

questions.question: Resting myocardium extracts 70-80% of delivered oxygen. Why does this make a narrowed coronary artery so dangerous on exertion?
options: A. Extraction is near-maximal, so more demand needs more flow — a stenosis prevents it
B. The myocardium switches to anaerobic metabolism and accumulates an oxygen debt it later repays
C. High extraction means venous blood still carries enough oxygen to mask the ischaemia
D. The coronary arteries fill during systole, so a stenosis matters only at high heart rates
questions.explanation: Because extraction is already near its ceiling, the heart cannot obtain much more oxygen by extracting harder; the only remaining route is increased blood flow, exactly what a stenosis blocks. So any rise in demand causes ischaemia. (Coronary flow is in fact greatest during diastole.)

questions.question: The prolonged cardiac action potential produces a long refractory period. The most important consequence of this is that it:
options: A. Speeds conduction through the ventricular muscle
B. Allows the SA node to override slower pacemaker sites
C. Prevents tetanus, so the ventricle relaxes and refills
D. Increases the force of each individual contraction
questions.explanation: A cell cannot be re-excited until it has nearly repolarised, so contractions cannot be stacked into a sustained tetanus. This forces a relax-and-fill gap between beats. It is unrelated to conduction speed, pacemaker dominance, or contractile force.

questions.question: If a cardiomyocyte's extracellular Na+ concentration fell while intracellular Na+ stayed the same, the sodium equilibrium potential (E_Na) would:
options: B. Stay the same, since E_Na depends only on temperature
D. Reverse sign to become negative immediately
questions.explanation: E_Na is proportional to ln([Na]o/[Na]i). Lowering [Na]o shrinks the outside-to-inside ratio, so the log term falls and E_Na becomes less positive. It would only turn negative if [Na]o dropped below [Na]i, not at the first small change.

questions.question: A patient's ECG shows a widened QRS complex of normal height. This pattern most directly indicates:
options: A. Increased ventricular muscle mass rather than a conduction problem
D. Slowed conduction through the ventricles rather than increased muscle mass
questions.explanation: Interval durations report on conduction, whereas wave amplitudes report on muscle mass. A wide but not tall QRS means depolarisation is taking longer to spread (e.g. a bundle branch block), not that there is more muscle. A tall QRS would suggest hypertrophy.

questions.question: Two patients both have an ejection fraction of 55%, but one has a much larger stroke volume. The most likely reason is that:
options: A. The patient with the larger stroke volume has a higher heart rate
B. The patient with the larger stroke volume has a lower end-systolic volume for the same EDV
C. Ejection fraction and stroke volume cannot differ if EF is equal
D. The patient with the larger stroke volume has a larger end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation: EF is the ratio SV/EDV. At the same fraction, a larger EDV yields a larger absolute SV (a dilated ventricle ejecting the same 55% moves more blood). A lower ESV at fixed EDV would raise EF, contradicting the equal-EF premise; heart rate affects cardiac output, not stroke volume per beat.

questions.question: A person has an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL, an end-systolic volume of 60 mL, and a heart rate of 80 bpm. Their cardiac output is closest to:
questions.explanation: SV = 130 - 60 = 70 mL; CO = SV x HR = 70 x 80 = 5600 mL/min = 5.6 L/min. The 10.4 L/min distractor comes from wrongly using EDV (130 x 80); 4.8 comes from a 60 mL SV error.

questions.question: In aortic stenosis (a narrowed aortic valve), how does the left-ventricular pressure-volume loop change during ejection, and why?
options: A. The peak pressure falls, because less blood is ejected each beat
B. The loop loses its vertical isovolumic-contraction limb, because a valve is leaking during contraction
C. The loop widens, because stroke volume increases to compensate
D. The peak pressure rises, because the ventricle must generate more force to drive blood through the narrowed valve
questions.explanation: A stenotic aortic valve resists outflow, so the ventricle must build a much higher pressure to eject, raising the top of the loop. Loss of a vertical isovolumic limb is the signature of a regurgitant (leaking) AV valve, not a stenotic outflow valve.

questions.question: If the left ventricle's contractility falls in isolation, which downstream consequence follows most directly from the circuits being in series?
options: A. The right ventricle immediately fails from the same cause
B. Blood backs up behind the left heart, congesting the pulmonary circulation
C. Systemic arterial pressure rises because the aorta receives more blood
D. The coronary arteries deliver less oxygen to the right ventricle
questions.explanation: In series, if the left ventricle ejects less than it receives, the blood arriving from the lungs has nowhere to go and backs up into the pulmonary circuit, causing congestion (breathlessness). The right ventricle is not directly damaged, and reduced forward output lowers, not raises, systemic pressure.

questions.question: Why does the intercalated disc contain both desmosomes and gap junctions rather than just one type of junction?
options: A. Desmosomes conduct the signal while gap junctions provide mechanical strength
B. Gap junctions store calcium while desmosomes release it during contraction
C. Desmosomes resist tearing while gap junctions spread the signal
D. Both junction types perform the same role, providing redundancy against damage
questions.explanation: Desmosomes give tensile strength so cells are not pulled apart under repeated contraction, while gap junctions pass current so the muscle acts as a functional syncytium. The two roles are distinct: glue for force, wire for signal.

ion_channels_medi2004_wk6.html.title: Ion Channels & Channelopathies
ion_channels_medi2004_wk6.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
ion_channels_medi2004_wk6.html.content: MEDI2004 Week 6 Lecture 11 — Introduction to Ion Channels & Ion Channel Diseases (Dr Chris Bladen). Covers channel structure, selectivity filters (GYG/EEEE/DEKA), electrochemical driving forces, Nernst equation, channel architecture (nAChR/ClC/Kv/Nav/Cav), action potential phases, tissue distribution of Ca2+ channels, channelopathies (Nav1.1/Nav1.5/hERG/KCNQ1/CFTR), pain pathway and T-type Ca2+ channels, gating states and drug targets (local anaesthetics, antiepileptics, Ca2+ channel blockers, ziconotide).

questions.question: Which part of a voltage-gated sodium channel acts as the primary voltage sensor?
options: A. The P-loop hairpin between S5 and S6
B. The N-terminal inactivation ball domain
C. The S1–S2 extracellular linker loop
questions.explanation: S4 carries positively charged arginine/lysine residues at every third position. Membrane depolarisation repels S4 outward, triggering the conformational change that opens the activation gate. The P-loop forms the selectivity filter, not the voltage sensor.

questions.question: What is the selectivity filter motif of the voltage-gated K⁺ channel?
questions.explanation: GYG (Gly-Tyr-Gly) is the universal signature of K⁺ channels. The carbonyl oxygens of this motif mimic the water hydration shell around K⁺, allowing dehydration and selective passage. EEEE (four glutamates) is the Ca²⁺ channel motif; DEKA is the Na⁺ channel motif.

questions.question: Which combination correctly matches ion and approximate equilibrium (Nernst) potential at 37°C?
questions.explanation: K⁺ equilibrium potential is approximately −90 mV (concentrated inside; diffusion drives it out until electrical attraction inward balances it). Na⁺ equilibrium potential is approximately +60 mV (concentrated outside; both electrical and diffusion forces drive it inward until the inside is very positive).
