The resting potential (−70 mV) sits between these two values.

questions.question: Which two simultaneous events drive membrane repolarisation after the peak of an action potential?
options: A. Nav channel inactivation and voltage-gated Kv channel opening
B. Nav channel opening and influx of K⁺ through Nav pores
C. Na⁺/K⁺ pump activation and closure of all Kv channels
D. Kv channel closing and secondary activation of more Nav channels
questions.explanation: Repolarisation requires stopping Na⁺ inflow (Nav channels inactivate via the ball-and-chain mechanism) and starting K⁺ outflow (voltage-gated Kv channels open with a short delay after Nav). Both events are required simultaneously — Nav inactivation alone slows depolarisation but Kv opening drives rapid repolarisation.

questions.question: How many Na⁺ and K⁺ ions does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase transport per ATP hydrolysed?
questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase exports 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP hydrolysed. The net loss of one positive charge per cycle makes the pump electrogenic, contributing a small hyperpolarising current. This stoichiometry maintains the concentration gradients that channels exploit.

questions.question: Which Ca²⁺ channel type primarily triggers insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells after glucose-induced depolarisation?
options: B. L-type (Cav1.x) at the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: L-type Cav1 channels open when the β-cell depolarises (after ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close in response to glucose). L-type Ca²⁺ entry triggers insulin vesicle exocytosis. Sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels to depolarise the cell and enhance this process in type 2 diabetes.

questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in which channel or transporter?
questions.explanation: CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel expressed on airway epithelial cells. The ΔF508 mutation causes misfolding and degradation, so CFTR never reaches the cell surface; without apical Cl⁻ exit the airway surface liquid dehydrates and mucus thickens. ClC-1 mutations cause myotonia congenita; hERG mutations cause Long QT syndrome.

questions.question: Ziconotide is a cone-snail-derived drug used for intractable chronic pain. Which channel does it block?
options: A. N-type Ca²⁺ (Cav2.2) at dorsal horn presynaptic terminals
B. T-type Ca²⁺ (Cav3.x) in thalamic relay neurons
C. L-type Ca²⁺ (Cav1.x) in vascular smooth muscle
D. Nav1.8 in dorsal root ganglion nociceptors
questions.explanation: Ziconotide (synthetic ω-conotoxin MVIIA) selectively blocks N-type Cav2.2 Ca²⁺ channels at presynaptic terminals in the spinal dorsal horn, preventing neurotransmitter release into the pain pathway. It is delivered intrathecally because it does not safely cross the blood-brain barrier at systemic concentrations.

questions.question: The nAChR is non-selective for cations. Which structural feature best explains this compared with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels?
options: A. nAChR lacks transmembrane helices, so ions bypass the lipid bilayer
B. Its DEKA motif admits Na⁺ and K⁺ with equal affinity at physiological pH
C. Its pentameric (5-fold) pore is too wide to form a precise selectivity filter
D. Ligand-gated channels structurally cannot form a selectivity filter
questions.explanation: The nAChR pentamer (2α, β, γ, δ) arranges five subunits around a central pore. This 5-fold geometry creates a wider pore with a general negative charge ring that excludes anions but cannot discriminate among monovalent cations. The 4-fold voltage-gated channels have a precisely constrained selectivity filter (GYG, DEKA, EEEE) that the 5-fold architecture cannot replicate. The DEKA motif belongs specifically to Nav channels; nAChR has its own pore-lining residues.

questions.question: K⁺ (ionic radius 1.38 Å) passes through K⁺ channels while Na⁺ (ionic radius 1.02 Å) does not. Which explanation is mechanistically correct?
options: A. The GYG pore diameter is too large to accommodate the smaller Na⁺, so it falls through without contacting the filter
B. Na⁺ retains its full hydration shell and is too bulky to enter, while K⁺ can squeeze through dehydrated
C. GYG carbonyl oxygens replace K⁺'s lost water; Na⁺ is too small for the same contacts, so it is excluded
D. Na⁺ is repelled by the positively charged lysine in K⁺ channels' outer vestibule
questions.explanation: K⁺ sheds its water shell and the four carbonyl oxygens of GYG provide energetically equivalent contacts, making dehydration cost-neutral. Na⁺ is too small — it cannot simultaneously contact all four oxygens, its dehydration energy is not compensated, and it is excluded. The pore is an energetic trap tuned to K⁺, not a steric sieve. Option A incorrectly applies a size-exclusion model; option B reverses which ion dehydrates.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential is −70 mV and E_K is −90 mV. What is the net K⁺ driving force at rest, and in which direction does K⁺ flow?
options: A. Zero net force; K⁺ is at equilibrium at −70 mV
B. 160 mV net inward; K⁺ is strongly attracted into the cell by Na⁺ exchange
C. 20 mV net inward; K⁺ diffuses in because the external concentration exceeds internal
D. 20 mV net outward; K⁺ has a small tendency to leave the cell
questions.explanation: Driving force = membrane potential − equilibrium potential. For K⁺: −70 − (−90) = +20 mV outward. The resting potential is more positive (less negative) than E_K, so electrical force inward does not fully cancel diffusion force outward — a small net outward driving force exists. K⁺ leaks out through resting K⁺ channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump compensates.

questions.question: Nav1.5 (SCN5A) gain-of-function and hERG (KCNH2) loss-of-function both prolong the QT interval. What do these two mechanistically different mutations have in common?
options: A. Both raise intracellular Ca²⁺ through L-type channels, slowing the plateau
B. Both reduce the outward K⁺ current that drives ventricular repolarisation
C. Both delay the return of membrane voltage toward E_K during ventricular repolarisation
D. Both activate the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which slows ion redistribution after each beat
questions.explanation: The shared endpoint is delayed ventricular repolarisation. Nav1.5 GoF sustains a persistent inward Na⁺ current that opposes repolarisation; hERG LoF reduces the outward K⁺ current that normally drives repolarisation. Despite opposite channel mechanisms, both delay the membrane returning toward E_K and lengthen the QT interval. Option B is only partially true — Nav1.5 GoF does not reduce K⁺ efflux; it adds inward Na⁺ instead.

questions.question: Nav1.5 (SCN5A) gain-of-function causes LQT3. Which cardiac consequence is most directly expected from this mutation?
options: A. Shortened QT interval due to faster K⁺ repolarisation
B. Right bundle branch block due to absent Nav current in conduction fibres
C. Prolonged QT interval due to persistent Na⁺ influx during the repolarisation plateau
D. Atrial fibrillation from enhanced SA node pacemaker current
questions.explanation: Nav1.5 GoF means the inactivation gate fails to close normally, allowing persistent (late) Na⁺ inward current during repolarisation. This sustained inward current opposes K⁺ efflux and prolongs the plateau — stretching the QT interval (LQT3). Nav1.5 loss-of-function causes Brugada syndrome or cardiac conduction disease.

questions.question: Which best explains the absolute refractory period that follows each action potential?
options: A. Nav channels occupy the inactivated state and cannot reopen regardless of stimulus strength
B. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump actively hyperpolarises the membrane to −120 mV until gradients are restored
C. Kv channels remain open and prevent any further inward Na⁺ movement for ~2 ms
D. The extracellular Na⁺ concentration is transiently depleted by each action potential
questions.explanation: Immediately after an AP, Nav channels enter the inactivated state (ball-and-chain occluding the inner pore). In this state they cannot reopen even if S4 is displaced by a second depolarisation — the activation gate can open but the inactivation gate blocks ion flow. Channels must first recover to the resting state (requires repolarisation and time) before another AP is possible.

questions.question: Ethosuximide is effective for childhood absence epilepsy but ineffective for tonic-clonic seizures. This selectivity is best explained by:
options: A. Ethosuximide stabilises Nav inactivation, which is only expressed in thalamic neurons
B. It reduces T-type (Cav3.1) current in thalamic relay neurons driving 3 Hz spike-wave activity
C. Ethosuximide blocks GABA-A receptors in the thalamus, reducing inhibitory surges
D. Ethosuximide inhibits L-type Ca²⁺ channels preferentially in cortical pyramidal cells
questions.explanation: Absence seizures arise from 3 Hz thalamo-cortical oscillations driven by T-type (Cav3.1) burst firing in thalamic relay neurons. Ethosuximide selectively reduces this T-type current, silencing the thalamic pacemaker without affecting Nav or L-type channels. Tonic-clonic seizures involve widespread Nav-dependent high-frequency firing where T-type blockade has little effect.

questions.question: After tissue injury, which signalling cascade most directly upregulates T-type Ca²⁺ channel activity in DRG neurons?
options: A. TNF-α → JAK/STAT → Nav1.8 transcriptional upregulation over 24–48 h
B. ATP → P2X receptor → direct mechanical coupling to T-type channel gating
C. Substance P → NMDA → Ca²⁺/calmodulin → T-type channel membrane trafficking
D. IGF/GPCR → PLC → PKCα phosphorylation of T-type channels within minutes
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the specific cascade: injury → IGF receptor and GPCRs activated → phospholipase C (PLC) recruited → protein kinase Cα (PKCα) activated → PKCα phosphorylates T-type Cav3 channels, increasing activity. This post-translational modification rapidly enhances T-type current within minutes, explaining fast peripheral sensitisation after injury.

questions.question: Verapamil and amlodipine both block L-type Ca²⁺ channels yet have different clinical profiles. Which statement best captures their mechanistic difference?
options: A. Verapamil binds the extracellular DHP site and remodels pore geometry; amlodipine plugs the intracellular vestibule
B. Amlodipine prefers the resting state in cardiac muscle; verapamil prefers the inactivated state in vascular smooth muscle
C. Both enter the pore during opening, but verapamil dissociates 10× faster in vascular than cardiac tissue
D. Verapamil plugs the pore internally; amlodipine binds an external site, with different state preferences
questions.explanation: Verapamil (phenylalkylamine) enters the inner vestibule of the open channel from the cytoplasmic side and physically occludes it — producing strong use-dependent block in heart. Amlodipine (dihydropyridine) binds an external allosteric site and remodels the pore; it has greater affinity for the inactivated state that vascular smooth muscle cells preferentially occupy at their resting potentials. Both block Ca²⁺ conduction, but through distinct sites and preferred states.

questions.question: Replacing glutamate-177 in domain II of a Cav channel with alanine (E177A) is expected to change which functional property most directly?
options: A. Inactivation kinetics slow because alanine cannot form the inactivation-gate hydrogen bond
B. Activation threshold shifts to more negative voltages because neutral alanine cannot repel S4
C. Ca²⁺/Na⁺ selectivity decreases because one of the four EEEE negative charges is neutralised
D. The channel constitutively inactivates because alanine occludes the inner pore via hydrophobic collapse
questions.explanation: The Ca²⁺ selectivity filter is formed by four glutamate residues (EEEE), one from each domain. Replacing Glu-177 with neutral alanine reduces the negative charge density from −4 to −3 equivalent charges. Experimental data show that systematically neutralising EEEE glutamates progressively converts Ca²⁺ selectivity toward monovalent permeation — a single E→A substitution measurably reduces Ca²⁺/Na⁺ selectivity. This is direct evidence that the EEEE motif, not pore geometry, determines Ca²⁺ selectivity.

questions.question: Dravet syndrome is caused by Nav1.1 (SCN1A) loss-of-function, yet carbamazepine (a Na⁺ channel stabiliser) worsens Dravet seizures. Which mechanism explains this paradox?
options: A. Nav1.1 is expressed equally in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, so net channel block has no directional effect
B. Carbamazepine metabolites act as Nav1.1 agonists in Dravet patients due to a pharmacogenomic CYP2C9 variant
C. LoF mutations allosterically convert Nav1.1 to a gain-of-function in inhibitory neurons, which carbamazepine then reverses inappropriately
D. Nav1.1 is mainly in inhibitory interneurons; blocking it deepens the inhibitory deficit and worsens disinhibition
questions.explanation: In healthy brain, Nav1.1 is predominantly expressed in fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons that require high-frequency Nav firing to sustain inhibitory output. In Dravet, LoF mutations mean these interneurons already fire inadequately — the excitatory network is disinhibited. Adding carbamazepine further reduces the firing of already-compromised interneurons, worsening disinhibition and precipitating more severe seizures. This is why Dravet is treated with Nav-channel-sparing drugs (clobazam, stiripentol, valproate) rather than conventional Na⁺ blockers.

questions.question: A drug reduces the cardiac IKr (hERG) current by 40% without affecting ICaL. Which outcome is most accurate for the ventricular action potential?
options: A. The plateau shortens because less inward Ca²⁺ current is opposed by K⁺
B. Repolarisation accelerates because remaining Kv channels upregulate to compensate
C. The resting potential shifts toward 0 mV because the K⁺ equilibrium potential changes
D. The plateau prolongs because the balance tips toward net inward current during repolarisation
questions.explanation: During the cardiac plateau, ICaL (inward) is roughly balanced by IKr and other K⁺ currents (outward). Reducing IKr by 40% tips the balance toward net inward current — the plateau voltage cannot fall as quickly, prolonging it and lengthening the QT interval. This is precisely how hERG-blocking drugs cause drug-induced LQT2 — they partially unbalance the plateau equilibrium without affecting ICaL.

questions.question: State-dependent block explains why lidocaine preferentially suppresses high-frequency firing in nociceptors. Which biophysical property makes this selectivity possible?
options: A. It binds inactivated channels ~100× tighter than resting; rapid firing accumulates inactivation, trapping more drug
B. Lidocaine promotes channel opening, so more frequent firing exposes more binding sites
C. Large motor fibres express lidocaine-resistant Nav1.4 exclusively, while small pain fibres express only lidocaine-sensitive Nav1.7
D. Lidocaine only enters the pore during the resting state, when the gate is maximally open
questions.explanation: Lidocaine binds the inactivated state with ~100-fold higher affinity than the resting state, and drug-bound channels recover far more slowly. At low firing frequencies, channels return to the resting state during long inter-spike intervals, drug dissociates, and little net block accumulates. At high frequencies (nociceptors in pain states), channels accumulate in the inactivated state with drug bound, and slow recovery means block builds progressively ('use-dependent block'). Motor fibres firing at physiological rates experience far less accumulation — this differential is the basis of differential nerve block.

questions.question: A KCNQ1 (Kv7.1) missense patient shows QT prolongation at rest but near-normal QT during exercise. Which mechanism best accounts for this exercise normalisation?
options: A. β-adrenergic cAMP signalling partially rescues the mutant Kv7.1 K⁺ current on exercise
B. Exercise raises body temperature, which increases ion diffusion rates and accelerates repolarisation
C. Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate, shortening each AP by reducing channel open time
D. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump accelerates during exercise, restoring K⁺ gradients faster and shortening the QT
questions.explanation: KCNQ1 normally forms the slow delayed rectifier IKs (with KCNE1), which is upregulated by β-adrenergic stimulation via cAMP → PKA → KCNQ1 phosphorylation. Some missense mutations reduce basal IKs but retain the ability to respond to cAMP potentiation. During exercise, the cAMP-boosted current from even a partially functional mutant may suffice to shorten the AP plateau toward normal QT. This genotype-phenotype nuance distinguishes certain LQT1 mutations and influences arrhythmia triggers.

questions.question: Nav1.8 in nociceptors is TTX-resistant due to a serine replacing the usual residue near the DEKA filter. What confers this resistance at a mechanistic level?
options: A. Serine can't make the aromatic contacts TTX's guanidinium needs, cutting affinity ~1000-fold
B. Serine is positively charged and electrostatically repels TTX's guanidinium group from the binding site
C. Serine's smaller side chain sterically occludes the outer pore before TTX can insert
D. Serine introduces a glycosylation site that physically blocks the outer vestibule against TTX entry
questions.explanation: TTX binds with nanomolar affinity to a site at the outer mouth of the Nav selectivity filter. TTX-sensitive channels (Nav1.1–1.7) have an aromatic residue (tyrosine or phenylalanine) that makes van der Waals and H-bond contacts with TTX's guanidinium. Nav1.8 carries serine at the equivalent position — the hydroxyl group cannot form the same high-affinity contacts, reducing TTX affinity by ~1000-fold. The mechanism is electrostatic/geometric complementarity, not steric exclusion.

questions.question: Blocking T-type Ca²⁺ channels in a neuropathic pain model reduces DRG firing from 80 Hz to 20 Hz but not to zero. Which best explains why firing persists?
options: A. T-type channels set burst frequency, but the APs come from Nav channels unaffected by the block
B. T-type channels are the sole Ca²⁺ source in DRG neurons; 80% block leaves 20% residual T-type current
C. Kv channels downregulate to compensate for reduced Ca²⁺ influx, preserving membrane depolarisation
D. T-type blockade partially inhibits Nav1.7 as a side effect, and residual Nav1.7 current sustains 20 Hz firing
questions.explanation: T-type channels operate near the resting potential and modulate the subthreshold depolarising envelope that primes DRG neurons for burst firing. They contribute to the low-threshold Ca²⁺ spike that drives repetitive burst patterns. However, the action potentials themselves are generated by Nav channels (Nav1.7, Nav1.8, Nav1.9) — T-type block removes the subthreshold scaffolding that drives repetitive bursting, but individual Nav-driven spikes still occur. Result: reduced burst frequency (80→20 Hz) without complete silence.

questions.question: Mutations in the Nav channel window-current region widen the overlap between activation and inactivation curves. A drug targeting only this window-current region would theoretically differ from a conventional inactivated-state blocker because:
options: A. Window-current blockers bind the resting state, reducing channel availability before any AP begins
B. They cut the persistent tonic current while sparing the transient current needed for normal APs
C. They would selectively suppress Nav1.5 in heart without affecting neuronal Nav subtypes
D. Window-current agents would act as channel activators at depolarised potentials, paradoxically enhancing repolarisation
questions.explanation: The window current is the small persistent inward current at voltages where both activation and inactivation curves have significant values — channels cycle between open and inactivated, maintaining a tonic leak. Disease mutations expand this window, dramatically increasing persistent current. A window-current-selective drug would suppress this pathological tonic leak (which delays repolarisation or raises resting excitability) while leaving the fast transient Nav current intact — preserving normal AP amplitude and propagation at therapeutic concentrations.

questions.question: Nav1.6 (SCN8A) gain-of-function mutations cause early-onset epileptic encephalopathy. Which cellular mechanism links this to seizures?
options: A. Nav1.6 LoF reduces inhibitory Purkinje cell firing, disinhibiting cortical excitation
B. GoF in excitatory pyramidal neurons raises their firing rate, causing cortical hyperexcitability
C. Nav1.6 GoF in GABAergic interneurons increases inhibitory output, causing rebound excitation
D. Nav1.6 is a cardiac channel; its GoF causes cerebral hypoxia that triggers secondary seizures
questions.explanation: Nav1.6 (SCN8A) is predominantly expressed in excitatory pyramidal neurons and is the channel responsible for their sustained high-frequency firing. GoF mutations enhance Nav1.6 current → increased excitatory neuron AP firing → focal or generalised hyperexcitability → epilepsy (early infantile epileptic encephalopathy). This contrasts with Nav1.1 (SCN1A), where LoF in inhibitory interneurons drives disinhibition. Nav1.6 GoF and Nav1.1 LoF both cause epilepsy, but through opposite cell-type mechanisms.

questions.question: At nanomolar Ca²⁺ concentrations, L-type Cav channels become anomalously permeable to Na⁺. Which mechanism best explains this 'anomalous mole fraction effect'?
options: A. EEEE filter glutamates become protonated at very low [Ca²⁺], neutralising the negative charge and allowing Na⁺ to pass
B. Ca²⁺ normally fills the high-affinity EEEE sites and blocks Na⁺; with Ca²⁺ absent, Na⁺ permeates freely
C. Na⁺ outcompetes Ca²⁺ at an external binding site, forcing Ca²⁺ out of the filter so Na⁺ can enter
D. At low Ca²⁺ the channel adopts the inactivated conformation, and Na⁺ permeates through the ball-and-chain inactivation gate
questions.explanation: The EEEE filter acts as a multi-ion pore with high-affinity Ca²⁺ binding sites. At physiological [Ca²⁺] (~1.2 mM), Ca²⁺ permanently occupies the filter sites and physically blocks the far more abundant Na⁺ (~140 mM) — Ca²⁺ plugs its own filter. At nanomolar [Ca²⁺], Ca²⁺ can no longer reliably occupy the filter; Na⁺ then permeates through the unoccupied EEEE cage. This paradox — increasing Ca²⁺ decreases Na⁺ current but very low Ca²⁺ renders the channel Na⁺-permeable — is direct evidence that Ca²⁺ selectivity relies on competition for high-affinity EEEE sites rather than a steric sieve.

drug_safety_medi2004_wk6.html.title: Drug Safety — Adverse Effects, Interactions & Poisoning
drug_safety_medi2004_wk6.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
drug_safety_medi2004_wk6.html.content: Adverse drug reactions (Type A vs B and the Rawlins–Thomson categories), the therapeutic index and window, factors predisposing to ADRs, drug–drug interactions (pharmacokinetic CYP450 induction/inhibition vs pharmacodynamic synergism/antagonism), and the management of poisoning — decontamination, enhanced elimination and specific antidotes.

questions.question: Among adverse events reported in Australian hospitals, where do drug-related events rank?
options: A. The single most common category
B. The third most common category
C. The second most common category
questions.explanation: Adverse drug effects are ~32% of hospital adverse events (AIHW 2015-16) — the second most common category after procedure-related events.

questions.question: Roughly what proportion of ADR-related hospital admissions are judged preventable?
questions.explanation: More than half of ADR-related admissions are considered preventable, which is why drug safety is emphasised.

questions.question: The therapeutic index (TI) of a drug is defined as:
options: C. The plasma half-life at steady state
D. The dose effective in 50% of people
questions.explanation: TI = TD50/ED50. A larger ratio means a wider gap between effective and toxic doses (a safer drug). ED50/TD50 is the inverse; the last option defines ED50 itself.

questions.question: A drug has ED50 = 10 mg and TD50 = 60 mg. Its therapeutic index is:
questions.explanation: TI = TD50/ED50 = 60/10 = 6. 0.17 is the inverse, 50 is the difference, 600 is the product.

questions.question: Which trio is the classic example of drugs with a LOW (narrow) therapeutic index needing monitoring?
questions.explanation: Digoxin, lithium and warfarin sit close to their toxic doses, so plasma levels or effect (INR) are monitored. The other trios have wide safety margins.

questions.question: How do the therapeutic WINDOW and therapeutic INDEX differ?
options: A. Window = the population toxic:effective dose ratio; index = the concentration giving benefit at acceptable risk
B. Index = the population toxic:effective dose ratio; window = the concentration giving benefit at acceptable risk
C. They are two names for the very same TD50/ED50 ratio
D. The window applies only to antibiotic dosing, the index to all drugs
questions.explanation: The index (TI) is the population-level TD50/ED50 ratio; the window is the concentration range in which benefit is likely and harm acceptable. Option 2 reverses the two.

questions.question: Type A (Augmented) adverse drug reactions are best described as:
options: A. Rare and idiosyncratic, unrelated to the dose given
B. Caused only by an immune hypersensitivity response
C. Appearing only once the drug has been stopped
D. Dose-related and predictable from known pharmacology
questions.explanation: Type A reactions are exaggerations of the drug's known pharmacology — dose-related, common, mostly reversible. The others describe Type B, a subset of B, and withdrawal reactions.

questions.question: Which is a typical Type B (Bizarre) reaction?
options: B. Digoxin toxicity after a dose rise
questions.explanation: Type B reactions are idiosyncratic and not dose-related — penicillin anaphylaxis is the archetype. The other three are dose/action-related Type A effects.

questions.question: A patient on lithium develops tremor and confusion after a dose increase. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: It is dose-related and flows from lithium's narrow therapeutic index — the definition of a Type A reaction.

questions.question: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by a volatile anaesthetic is which type of ADR?
questions.explanation: It is a rare, genetically-determined idiosyncratic reaction unrelated to dose — Type B.

questions.question: Under the Rawlins & Thomson scheme, thalidomide-induced phocomelia is categorised as:
questions.explanation: Teratogenesis is a time-related reaction tied to a critical developmental window, distinct from simple dose-related Type A effects.

questions.question: Prolonged glucocorticoid use suppressing the HPA axis fits which Rawlins & Thomson category MOST precisely?
questions.explanation: HPA suppression depends on both cumulative dose and duration, so it is dose-AND-time-related — more precise than 'time-related only'.

questions.question: Which patient factor most directly reduces drug clearance and predisposes to toxicity?
questions.explanation: The liver and kidney are the main routes of drug elimination; impairing either raises plasma levels toward toxicity.

questions.question: Why are BOTH neonates and the elderly at higher ADR risk?
options: A. Both have reduced drug-clearance capacity
B. Both have faster hepatic metabolism
C. Both have increased renal GFR
D. Both differ only in protein binding
questions.explanation: Neonates have immature hepatic enzymes and the elderly have reduced GFR and liver mass/flow — the shared theme is lower clearance, not faster metabolism.

questions.question: Polypharmacy raises ADR risk mainly because it:
options: A. Multiplies the chance of drug–drug interactions
C. Slows gastric emptying of each drug
questions.explanation: Each added drug increases the combinations that can interact pharmacokinetically or pharmacodynamically; the other options are not the primary mechanism.

questions.question: The four mechanisms of drug–drug interaction are behavioural, pharmaceutic, pharmacokinetic and:
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamic interactions alter the effect at the target; the other three terms are real words but not interaction mechanisms.

questions.question: A CYP450 INDUCER such as rifampicin will do what to a substrate drug's plasma level?
options: D. Convert it to an antidote
questions.explanation: Induction upregulates the metabolising enzyme, speeding clearance and lowering the substrate's level — risking therapeutic failure.

questions.question: A patient stabilised on warfarin starts rifampicin for TB. The expected effect is:
options: A. Increased warfarin effect and bleeding risk
B. No change, since warfarin is renally cleared
C. Reduced warfarin effect and higher clotting risk
questions.explanation: Rifampicin induces CYP2C9/3A4, increasing warfarin clearance; the INR falls (subtherapeutic) and clot risk rises. The tempting trap is inhibitor-style bleeding.

questions.question: Grapefruit juice raises plasma atorvastatin because it:
options: D. Blocks renal excretion of atorvastatin
questions.explanation: Furanocoumarins irreversibly inhibit gut-wall CYP3A4, cutting first-pass metabolism and raising bioavailability. Induction would do the opposite.

questions.question: Alcohol taken with diazepam causes dangerous CNS and respiratory depression. This is:
questions.explanation: Both potentiate GABA-A chloride influx, so their depressant effects add at the same target — a pharmacodynamic (synergistic) interaction.

questions.question: Which interaction is PHARMACODYNAMIC rather than pharmacokinetic?
options: A. A beta-blocker opposing a beta-agonist at its receptor
B. Fluconazole raising plasma phenytoin concentrations
C. Rifampicin lowering plasma ciclosporin concentrations
D. Antacids binding tetracycline to reduce absorption
questions.explanation: The beta-blocker/beta-agonist pair act at the same receptor with opposing effects (pharmacodynamic). The rest change concentration via metabolism or absorption (pharmacokinetic).

questions.question: Probenecid prolongs penicillin's action by:
options: A. Blocking renal tubular secretion of penicillin
C. Displacing penicillin from plasma protein
questions.explanation: Probenecid competes for the organic-acid transporter that secretes penicillin into urine, slowing its renal elimination — historically used to extend penicillin action.

questions.question: Displacing a highly protein-bound, narrow-TI drug from albumin will transiently:
options: B. Have no effect on free drug
D. Permanently increase total body drug
questions.explanation: Only free drug is active; displacement shifts bound to free, transiently raising the active fraction until redistribution and clearance compensate.

questions.question: The Paracelsus principle 'the dose makes the poison' means:
options: A. Only illegal substances are poisons
B. Natural substances are never poisonous
C. Any substance can be toxic at a high enough dose
D. Toxicity depends only on the route
questions.explanation: Toxicity is dose-dependent — even water or oxygen is harmful in excess, and any drug can poison at a high enough dose.

questions.question: The specific antidote for opioid overdose is:
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid antagonist. The distractors are antidotes for benzodiazepines, cholinergic/organophosphate excess, and paracetamol respectively.

questions.question: Activated charcoal is MOST effective when given:
options: C. After a session of haemodialysis
D. Within about an hour of ingestion
questions.explanation: Charcoal adsorbs drug still in the gut, so it works best before absorption is complete — within roughly an hour.

questions.question: N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol overdose by:
options: B. Chelating free iron in plasma
D. Replenishing glutathione to detoxify NAPQI
questions.explanation: It restores hepatic glutathione, which conjugates the toxic metabolite NAPQI and prevents hepatocellular necrosis. The distractors are other antidotes' mechanisms.

questions.question: Why does urinary alkalinisation (IV bicarbonate) enhance salicylate elimination but not digoxin?
options: A. Digoxin is the weak acid trapped in alkaline urine, not salicylate
B. Digoxin is not eliminated by the kidney whatsoever
C. Salicylate is a weak acid ion-trapped in alkaline urine; digoxin is not
D. Bicarbonate chemically chelates the salicylate molecule
questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionises weak acids like salicylate, trapping them in the tubule (ion trapping) so they cannot be reabsorbed. Digoxin is not a weak acid, so pH-manipulation does not trap it.

questions.question: Ethanol or fomepizole is used in methanol / ethylene-glycol poisoning because it:
options: A. Chelates the parent alcohol for renal excretion
B. Directly neutralises the formic acid produced
C. Induces CYP2E1 to clear methanol more quickly
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol/ethylene glycol into their toxic acids; ethanol/fomepizole outcompete the substrate at that enzyme, buying time for elimination.

questions.question: Repeated-dose activated charcoal ('gut dialysis') boosts elimination of drugs that:
options: A. Are large, entirely protein-bound molecules
B. Undergo enterohepatic or entero-enteric recirculation
C. Are excreted unchanged only by the kidney
D. Cannot cross any biological membrane
questions.explanation: By keeping the gut lumen drug-free, repeated charcoal maintains a blood-to-gut gradient that pulls recirculating drug (e.g. theophylline, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) back for adsorption.
